## High-throughput chains with modified gas models

- Monad, cycle 1. A1: whether an unlock flag, a currency delta or a synced currency can survive from one Monad transaction into another, through optimistic parallel execution, a retried transaction, or a system transaction. Result: The client builds a new State for every execution attempt of every transaction, and transient storage is a field of the per-account state inside it. A retry discards the first State. System transactions get their own State and only run the staking syscall. The lock, delta, counter and reserve slots at src/libraries/Lock.sol:13-25, src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:21-39, src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:14-32 and src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:17-36 therefore start at zero in each transaction. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/execution/ethereum/execute_transaction.cpp lines 454 and 480; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/execution/ethereum/state3/account_state.hpp line 70; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/execution/monad/execute_system_transaction.cpp
- Monad, cycle 1. A3: whether Monad's reserve balance rule can block a native payout from the PoolManager, or revert a transaction because the PoolManager's MON balance fell below 10 MON. Result: The check skips every account whose code is not empty and not an EIP-7702 delegation ('Skip if not EOA'). The PoolManager has 24009 bytes of ordinary code, so its balance is never tested. A recipient's balance only rises in take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), which cannot count as a dip. The rule can still revert a user's own transaction when the user pays MON into settle (src/PoolManager.sol:300-302) from an account that ends below its threshold. That is a failed transaction for that user and moves no pool funds. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/execution/monad/reserve_balance.cpp lines 81 to 98 and 191 to 210; https://docs.monad.xyz/developer-essentials/reserve-balance.md
- Monad, cycle 1. A3: whether MON has an ERC-20 face, so that a pool on address(0) and a pool on a token could draw on one balance. Result: No. WMON is a 3249 byte contract with no proxy slot, and its totalSupply equals the MON it holds. balanceOf(PoolManager) on WMON is 927,086 while the PoolManager's native balance is 216,079,353. The staking and reserve precompiles revert on balanceOf and transfer. Native settlement uses msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354) and token settlement uses a balance difference (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and no Monad contract found here links the two. Evidence: rpc https://rpc.monad.xyz, queries at blocks 124417992 to 124420045 on 2026-11-22
- Monad, cycle 1. A4: whether a Monad precompile can serve as a currency whose balanceOf or transfer gives credit without payment, or as a hook that the PoolManager calls with effect. Result: The staking precompile (0x1000) and the reserve balance precompile (0x1001) reject STATICCALL, so sync (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288) reverts at balanceOf for either address. Under CALL they revert on the transfer selector, so take reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86. The staking precompile also reverts on afterInitialize and on empty calldata with value, so it cannot be a hook and cannot receive a native take. P256 at 0x0100 returns empty data to balanceOf, which fails ABI decoding. Hook calls carry zero value (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134) and a fixed selector, and the PoolManager has no stake or delegation that a staking call from it could move. Evidence: rpc https://rpc.monad.xyz, queries at blocks 124417992 to 124420045 on 2026-11-22; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/execution/monad/monad_precompiles.cpp lines 43 to 49
- Monad, cycle 1. A10 and A3: whether the higher cold access costs (10100 per account, 8100 per storage page) break a payout or a hook call that relies on a fixed gas amount. Result: The PoolManager passes gas() on the native transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:48), on the ERC-20 transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:73) and on hook calls (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134). It never uses the 2300 stipend or a hard-coded gas value. Contracts around it that do are outside the PoolManager. Evidence: https://docs.monad.xyz/developer-essentials/opcode-pricing.md
- Monad, cycle 1. A9: whether the 30 million per-transaction gas cap together with MIP-8 storage pricing can make a swap or a liquidity removal impossible to include. Result: A tick crossing reads one bitmap word and updates one tick record. Under MIP-8 that is one page load (8000), one page write (2800), small base charges and at most two new slots at 17000 each, so tens of thousands of gas per tick and several hundred ticks per transaction in the worst case. A swap stops at the caller's price limit (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344) and can continue in the next transaction. modifyLiquidity touches two ticks and one position (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238), which is constant work. The per-tick figure is computed from the documented schedule and was not measured on chain. Evidence: https://docs.monad.xyz/developer-essentials/opcode-pricing.md; https://docs.monad.xyz/ai/current-facts.md
- Monad, cycle 1. Whether charging gas on the gas limit, or the reserve balance precompile, gives a hook or token a way to change PoolManager accounting. Result: Both act on the transaction sender's MON balance or report a read-only flag. Neither changes a token balance at the PoolManager, a delta or a storage slot. The deltas must still net to zero at src/PoolManager.sol:112. Evidence: https://docs.monad.xyz/developer-essentials/gas-pricing.md; https://docs.monad.xyz/developer-essentials/precompiles.md
- Monad, MegaETH, cycle 1. A12: whether anyone can call the PoolManager as the zero address, which is the protocol fee controller on both networks, and what that caller could take. Result: No transaction type documented for either chain produces msg.sender zero. Monad system transactions come from 0x6f49a8F621353f12378d0046E7d7e4b9B249DC9e and must target the staking address. MegaETH system transactions come from the registry's system address and may only call the Oracle, pre-block calls come from 0xff...fe to fixed contracts, and a deposit carries its L1 sender. With no controller, setProtocolFee (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41) cannot run, so protocol fees stay zero, and protocolFeesAccrued reads zero for the currencies checked. collectProtocolFees subtracts with overflow checks at src/ProtocolFees.sol:55, so a caller could not withdraw more than the accrued amount in any case. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/execution/monad/validate_system_transaction.cpp lines 53 to 65; https://docs.megaeth.com/spec/system-contracts/system-tx.md; rpc https://rpc.monad.xyz, queries at blocks 124417992 to 124420045 on 2026-11-22; rpc https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc, queries at blocks 32548426 to 32549054 on 2026-11-22
- MegaETH, cycle 1. A1: whether MegaETH has an execution context with its own transient storage that shares persistent state with a running PoolManager call. A second context would let a stale sync in one context be paid by a transfer made in the other. Result: The only nested context is the KeylessDeploy sandbox. It runs a separate EVM with its own journal over the parent state, and the node starts it only when the KeylessDeploy call is the top-level call of the transaction. A contract that calls it mid-transaction reaches bytecode that reverts with NotIntercepted. The outer transaction therefore has no PoolManager activity before or after the sandbox, and the sandbox itself is one ordinary context. Mini-blocks and EVM blocks do not split a transaction, and detention and resource counters reset per transaction. Evidence: https://docs.megaeth.com/spec/system-contracts/keyless-deploy.md; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/sandbox/mod.rs; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/sandbox/execution.rs
- MegaETH, cycle 1. A3 and A8: whether an OP Stack deposit can raise the PoolManager's native balance in a way that counts as payment, or let an L1 actor call as the PoolManager or as its owner. Result: A deposit mints ETH to its from account, never to the target. The PoolManager accepts value only in settle and settleFor (src/PoolManager.sol:300-307), both of which require an unlocked manager, and it has no receive or fallback function. Native settlement credits msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354), so ETH that reaches the balance another way, for example through SELFDESTRUCT, is credited to nobody. A contract sender on L1 is aliased by a fixed offset, and an externally owned sender keeps its address, so reaching the PoolManager address or the receiver address as sender needs control of that externally owned account or an L1 contract at the address minus the offset. Evidence: https://specs.optimism.io/protocol/deposits.html
- MegaETH, cycle 1. A3: whether ETH on MegaETH has an ERC-20 face, through the WETH predeploy or the LegacyERC20ETH address. Result: WETH at 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000006 has ordinary code, empty proxy slots and totalSupply equal to the ETH it holds. Its balanceOf(PoolManager) is 0.0058 while the PoolManager's native balance is 2.2648 ETH. 0xDeadDeAddeAddEAddeadDEaDDEAdDeaDDeAD0000 has no code. Evidence: rpc https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc, queries at blocks 32548426 to 32549054 on 2026-11-22
- MegaETH, cycle 1. A4 and A7: whether a MegaETH system contract or OP Stack predeploy can be used as a hook, or made to act on a call the PoolManager issues. Result: The six system contract addresses end in 1 to 6, and each of those bit patterns fails isValidHookAddress (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:111-120). The calls the PoolManager can be made to issue are limited to hook selectors with zero value (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134), transfer(to, amount) on a currency (src/types/Currency.sol:60-73), balanceOf(self) (src/types/Currency.sol:94), unlockCallback on the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:110) and a native transfer with empty calldata (src/types/Currency.sol:48). Each of the last two fund-moving calls creates a negative delta that the caller must repay before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112), so sending pool ETH to a predeploy such as L2ToL1MessagePasser costs the caller the same amount. Evidence: https://docs.megaeth.com/spec/system-contracts/overview.md; rpc https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc, queries at blocks 32548426 to 32549054 on 2026-11-22
- MegaETH, cycle 1. A7 and A9: whether the 98/100 forwarding rule, the per-frame resource budgets, the 200 million compute gas cap or the cap of 1,000 new state entries per transaction can trap funds in the PoolManager. Result: The PoolManager treats a failed hook or token call as a revert (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:137, src/types/Currency.sol:82-86), so a frame that runs out of any budget cannot leave partial state. A swap that crosses ticks for the first time writes up to two new slots per tick in crossTick (src/libraries/Pool.sol:602-612), so one transaction can cross a few hundred fresh ticks before the state growth cap. It can stop at a price limit and continue later (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344). Removing liquidity touches two ticks and one position (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238). The per-block cap of the same size is left as a lead. Evidence: https://docs.megaeth.com/spec/megaevm/resource-limits.md; https://docs.megaeth.com/spec/megaevm/gas-forwarding.md
- MegaETH, cycle 1. A7: whether code at a hook or token address on MegaETH can disappear after pool creation through SELFDESTRUCT. Result: SELFDESTRUCT follows EIP-6780 since Rex2 and was disabled before that. A contract loses code only in the transaction that created it. EIP-7702 delegation works as on Ethereum Prague and is the same risk class as an upgradeable hook. Evidence: https://docs.megaeth.com/spec/megaevm/selfdestruct.md
- MegaETH, cycle 1. A9: whether the SALT bucket multiplier lets an attacker raise storage gas until a liquidity removal or a take cannot be paid for. Result: Storage gas applies to zero to nonzero writes and to account creation, at 20,000 or 25,000 times (multiplier minus 1). A removal writes at most a few such slots (position fee growth fields) and a take to a new address creates one account. The gas limit is 10,000,000,000 and the base fee read on chain is 0.001 gwei, so even a multiplier in the thousands leaves the exit affordable. How an attacker would grow a chosen bucket was not analysed, because the bound already clears the freeze question. Evidence: https://docs.megaeth.com/developer-docs/overview-3/gas-model.md; rpc https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc, queries at blocks 32548426 to 32549054 on 2026-11-22
- Monad, MegaETH, cycle 1. Whether a protocol address with hook flag bits and no hook interface (Monad 0x0100, OP Stack predeploys such as 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000010) adds a hazard beyond what any address without code already gives. Result: No. For such an address the hook call either reverts or returns fewer than 32 bytes, and the PoolManager reverts at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:137 or src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154. That is the same result as a flagged address with no code on any chain. A pool created with such a hook address can lock the operations whose flags are set. The hook address is part of the pool identity, so a liquidity provider can read it before depositing. Evidence: rpc https://rpc.monad.xyz, queries at blocks 124417992 to 124420045 on 2026-11-22
- Monad, cycle 2. Sweep of every Monad precompile and system address (0x01 to 0x11, 0x0100, 0x1000, 0x1001, the EIP-2935, EIP-4788, EIP-7002 and EIP-7251 addresses, SYSTEM_SENDER, 0xff...fe, the MIP-11 fee account and WMON) with calls from the PoolManager address: empty calldata with zero and nonzero value, transfer with amounts 0, 1 and 1e18, balanceOf(PoolManager), the ten IHooks selectors and unlockCallback. Result: No address gives credit without payment and none moves PoolManager value on a transfer call except WMON, which is an ordinary wrapper. 0x01 and 0x0100 return success with empty data, so a take of those ids debits the caller and moves nothing (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), and sync reverts on the empty answer. 0x02, 0x03 and 0x04 answer balanceOf with a constant, so settle after sync credits zero (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and they fail the transfer test because the first word is not 1. 0x1000 and 0x1001 revert on every shape and fail under STATICCALL. Addresses without code behave as on Ethereum. Evidence: rpc https://rpc.monad.xyz, eth_call with from set to the PoolManager, eth_getCode, eth_getBalance and eth_getStorageAt at blocks 124455000 to 124466634 on 2026-11-22
- MegaETH, cycle 2. Sweep of 0x01 to 0x11, 0x0100, all 256 addresses 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000000 to 00ff, 0x6342000000000000000000000000000000000001 to 0007, the EIP-2935 and EIP-4788 contracts, the EIP-7002 and EIP-7251 addresses, LegacyERC20ETH, the L1 attributes depositor, the system address and 0xff...fe with the same call shapes from the PoolManager address. Result: No address gives credit without payment. Only WETH returns success on transfer with a true word, and it is an ordinary wrapper. Seven predeploys accept a native payout (L2ToL1MessagePasser, four fee vaults, WETH and L1BlockNumber), and in each case the caller of take is debited the full amount at src/PoolManager.sol:294 before the transfer. The six MegaETH system contracts revert on all shapes, with NotIntercepted (0x1894f076) for MegaAccessControl and MegaLimitControl. The precompiles behave as on Ethereum. Evidence: rpc https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc, eth_call with from set to the PoolManager and with state overrides, eth_getCode, eth_getBalance, eth_estimateGas and eth_getBlockByNumber at blocks 32558000 to 32563302 on 2026-11-22
- MegaETH, cycle 2. Whether the L1BlockNumber predeploy at 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000013, which answers balanceOf(PoolManager) with a number that rises over time, can serve as a currency that yields credit. Result: No. The answer equals L1Block.number(), which changes only through the L1 attributes transaction at the start of a block. Inside one transaction sync and settle read the same value and the credit is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). Transient storage does not survive the transaction, so a sync from an earlier block cannot be used. A transfer call returns the same word, which is not 1, so take reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:68 and 82-86. Its low bits are 0x13, which isValidHookAddress rejects because bit 1 is set without bit 10 (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:113-116). Evidence: rpc https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc, eth_call with from set to the PoolManager and with state overrides, eth_getCode, eth_getBalance, eth_estimateGas and eth_getBlockByNumber at blocks 32558000 to 32563302 on 2026-11-22
- MegaETH, cycle 2. What a native payout from the PoolManager does at each predeploy that accepts it, and whether the caller owes the full value: take(address(0), predeploy, amount) for L2ToL1MessagePasser, the four fee vaults, WETH, L1BlockNumber and L2StandardBridge. Result: The caller owes the full amount in every case, because take records the debit before the transfer and unlock reverts unless it is settled (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 294-295). L2ToL1MessagePasser keeps the ETH and registers a withdrawal whose sender and target are the PoolManager address, so the value is lost to the caller. The fee vaults and L1BlockNumber keep the ETH. WETH credits the PoolManager with the same amount of WETH. L2StandardBridge rejects the call when the PoolManager is called by another account. The op-stack-eth unit recorded the same self-inflicted loss as a low finding in this cycle, and chain 4326 can be added to it. Evidence: rpc https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc, eth_call with from set to the PoolManager and with state overrides, eth_getCode, eth_getBalance, eth_estimateGas and eth_getBlockByNumber at blocks 32558000 to 32563302 on 2026-11-22
- Monad, MegaETH, cycle 2. Faces of the native asset through the wrapper: sync(wrapper), take(address(0), wrapper, X) so that the PoolManager itself deposits X into WMON or WETH, settle, then take, mint, burn and native settle in every order. Result: The sequence nets to zero. The native payout debits the caller X of currency address(0) and lowers the native balance by X. The wrapper credits the PoolManager with X, and settle credits the caller X of the wrapper id, which is the measured rise since sync. The caller then holds a debt of X native and a credit of X wrapped, and unlock requires both to be closed (src/PoolManager.sol:112). Closing them returns X native to the PoolManager or removes X wrapped from it. Without the earlier sync the wrapped tokens stay with the PoolManager as unowned surplus and the caller still owes X. mint and burn only move the same deltas into claims (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). The one to one credit was confirmed on both chains with a probe of 0.001 native units. Evidence: rpc https://rpc.monad.xyz, eth_call with from set to the PoolManager, eth_getCode, eth_getBalance and eth_getStorageAt at blocks 124455000 to 124466634 on 2026-11-22 and rpc https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc, eth_call with from set to the PoolManager and with state overrides, eth_getCode, eth_getBalance, eth_estimateGas and eth_getBlockByNumber at blocks 32558000 to 32563302 on 2026-11-22
- Monad, MegaETH, cycle 2. Whether any address on either chain exposes the PoolManager's native balance, or the balance of a token it holds, under a second currency id, and whether two ids on one balance could be credited twice. Result: No second face was found. MON and ETH have no ERC-20 interface among the precompiles and predeploys swept, LegacyERC20ETH has no code on MegaETH, and no listed Monad token mirrors the native balance. For the general case the code keeps one synced currency in one transient slot (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:17-36), settle credits only the rise of that one currency or msg.value and rejects msg.value while an ERC-20 is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:353-361), and take debits exactly the amount it sends (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295). Each credit therefore needs its own payment even if two ids shared one balance. Tokens outside the lists checked were not enumerated on Monad. Evidence: rpc https://rpc.monad.xyz, eth_call with from set to the PoolManager, eth_getCode, eth_getBalance and eth_getStorageAt at blocks 124455000 to 124466634 on 2026-11-22 and rpc https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc, eth_call with from set to the PoolManager and with state overrides, eth_getCode, eth_getBalance, eth_estimateGas and eth_getBlockByNumber at blocks 32558000 to 32563302 on 2026-11-22
- Monad, cycle 2. Opcode differential from the Monad client source for the patterns the PoolManager relies on: CALL with value, gas forwarding, calls to addresses without code, return data, STATICCALL, TSTORE and TLOAD with rollback, and precompile dispatch. Result: No departure from Ethereum was found. call_impl applies the 63/64 rule, the 2300 stipend and the depth limit and reports success only for status Success. pre_call moves value for CALL and CALLCODE inside a pushed state version, and post_call rejects that version on any failure, which restores balances, storage and transient storage. Precompile dispatch happens after pre_call, so a reverted precompile call returns the value. The Monad precompiles return Rejected for any call kind other than CALL, which the caller sees as a failed call. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/runtime/call.cpp
- Monad, cycle 2. Whether the 8 MB memory cap per transaction (MIP-3) can break a PoolManager path that copies return data, or freeze a withdrawal. Result: No. The PoolManager copies hook return data and revert data in full (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:140-149, src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119) and copies 32 bytes after a token transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:73). A callee that returns more than the remaining memory makes the PoolManager frame halt, which reverts the call. Only a hook or token chosen for the pool can do this, and that case is F-004. A removal in a pool without such a hook uses a few hundred bytes of memory. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monad-crypto/MIPs/main/MIPs/MIP-3.md
- MegaETH, cycle 2. Opcode differential from the mega-evm source: TSTORE, TLOAD, CALLVALUE, RETURNDATASIZE, RETURNDATACOPY, MCOPY, PUSH0, CALL with value, the 98/100 forwarding rule, per-frame resource budgets and the storage call stipend. Result: The opcode bodies are the revm handlers with accounting wrappers, so results are those of Ethereum Prague. The changed rules are fail-closed for the PoolManager. A child that receives less gas or exceeds its resource share reverts, and the PoolManager reverts on a failed native transfer, token transfer, hook call or unlock callback (src/types/Currency.sol:51-53 and 82-86, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:137). No path treats a failed call as success. The extra 23,000 gas stipend on value calls cannot pay computation, and the PoolManager forwards all gas anyway. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/evm/instructions.rs
- MegaETH, cycle 2. A1 from the node source: does transient storage end with the transaction, including after an error or a panic, and does the KeylessDeploy sandbox share it. Result: Yes for the transaction boundary and no for the sandbox. Every transaction ends with the journal finalize step that clears transient storage, and the panic recovery path calls the same step. The sandbox database reads accounts and storage from the parent journal state and has its own journal. Together with the cycle 1 reading of the Monad client this answers the open question on transient storage for chains 143 and 4326. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/evm/mod.rs
- MegaETH, cycle 2. Whether an attacker can inflate the SALT bucket that holds a victim's storage slot until a zero to nonzero write there becomes unaffordable, given that the bucket index comes from a fixed-seed hash. Result: Not on the normal path. A bucket doubles when it is more than 80 percent full, so reaching multiplier 2^k needs about 205 times 2^k entries in that bucket, each paying 20,000 times (multiplier minus 1) storage gas at the multiplier in force. The total is about 2.7 million times 4^k gas. Multiplier 1,024 costs the attacker about 2.8 ETH at the current base fee and adds 20.5 million gas, about 0.00002 ETH, to one write by the victim. A write that exceeds the 10 billion gas transaction limit needs a multiplier near 500,000 and about 740,000 ETH. A removal mostly clears slots or rewrites nonzero slots, and the recipient of a payout can choose an address that already holds the token. The figures are computed from the documented rule, and the value of NUM_KV_BUCKETS was not read. Evidence: https://docs.megaeth.com/spec/megaevm/dual-gas-model.md
- MegaETH, cycle 2. Whether a call that the PoolManager issues can match a MegaETH call interceptor (Oracle sendHint, KeylessDeploy, MegaAccessControl, MegaLimitControl) and produce a synthetic success. Result: No. Each interceptor requires the target address and a specific four-byte selector. The PoolManager can address a system contract only as a currency or as a hook, with transfer, balanceOf, an IHooks selector or empty calldata. None of these matches, the call falls through to the contract code, and the code reverts on all of them. The hook route is closed earlier, because the addresses end in 1 to 6 and fail isValidHookAddress (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:111-120). Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/system/intercept.rs
- MegaETH, cycle 2. Whether gas detention or disableVolatileDataAccess can be imposed on another user's PoolManager transaction. Result: No. Detention state is reset at the start of each transaction and applies to the transaction that made the volatile read. The access control switch covers the caller's frame and its descendants. A third party is in neither position for a victim's transaction unless the victim's pool uses that party's hook or token, which is F-018. Since REX4 the cap is relative, so a transaction can always spend 20 million compute gas after the read. Evidence: https://github.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/blob/main/docs/spec/evm/gas-detention.md
- Monad, cycle 2. Known weakness: the Spearbit finding that DELEGATECALL to the staking precompile credited stake without moving MON, and its STATICCALL variant. Can an ordinary account use the precompile against PoolManager funds today. Result: No. The fix rejects every message whose kind is not CALL or whose flags are nonzero before dispatch, and the STATICCALL probe from the PoolManager address fails. The PoolManager never issues DELEGATECALL (no use in src outside tests) and cannot send a staking selector. The precompile takes funds only from msg.value of its caller. Evidence: https://cantina.xyz/portfolio/d90b081f-fb8c-4ca7-8e68-6a9219288ae1
- Monad, cycle 2. Known weaknesses in the reserve balance rule: the Code4rena finding on EIP-7702 delegation status that let a sender stall block proposals for free, the testnet crash of 2025-09-27 from relaxed balance merging, and the three bugs described by Category Labs. Can any of them be used against funds in the PoolManager. Result: No path was found. All of them concern whether a sender can pay its fee and whether consensus and execution agree on that. Their effect is a stalled or halted chain, which delays every user alike and moves no balance. The execution check skips accounts whose final code is contract code, so the PoolManager is never the account under test. A user who adds MON and ends below the reserve can have the deposit reverted when the emptying exception does not apply, and a payout only raises the recipient's balance. Evidence: https://code4rena.com/reports/2025-09-monad and https://github.com/code-423n4/2025-09-monad/blob/3d1f9a1d/README.md and https://www.category.xyz/blogs/finding-bugs-that-frontier-models-miss
- MegaETH, cycle 2. Known weaknesses: the BlockSec findings on MegaEVM (unbounded TSTORE, cheap KZG, KZG gas cost crash, costly opcode loops) and the REX4 audit fixes. Can an ordinary account use them against funds in the PoolManager. Result: No path was found. Each is a way to load or crash the node or to escape a resource limit. The PoolManager writes transient storage at fixed slots and at one slot per account and currency (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41), which a caller can multiply only at its own gas cost, and the effect is on node memory. Three of the four BlockSec findings are marked confirmed without a stated fix, so node availability under these loads stays an operator matter. Only the report index was read. Evidence: https://blocksec.com/audit-report/audit-report-megaeth--megaevm--stateless-validator---salt

Result: Monad has three (0x10, 0x0100, 0x1000) and MegaETH has 39 among the swept addresses. 0x1000 on Monad, the EIP-4788 contract and 0xff...fe on MegaETH carry an initialize flag and fail the hook call, so no pool can be created with them. The others let a pool be created and then block only the flagged action: donate, swap, or for 0x0100 every call with liquidityDelta of zero or less. A provider would have to choose such a pool. The 0x0100 case is the one cycle 1 recorded, and it also exists on any chain with the P256 precompile. - MegaETH, cycle 4. Lead L-171: are L1 deposits placed ahead of sequencer transactions, and can a deposit be skipped because the block's state growth counter has reached 1,000 while deposits remain?. Result: Deposits come first. In 25 of 25 sampled deposit blocks the user deposit is at index 1, after the L1 attributes transaction and before every system and sequencer transaction, so the counter is near zero when deposits run. The OP Stack derivation rule places the user deposits of an L1 block in the first L2 block of its epoch. The L1 portal sells at most 20,000,000 gas of deposits per L1 block, and cycle 2 measured 20,333,678 gas for 900 new slots, so the deposits of one L1 block cannot create 1,000 entries. The limiter also applies its test before a transaction and admits the one that reaches the limit. A deposit can fail on its own transaction limits and is then included as failed with its mint kept. - Monad, cycle 13. Monad interpreter refactor from v0.16.5 to v0.16.7 (StackTop one-past stack pointer): DUPn, SWAPn, push, pop, pop_for_overwrite, top_two, check_requirements stack size, call_runtime argument pointers and result slot, the runtime context stack pointer and size, and the initial pointer in execute.cpp. Result: Old code held a pointer to the top word with the empty stack at bottom minus one; new code holds a pointer one past the top with operator[](i) = *(ptr + i - 1). Old *(top - N) equals new top[-N], old top + 1 equals new next_slot(), old top - bottom equals new next_slot() - bottom (bottom moved by one with the pointer), so every changed expression names the same word. A new vector set, stackedge.py, runs DUPn and SWAPn for n = 1 to 16 at the needed depth and one short, pushes to depths 1,014 to 1,025 followed by DUP1, DUP16 and SWAP16, and memory, hashing and copy runtime calls at stack depth 0 to 1,019: 117 of 117 cases equal the model and Ethereum on Monad and on MegaETH, failures included. The PoolManager uses DUP and SWAP up to 16 in every function, so this is the path every eth_call on the 0.16.7 fleet takes. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/vm/interpreter/stack_top.hpp ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/vm/interpreter/stack.hpp lines 33-98 ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/vm/interpreter/call_runtime.hpp lines 30-55 ; research/network-risk/cycles/013/high-throughput.work/stackedge.json
- Monad, cycle 13. Result: The new loop keeps the value from the most significant nonzero word: 192 - 64 i + clz(word i), and 256 for zero. A transcription agrees with 256 minus the bit length on 200,007 inputs that include every word boundary. The interpreter uses it only for CLZ (opcode 0x1e), which the PoolManager bytecode does not contain; the compiled MULMOD by 2^96 and 2^128 sites of src/libraries/FullMath.sol:48 reach it through bit_width at compile time only. - Monad, cycle 13. Correction and extension of the cycle 12 clearance that the only emitter change from v0.16.5 to v0.16.7 is the constant-by-variable shift. Four more compiled-path changes exist. (1) touch_memory, used by every compiled MLOAD and MSTORE with a non-literal offset, skips the bounds and expansion check when the same stack element already passed it for at least the same size. Result: Safe as read. The size is recorded on the StackElem object (virtual_stack.hpp lines 216-227 and 279). Every StackElem is constructed fresh by placement new with touched_memory_size_ zero (rc_ptr.hpp line 64, virtual_stack.cpp lines 90-94 and 346-361), and every operation that produces a new value returns a new element: release_general_reg, release_avx_reg and alloc_or_release_* move the register into a new_stack_elem (virtual_stack.cpp lines 821-856, emitter.cpp lines 1161-1233); operations that return an input unchanged (x - 0, x & ~0, shift by 0) return the same value. A cached element therefore always holds the value that was checked, memory never shrinks within a frame, and the data pointer is reloaded from the context on each access, so a reallocation by expansion is followed. Literal offsets, such as mload(0) in src/types/Currency.sol:68, are never cached. The cached path is taken for example by mstore(fmp, 0) at src/types/Currency.sol:77 after mstore(fmp, selector) at line 60. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/emitter.cpp lines 6276-6313 ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/virtual_stack.hpp ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/vm/utils/rc_ptr.hpp
- Monad, cycle 13. (2) Monad v0.16.7 write_to_final_stack_offsets, which writes the virtual stack back at the end of every compiled basic block: dependency counts moved from an unordered_map keyed by heap address to an array indexed by each element's lowest stack index, elements are visited in stack index order, and stack words that were stored from general registers are loaded word by word into an AVX register (mov_words_to_ymm). Result: The algorithm is the same topological write with cycle breaking; only the order in which dependency-free elements are taken changes, and the result does not depend on that order. blockexit.py models the code as written on 200,000 random block-exit states (elements in any mix of stack slot, general register, AVX register and literal, one to three stack indices each): both the stack index order and a shuffled order standing for v0.16.5 leave every final stack index with its element's value, and a planted fault that ignores dependencies is caught in 9,479 of 20,000 cases. mov_words_to_ymm puts word 0 and 1 in the low half and 2 and 3 in the high half, matching the little endian slot layout of stack_offset_to_mem256 (emitter.cpp lines 109-116). The scratch register it uses is free at allocation and distinct from the init register and from every element register. The array index stays in range under the invariant v0.16.5 already needed (an element at a slot in [min_delta, top] has its lowest index there). Every JUMP and JUMPI of the PoolManager, among them the TickBitmap and BitMath branches, passes through this code. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/emitter.cpp lines 1384-1690 ; research/network-risk/cycles/013/high-throughput.work/blockexit.py ; research/network-risk/cycles/013/high-throughput.work/blockexit-planted.json
- Monad, cycle 13. (3) Monad v0.16.7 block_prologue stack bound check, changed from 'min_delta < -1024 or max_delta > 1024' to 'max_delta - min_delta > 1024' before the two runtime checks, and (4) MSTORE8 of a value held in a stack slot and the branchless CLZ. Result: With min_delta at most 0 and max_delta at least 0, every block the new static test rejects is one whose two runtime checks (size at least -min_delta and size at most 1024 - max_delta) no stack size passes, and the old static test is implied by the new one, so both versions fail exactly the same stack sizes and an exceptional halt consumes all gas either way. MSTORE8 now reads four bytes of the little endian slot and stores the low byte, the same byte as before. The PoolManager bytecode has no MSTORE8 (0x53) and no CLZ (0x1e) by linear disassembly of build/PoolManager.json. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/emitter.cpp lines 1325-1365 and 3395-3412 ; research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json

Block execution with a cold cache calls cached_compile_and_execute_raw, compiling synchronously on the first call; with a warm cache it interprets and starts asynchronous compilation once interpretation of the code hash has used max_code_size(10,240, size) gas. - Monad, cycle 16. Monad main, EIP-8024 and SLOTNUM: can the new opcodes or their immediates change the jump destination map or the execution of the deployed PoolManager?. Result: No. The opcodes are gated on Amsterdam, which only MONAD_NEXT selects, and mainnet's revision function ends at MONAD_TEN. The interpreter's jump analysis has no EIP-8024 case, because an allowed immediate is never 0x5b or a PUSH. The compiler consumes an immediate only when it is allowed and otherwise ends the block as invalid, so 0x5b after 0xe6 to 0xe8 stays a JUMPDEST. A linear scan of the 24,009 byte runtime finds no 0x4b, 0xe6, 0xe7 or 0xe8 outside push data, so no PoolManager instruction changes meaning. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/compiler/ir/basic_blocks.hpp ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/interpreter/intercode.cpp ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/execution/monad/chain/monad_mainnet.cpp lines 33-51 ; research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json
- Monad, cycle 16. Monad main, generic 256 bit division and modular arithmetic that DIV, MOD, ADDMOD and MULMOD call (udivrem, addmod, mulmod), read against v0.16.7 for the paths FullMath.mulDiv (src/libraries/FullMath.sol:24 and 48) and UnsafeMath.divRoundingUp use. Result: Equivalent as read. udivrem now forms the remainder from the n significant divisor words. After Knuth division the normalised remainder is below the normalised divisor, so the words at n and above are zero, and v0.16.7 read the same zeros. The short path zero fills the remainder and copies min(M, N) words, which also removes an over-read when M is less than N. addmod's fast path returns the same value through one variable. mulmod's wide_mul is truncating_mul of width M+N. Not run, because the library could not be built here. L-836: the 61 whole-transaction reruns of cycle 13 that still mismatched after the DELEGATECALL fix (38 Monad, 23 MegaETH), rerun with replay17.py and sorted by the first PoolManager frame whose input or output differs from the chain's call tracer. Result: MegaETH: 15 now match in every PoolManager frame's input, success and output; in 8 all shared PoolManager frames are equal and the calling contract made fewer calls after two failed unlock attempts, a gas-dependent decision of the caller. Monad: 19 have every PoolManager frame equal (the difference is a caller frame that reverts or logs differently), 7 differ only in the number of later calls, 2 receive a different input from the caller, and 10 differ at a swap of dynamic fee pools with hook 0x5ec8dd7d84fc91bf016d79b125d15aff97c32888. In the one of those traced in full, the hook's beforeSwap returned a different unspecified delta in the rerun for the same input; its library 0x1e32de59 (127,091 bytes) holds 154 GAS instructions and makes a STATICCALL with zero gas that fails out of gas on chain, and the reference interpreter has no gas model. No case shows the PoolManager returning a different result for the same input and the same hook answers, which the PoolManager-only replays of cycles 13 and 14 cover. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/019/high-throughput.work/l836/l836-summary.json, first-*.json, hook-0x3a286a.json, divergent-swaps.json, oog-*.json, firstpm.py, hookio.py; rpc https://rpc-mainnet.monadinfra.com and https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc
- Monad, cycle 19. Whether Monad's prestateTracer, which the whole-transaction reruns start from, returns the state left by earlier transactions of the same block. Result: For transaction 0x00cefb67 (index 111 of 124 in block 124,744,439) the two PoolManager slots of pool ee7e75fa that an earlier transaction of the block wrote are reported with the value that transaction wrote, not the parent-block value, and the other four slots equal the parent value. The rerun mismatches of that transaction therefore do not come from a wrong pre-state. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/019/high-throughput.work/l836/prestate-0x00cefb.json, prestate_check.py; rpc https://rpc-mainnet.monadinfra.com
- Monad, cycle 19. L-813 for Monad: does the reserve balance check report a frame as failed while keeping its writes?. Result: No. revert_transaction calls dipped_into_reserve after the transaction has executed, for MONAD_FOUR and later, and a positive answer reverts the whole transaction; there is no frame-level outcome. The check skips accounts with contract code, so the PoolManager (24,009 bytes of code) is never tested, and a revert of the whole transaction discards every PoolManager write with it (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/execution/monad/reserve_balance.cpp lines 54-130 and 392-419
- Monad, cycle 19. Upcoming Monad forks and releases in the next six months. Result: MonadMainnet::get_monad_revision on main returns MONAD_TEN from timestamp 1788359400 and names no later revision; MONAD_NEXT and MONAD_NEXT_AMSTERDAM exist in revision.h without a mainnet timestamp. The only pending mainnet step is the rolling v0.16.7 upgrade, a snapshot memory fix on top of v0.16.6, whose EVM changes (memory bounds checked once per offset, literal shifts, CLZ, block-exit writes) cycles 16 to 18 already tested against the PoolManager. Nothing changes for funds already in the PoolManager, and no new lever appears for an ordinary account. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/execution/monad/chain/monad_mainnet.cpp lines 31-51; https://docs.monad.xyz/node-ops/upgrade-instructions/v0.16.7; https://github.com/category-labs/monad-bft/releases/tag/v0.16.7
- MegaETH, cycle 19. Upcoming MegaETH forks in the next six months. Result: mega-evm v1.7.3 removed REX7 (pull request 402), chain.rs on main ends the mainnet schedule at Rex6 (1787626800), and the upgrade overview lists MiniRex to Rex6 only. No fork is scheduled, so nothing changes for funds in the PoolManager. - Monad, cycle 19. Monad main, Barrett reduction module in uint256.hpp: does anything on the interpreter or compiler path of MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV or MOD call it?. Result: Not on main as read. category/vm/runtime/math.hpp lines 74 to 95 call the generic addmod and mulmod, which compute a full 512 bit product and a long division (uint256.hpp lines 921 to 962), and emitter.cpp and emitter.hpp have no reference to barrett or reciprocal. Only files fetched by path were searched; no release carries the module. FullMath.mulDiv (src/libraries/FullMath.sol:24 and :48) therefore still meets the long division on Monad. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/core/runtime/uint256.hpp; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/runtime/math.hpp; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/emitter.cpp
- Monad, MegaETH, cycle 21. Opcode battery (99,985 vectors) and targeted set (85,544 vectors) rerun on Monad/0.16.7 and on the MegaETH replica mega-reth/v2.3.1-4499c42. Result: Every vector ran and none mismatches on either network: 0 of 99,985 and 0 of 85,544. That covers the 8,908 MULMOD and mulDiv inputs of the ruint 1.21.0 fault shape and all edges of DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, JUMPI, KECCAK256, MCOPY and CALLDATALOAD in OPCODES.md. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/021/high-throughput.work/battery.json and targeted.json, with client versions logged in run.log
- Monad, MegaETH, cycle 21. PoolManager script sets pmdiff (250 scripts, 12,322 calls) and pmdiff2 (300 scripts, 16,263 calls, run on this checkout's build, whose bytes equal the deployed code) against Ethereum's reth v2.11.0 under identical state. Result: MegaETH is identical on 250 of 250 and 300 of 300. Monad is identical on 229 of 250 and 280 of 300. The differing indices are exactly the 21 and 20 that cycle 19 attributed to heavy swaps meeting Monad's gas prices, so nothing new differs. - Monad, MegaETH, cycle 21. Mined swaps: tick relation and single-step amounts for recent Swap events, and step-by-step replay of the multi-step and unexplained ones. Result: Monad: 1,761 swaps all pass the tick relation, and of 1,682 pairs 1,669 match a single-step formula to the unit (1,477 exact in, 88 exact out, 104 to target) with 13 multi-step. MegaETH: 5,890 swaps all pass, and of 5,568 pairs 5,411 match a single step, 119 are multi-step and 38 other. The replay reproduces all 13 Monad multi-step swaps, 25 MegaETH multi-step swaps and all 38 MegaETH other swaps to the unit. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/021/high-throughput.work/swaps.json and replay.json
- MegaETH, cycle 21. Lead L-941: re-execution in the public stateless validator (mega-evm v1.7.3 build of cycle 16), with the pre-state tied to the parent block hash, of every MegaETH block with a PoolManager log from 32,826,735 to head 32,842,064. Result: 75 blocks hold PoolManager logs in that window, and all 75 validate (count=1, exit 0, no mismatch line). The producer's results in these blocks equal stock revm 40.0.3 under mega-evm. A native-only settle or clear emits no log, so blocks holding only those were not selected. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/021/high-throughput.work/anch-results.txt and anch/*.log
- Monad, cycle 21. Monad PR #2667 (v0.16.6), which checks memory bounds once per offset stack element in compiled code. Can a compiled MLOAD or MSTORE skip an expansion it needs?. Result: No. touch_memory serves only accesses of at most 32 bytes (MLOAD, MSTORE, MSTORE8) and skips the check only when the same immutable stack element has already been checked for at least as many bytes. That earlier check runs before it in the same straight-line block, or in a fall-through block that is not a jump destination (emitter.cpp jumpi, lines 3516 to 3536 on main). Memory never shrinks within a frame, and a failed check leaves the frame. The path exists only in v0.16.6 and later, which validators do not run, and simulated calls use the interpreter. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/emitter.cpp
- Monad, cycle 21. Monad MONAD_NINE memory cap (8 MB per transaction, counted over the current frame and its parents), measured on the live interpreter. Can an ordinary account use it to make a PoolManager call of another user fail, or to make the PoolManager continue after a failed sub-call?. Result: The cap holds at its exact edge: a write ending at byte 8,388,608 succeeds and one ending at 8,388,640 fails as out of gas. Only frames of the same transaction count, so an outside account can reach a victim's PoolManager call only through a hook or token in the victim's pool (pool-creator). Every PoolManager sub-call treats failure as a revert of the whole call: hook calls at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-135, payouts at src/types/Currency.sol:44-80, and the revert wrapper at src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:84-112. No path continues past a frame that the cap stopped. A hook that returns several MB makes its own pool's calls fail through the copy at Hooks.sol:140-149, which is a pool-creator hazard already covered by F-004. Evidence: https://docs.monad.xyz/developer-essentials/opcode-pricing and eth_call on https://rpc.monad.xyz with initcode 0x6001627fffe05200 (result 0x) and 0x600162800000520000 (out of gas)
- Monad, cycle 21. Lead L-933: can a transaction from Monad SYSTEM_SENDER, whose key system_sender.hpp calls known, reach the staking reward, snapshot or epoch change functions?. Result: No such path was found. The three syscalls are dispatched only in ExecuteSystemTransaction::execute_staking_syscall (execute_system_transaction.cpp lines 209 to 233). The staking precompile's dispatch table has no REWARD, SNAPSHOT or ON_EPOCH_CHANGE case and falls back to precompile_fallback. A system transaction must be legacy, addressed to the staking contract, with gas limit and fee 0 (validate_system_transaction.cpp lines 41 to 75), which an ordinary transaction cannot pass because of its intrinsic gas. The system sender cannot appear in an authorization list (validate_monad_transaction.cpp line 53). eth_call from the system sender with REWARD and SNAPSHOT reverts with 'method not supported'. Whether the key itself is published was not found. The address is not the PoolManager or its owner. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/execution/monad/execute_system_transaction.cpp
- MegaETH, cycle 21. Lead L-932: has the MegaETH OptimismPortal2 proxy on Ethereum ever pointed at a temporary implementation?. Result: No. eth_getLogs for Upgraded(address) from block 0 to head returns two events: 0x31f6e6a37ce650723ebf082ec59a48779be9af99 (version() 3.14.0) in the creation transaction at block 23,770,457, and 0x55400445e384393f9c1be23e7e734e8d44ed9fd9 (version() 3.15.2) at block 24,036,326 through ProxyAdmin 0x15fcb0120d414f246ead019ca4bdf97447cd8d90 upgrade(). The EIP-1967 slot holds 0x55400445 today. Both are versioned OptimismPortal2 releases, and the upgrader power remains the governance hazard of F-140. Evidence: eth_getLogs and eth_call on https://mainnet.gateway.tenderly.co; https://eth.blockscout.com/api/v2/addresses/0x7f82f57F0Dd546519324392e408b01fcC7D709e8
- Monad, MegaETH, cycle 21. Upcoming forks for the next six months on both networks. Result: None is scheduled. monad_mainnet.cpp on main still ends at MONAD_TEN (2026-09-02), the v0.16.7 upgrade instructions apply to testnet only, and no later tag exists. MegaETH's chain.rs on main ends at Rex6 (timestamp 1787626800), and the upgrade overview lists nothing after Rex6. With nothing scheduled, nothing changes for funds already in the PoolManager. ## HyperEVM

- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Do PUSH0, MCOPY, TLOAD, TSTORE and SELFBALANCE exist and behave as the bytecode expects (A10)?. Result: Yes. A read-only creation style eth_call that stores 0x2a with TSTORE, loads it with TLOAD, copies it with MCOPY and reads SELFBALANCE returned 0x2a in both words. The docs state Cancun without blobs and the replay client uses SpecId::CANCUN. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call init code 0x602a5f5d5f5c5f5260205f60205e475060405ff3; https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hyperliquid-dex/hyper-evm-sync/main/src/run.rs
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Is EIP-7702 active, which would let code at a hook address change after pool creation (A7)?. Result: No sign of Prague. The BLS12-381 precompile address 0x0b and the P256 address 0x0100 return empty data, block headers have no requestsHash, the docs state Cancun, and the replay client passes no authorization list. A hook address that has code keeps it under the Cancun SELFDESTRUCT rule. This needs a re-check when HyperEVM announces a fork. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call to 0x0b and 0x0100; eth_getBlockByNumber latest; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hyperliquid-dex/hyper-evm-sync/main/src/run.rs
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Does transient storage (unlock flag, deltas, synced currency and reserves) leak between a system transaction and a user transaction, or between two user transactions in one block (A1)?. Result: No. The replay client builds a new EVM and calls transact once per system transaction and once per signed transaction, and commits state after each (run.rs lines 155 to 168 and 216 to 258). It asserts that its receipts equal the receipts recorded by the production node, so the production node gives the same per transaction lifetime. src/libraries/Lock.sol:10-27, src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:15-38 and src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:12-34 therefore see Ethereum's behaviour. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hyperliquid-dex/hyper-evm-sync/main/src/run.rs
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Can a HyperCore to HyperEVM credit raise the PoolManager token balance between sync and settle and be claimed by the settler (A2, src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365)?. Result: No. A credit is a separate system transaction that runs before the user transactions of the block, and the recipient is the HyperCore sender's own address. sync and settle of one payment run inside one user transaction. A credit that lands earlier is already inside the reserves that sync records. Evidence: https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm/hypercore-less-than-greater-than-hyperevm-transfers; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hyperliquid-dex/hyper-evm-sync/main/src/run.rs
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Can any party make a system transaction call the PoolManager, or reach it with msg.sender equal to the owner or to the zero address fee controller (A8, A12)?. Result: No path found. Observed and documented system transactions target the linked contract of a token or the HyperCore sender's own address, and their senders are 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222, a 0x20 system address, or the two AQAv2 addresses. The PoolManager would become a target only if a token were linked to it, which needs a finalize action from the owner in storage slot 0. No sender is the zero address. With the controller at zero, setProtocolFee and collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-57) are unreachable and no protocol fee can accrue. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_getSystemTxsByBlockNumber over 120 blocks ending 51,941,801; https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm/hypercore-less-than-greater-than-hyperevm-transfers
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Does the native asset have an ERC-20 face, so that pools on address(0) and pools on a token address draw on one balance (A3)?. Result: No. HYPE links to the native balance and has no linked EVM contract. WHYPE is a wrapper whose totalSupply equals its own native balance. A native payment is msg.value and a native payout is a value call (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354, src/types/Currency.sol:48), in the same 18 decimal unit as address(this).balance. Evidence: https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm/hypercore-less-than-greater-than-hyperevm-transfers; https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call totalSupply() and eth_getBalance on 0x5555555555555555555555555555555555555555
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Do the 3,000,000 gas fast blocks or the 30,000,000 gas slow blocks freeze liquidity removal or swaps (A9)?. Result: No freeze found. modifyLiquidity updates two ticks, the bitmap and one position with no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238), which fits a fast block. A swap that would cross more ticks than one transaction can pay for can be cut with sqrtPriceLimitX96 and continued in the next transaction, because the loop stops at the limit and stores the reached price (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-439). A sender that needs more than 3,000,000 gas can opt in to slow blocks with the HyperCore action evmUserModify. That costs latency and does not block funds. Evidence: https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm/dual-block-architecture; https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_getBlockByNumber for 75 blocks ending 51,942,345
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Can anyone make the PoolManager send a HyperCore action through CoreWriter, for example add API wallet or spot send, and so control what the PoolManager address holds on HyperCore?. Result: No. CoreWriter's code dispatches only selector 0x17938e13. The PoolManager can call an arbitrary address only with transfer(address,uint256) calldata, balanceOf(address) calldata, hook selectors, or empty calldata with value (src/types/Currency.sol:48, 60-75, 94 and src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155), and it calls unlockCallback only on msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:110). None of these matches sendRawAction. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_getCode 0x3333333333333333333333333333333333333333; https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm/interacting-with-hypercore
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Can the HYPE bridge address or CoreWriter be used as a hook address so that the PoolManager calls them inside a pool action?. Result: No. The low 14 bits of 0x2222 and 0x3333 both set AFTER_ADD_LIQUIDITY_RETURNS_DELTA (bit 1) without AFTER_ADD_LIQUIDITY (bit 10), so isValidHookAddress returns false and initialize reverts (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127, src/PoolManager.sol:126). Both contracts also revert on hook selectors. Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127; https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_getCode on both addresses
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Can a read precompile used as a currency address create credit, since 0x0809 answers balanceOf with a number that grows over time (A2, A4)?. Result: No effect on other currencies. Inside one transaction the precompile value is fixed, so settle computes a paid amount of zero (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). take of that currency always reverts, because the precompile returns 32 bytes that are not 1 and Currency.transfer treats that as failure (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74 and 82-86). Deltas, reserves and claims are tracked per currency address (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41), so a currency with odd balance behaviour cannot draw on the balance of a real token. The other precompiles tested fail on balanceOf calldata, so sync reverts. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call to 0x0809 and neighbours with balanceOf and transfer calldata; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hyperliquid-dex/hyper-evm-sync/main/src/precompile.rs
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Does holding a pool token for part of one transaction have value on HyperEVM, given that take lends everything for free inside unlock (A5)?. Result: No use found. Gas is paid only in HYPE by the transaction sender. Read precompiles report HyperCore state fixed when the EVM block is built and do not read EVM balances. Bridging a borrowed balance to HyperCore removes it from the EVM, so the borrower cannot settle, unlock reverts on the unsettled delta (src/PoolManager.sol:112) and the bridge log is discarded with the revert. Evidence: https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm/interacting-with-hypercore; https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm/interaction-timings; https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. What happens if a HyperCore spot token is linked to the PoolManager address as its EVM contract?. Result: Nothing that touches pool funds, in the documented linking behaviour. HyperCore to EVM transfers would call transfer(address,uint256) on the PoolManager, which has no such function and no fallback (the ERC-6909 transfer takes three arguments, src/ERC6909.sol:25), so the call reverts. EVM to HyperCore credits need an ERC-20 Transfer log from the linked contract. The PoolManager emits only the five field ERC-6909 Transfer event (src/interfaces/external/IERC6909Claims.sol:14) and its deployed bytecode does not contain the ERC-20 Transfer topic 0xddf252ad. Linking also needs a finalize action from the owner stored in slot 0. The interaction with AQAv2 sender rules is left as a lead. Evidence: https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm/hypercore-less-than-greater-than-hyperevm-transfers; https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_getCode and eth_getStorageAt on the PoolManager
- HyperEVM, cycle 1. Can a reorg or equivocation undo a settlement after funds have left the PoolManager (A14)?. Result: Not under the stated consensus rules. HyperEVM blocks are part of HyperBFT execution, honest nodes agree on the ordered list of committed rounds, and a quorum is more than two thirds of stake. Settlement in core is atomic inside one transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), so there is no state that spans blocks. Evidence: https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/hypercore/staking; https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Sweep of the standard precompile range 0x01 to 0x20 and 0x0100 with the PoolManager as caller, using empty calldata, transfer(address,uint256) with a nonzero amount and balanceOf(PoolManager): does any address act as a currency or recipient in a way Ethereum's does not (P1, P2, P3)?. Result: No. 0x01 returns nothing, 0x02 and 0x03 return a 32 byte hash, 0x04 returns its input, 0x05, 0x06, 0x07 and 0x09 fail on the transfer and balanceOf shapes, and 0x08 and 0x0a fail on them as well when given enough gas (0x08 answers empty calldata with a 32 byte 1, as on Ethereum, which no PoolManager call shape for a currency can produce). 0x0b to 0x20 and 0x0100 answer like accounts without code. This is Ethereum's Cancun behaviour. None of these addresses returns a 32 byte 1 or empty data for the transfer shape while holding a balance, so take either reverts or moves nothing and still debits the caller (src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). 0x02, 0x03 and 0x04 answer balanceOf with a constant, so settle computes zero (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). Only the gas price of seven of them differs, see the MRB finding. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call from 0x12D4Fd9C5DeDd00ab8a0bCe2CF0167bbf94b6B1F to each address with three call shapes, latest, 2026-11-22
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Sweep of 0x0700 to 0x09ff and 0x1000 to 0x1010 with the same three call shapes: which addresses are read precompiles today and can any of them serve as currency, recipient or hook?. Result: Read precompiles occupy 0x0800 to 0x0814. Twenty of them fail on every PoolManager call shape, including all ten IHooks selectors on 0x0800 and 0x0810, the only two whose low 14 bits pass Hooks.isValidHookAddress. A failed call burns the gas forwarded and the PoolManager reverts (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-137, src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, and the balanceOf call at Currency.sol:94). A pool created with 0x0800 or 0x0810 as hook can be initialized, since neither has an initialize flag, and can never receive liquidity, because beforeAddLiquidity fails. Nobody else's funds are involved. All other addresses in the ranges answer like accounts without code. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call from 0x12D4Fd9C5DeDd00ab8a0bCe2CF0167bbf94b6B1F, three shapes for 785 addresses and fifteen shapes for 0x0800, 0x0809 and 0x0810
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Can 0x0809, which answers every call with the L1 block number, give a credit when used as currency, given that the number grows by about 20 per second (A2, A4)?. Result: No. Two calls to 0x0809 inside one execution returned the same value (0x495c881c and 0x495c881c), while separate executions about a second apart returned 0x495c8830 and 0x495c8846. sync and settle run in one transaction because the synced currency is transient (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-38), so paid is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). take under this id reverts, because the 32 byte answer is not 1 (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). This confirms the cycle 1 clearance with a measurement inside one execution. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call creation probe 0x60205f5f5f6108095afa50602060205f5f6108095afa5060405ff3, three runs
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Do the HYPE bridge 0x2222...2222, CoreWriter 0x3333...3333, the CoreDepositWallet, a token system address and the system interest address accept any PoolManager call shape other than the native payout already recorded in F-021?. Result: No. The bridge accepts empty calldata with or without value and reverts on transfer, balanceOf and all ten hook selectors. CoreWriter reverts on all fifteen shapes. The CoreDepositWallet reverts on all fifteen, and its transfer function names the reason: Caller is not the system address. 0x2000000000000000000000000000000000000077 and 0x5000000000000000000000000000000000000000 have no code, so a take to them is an ordinary transfer by the PoolManager that the caller pays for, and a take that names them as currency moves nothing and debits the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call from 0x12D4Fd9C5DeDd00ab8a0bCe2CF0167bbf94b6B1F with fifteen shapes per address, latest
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Which special addresses pass the hook address check, and can the PoolManager be made to call them inside a pool action with an accepted answer (P5)?. Result: Four pass Hooks.isValidHookAddress (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127): WHYPE, EntryPoint v0.6, 0x0800 and 0x0810. WHYPE has the afterInitialize flag and its fallback returns no data, so callHook reverts with InvalidHookResponse and initialize reverts (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154, src/PoolManager.sol:141). EntryPoint v0.6 has the beforeInitialize flag and reverts on the selector, so initialize reverts. The two precompiles are covered above. Every other special address fails the flag check. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call with the IHooks selectors from 0x12D4Fd9C5DeDd00ab8a0bCe2CF0167bbf94b6B1F; flag bits computed from the addresses against src/libraries/Hooks.sol:29-47
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Can a native payout to WHYPE, whose fallback wraps the value for the sender, leave the PoolManager owing native HYPE that it no longer holds, or give the caller a WHYPE credit it did not pay for?. Result: No. take(address(0), WHYPE, x) debits the caller x of the native id before the call (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295) and WHYPE credits the PoolManager x WHYPE. If the caller had synced WHYPE first, settle credits it x under the WHYPE id (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364). The caller then holds a debit of x native and a credit of x WHYPE and must clear both before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112). Whichever way it clears them, the native balance and the native amounts owed fall together and the WHYPE balance and amounts owed rise together. This is an in place wrap paid by the caller. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call from 0x12D4Fd9C5DeDd00ab8a0bCe2CF0167bbf94b6B1F to 0x5555555555555555555555555555555555555555 with empty calldata and value; WHYPE runtime code in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hyperliquid-dex/hyper-evm-sync/main/src/run.rs lines 47 to 53
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. stHYPE and wstHYPE: can one deposit be credited under both currency ids, can an ordinary account raise the stHYPE balance of the PoolManager inside its own sync window, and does rounding between the two units pay out more than a dust amount?. Result: No to all three. The synced currency is one transient slot, so only one measuring window is open at a time and a second sync replaces the first (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). Each window credits the rise of one balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and both balances rise only when shares arrive: the stHYPE rate depends on block.timestamp alone between rebases (stHYPE.sol lines 495 to 513), mint and burn keep the rate (lines 244 to 256), and rebase is role gated. Every take is debited in full under the id it names (src/PoolManager.sol:294). The sum of credits therefore never exceeds the shares paid in. Rounding: an stHYPE transfer moves floor(amount times shares per unit) of 24 decimal shares and wstHYPE moves multiples of 1e6 shares, so one settle can be off by at most one base unit of either token, far below the gas cost of the call. The effects that remain need the issuer and are in the stHYPE finding. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/999/0xe71caf5c1fe56d8897c7b604295d23968049e057?fields=sources; https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/999/0x104324863cfb2220756c60384efa9bb67a57aaf7?fields=sources; https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call rebase() from an unprivileged address
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Recheck of assumption A3 on 2026-11-22: does native HYPE now have an ERC-20 face or a linked EVM contract, and is any HyperCore token linked to the PoolManager, to WHYPE or to a system address?. Result: No. spotMeta returns evmContract null for HYPE (index 150). Of 194 linked tokens no two share an address and none points at the PoolManager, WHYPE, the bridge, CoreWriter or a 0x20 address. WHYPE remains a plain wrapper whose code has no path that reads another account's native balance. Evidence: https://api.hyperliquid.xyz/info spotMeta, 519 tokens
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Assumption A1 for system transactions, including the AQAv2 ones whose sender is the CoreDepositWallet or the treasury address: can an unlock flag, a delta or a stale sync written in one transaction be read by the next transaction of the block?. Result: No, on the evidence of the maintained archive client. It runs every system and signed transaction through one transact call (src/node/evm/executor.rs lines 192 to 213), and the revm fork it pins clears transient storage in commit_tx, discard_tx and finalize and restores it on checkpoint revert (journal/inner.rs lines 97 to 180 and 461 to 476). The client recovers any 20 byte sender from the s value, so the AQAv2 senders are covered, and it rejects a block whose gas used, receipts root or logs bloom differs from the header written by the validator node (src/node/consensus/reth_copy.rs lines 27 to 45). Lock, CurrencyDelta, CurrencyReserves and NonzeroDeltaCount (src/libraries/Lock.sol:10-27, CurrencyDelta.sol:28-41, CurrencyReserves.sol:21-38, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:12-34) therefore start each transaction at zero. This closes the gap the critic named for the replay client. The limit of the evidence: a header comparison shows a difference only if some past transaction depended on leaked transient state, and the validator binary itself is closed. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hl-archive-node/nanoreth/master/src/node/evm/executor.rs; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hl-archive-node/revm/fdf9b16bdd4388a680c97440c6e7f085647ece01/crates/context/src/journal/inner.rs; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hl-archive-node/nanoreth/master/src/node/consensus/reth_copy.rs
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Can system transactions crowd signed transactions out of a block and so delay a liquidity removal, given that an ordinary account can trigger them through HyperCore transfers?. Result: No. The archive client adds gas to the block total only for transactions that are not system transactions (src/node/evm/executor.rs lines 225 to 227) and checks each signed transaction against the remaining block gas without them (lines 196 to 206). A removal needs no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238) and fits a fast block. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hl-archive-node/nanoreth/master/src/node/evm/executor.rs
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Does the PoolManager address have a HyperCore account, a HyperCore balance or the big block flag, and can a third party set any of these in a way that changes how the PoolManager behaves on the EVM?. Result: No account exists: spotClearinghouseState returns no balances, userRole returns missing and preTransferCheck returns userExists false. A third party can create the account and fund it by sending HyperCore assets to the address, which changes nothing on the EVM. The big block flag and every HyperCore action need a signature of the account or a CoreWriter call by it, and the PoolManager can make neither (cycle 1 clearance on CoreWriter, rechecked: CoreWriter reverts on every PoolManager call shape). Evidence: https://api.hyperliquid.xyz/info spotClearinghouseState, userRole, preTransferCheck for 0x12D4Fd9C5DeDd00ab8a0bCe2CF0167bbf94b6B1F
- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Opcode differential for the opcodes and call patterns the PoolManager relies on: do TSTORE, TLOAD, SSTORE, SLOAD, MCOPY, KECCAK256, LOG, BALANCE, EXTCODESIZE, SELFBALANCE, CALL with and without value, STATICCALL, RETURNDATASIZE, PUSH0 and CREATE cost what they cost on Ethereum, and does the client change any of them?. Result: They cost the same in 23 measured snippets, to the unit of gas. The archive client uses revm's mainnet instruction table and replaces only BLOCKHASH for blocks below 243,538 (src/evm/api/mod.rs lines 33 to 43). Core does not use BLOCKHASH. The measured differences are confined to seven precompiles that core never calls. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm and https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com eth_call creation probes bracketed by GAS; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hl-archive-node/nanoreth/master/src/evm/api/mod.rs

- HyperEVM, cycle 2. Can an EntryPoint address used as currency draw on any balance that belongs to other users, since both EntryPoints answer balanceOf(PoolManager) and accept native value from the PoolManager?. Result: No. The EntryPoint deposit of the PoolManager rises only when native value is sent for it. If the PoolManager sends it through take, the caller is debited the native amount (src/PoolManager.sol:294). A credit under the EntryPoint id can be minted as a claim and can never be paid out, because transfer(address,uint256) reverts on both EntryPoints (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). Deltas and claims are separate per currency address (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16), so this id cannot reach HYPE, WHYPE or USDC held for pools.
