## Reading of the source (flow-liquidity)

- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Can one owner change or withdraw another owner's position through modifyLiquidity, including by reusing a salt, by passing ticks of another position, or by removing more than it holds. Result: No. The position is looked up under keccak256 of owner, tickLower, tickUpper and salt, and the owner is always msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161, src/libraries/Position.sol:34-41). The assembly lays the four fields out as 20, 3, 3 and 32 bytes without overlap, and bytes above the address fall outside the hashed range (Position.sol:54-66). I rebuilt the layout byte for byte and compared it with the packed encoding that test/libraries/Position.t.sol:75-80 expects on 3,000 random inputs, with dirty upper bits in the owner word. A removal larger than the position reverts in LiquidityMath.addDelta (Position.sol:88, src/libraries/LiquidityMath.sol:10-18), after the tick updates, and the revert undoes those. In 6,000 random sequences on a Python transcription, every attempt by a second owner, by the same owner under a different salt, or for one unit more than the position held reverted. Evidence: src/libraries/Position.sol:34-67
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Order of the steps inside Pool.modifyLiquidity: tick update, bitmap flip, fee growth read, Position.update, tick clearing, and the three price cases for the amounts. Covered add, remove, zero delta, full range, one spacing, ranges above, below and around the current tick, and several owners on shared ticks. Result: The order is sound. A new tick gets its feeGrowthOutside before the fee growth inside the range is read (src/libraries/Pool.sol:160-162, 533-539, 184-185). A tick whose liquidityGross returns to zero is deleted only after the last position has been paid from its values (Pool.sol:187-203). A position that still has liquidity keeps both its ticks alive, because liquidityGross is the sum of the positions on the tick, so its checkpoint can never meet a re-initialized tick. A position with zero liquidity earns nothing at its next update because fees use the liquidity held before the update (src/libraries/Position.sol:82-97). Amounts use slot0.tick for the range test and the stored sqrt price for the in range case, add rounds up and remove rounds down (Pool.sol:206-237, src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:261-288). I transcribed Pool, Position, TickBitmap, LiquidityMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath and TickMath into Python and ran 6,000 random sequences (254,069 operations, 50,789 of them reverts) with four owners, two salts, spacings 1, 10, 60, 200, 2000 and 32767, start prices in the middle and within 3,000 ticks of both ends, swaps, donations and protocol fees. After every operation liquidityGross and liquidityNet of each tick equalled the sums over positions, the bitmap bit was set exactly for ticks with liquidityGross above zero, pool liquidity equalled the liquidity of positions in range at slot0.tick, and the pool never owed more of either currency than it had received. At the end every position could be removed in full and all tick data was gone. A second set of 6,000 sequences without swaps or donations, 3,614 of them started in the state where slot0.tick is one below the tick of the price, paid no fees to anyone and left no owner with more than it had paid in. Evidence: src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Can an ordinary account make a hookless victim position impossible to remove, or leave a tick that can no longer be updated. Listed every revert on the removal path. Result: No path found for a token with fewer than 2^127 base units. On removal the cap is not checked (src/libraries/Pool.sol:165). liquidityGross cannot underflow because it is the sum of the positions. liquidityNet stays inside int128 because its size is bounded by liquidityGross, and the cap is at most 6076470837873901133274546561281575204 (spacing 32767), below 2^127. The same bound keeps pool liquidity inside uint128 when ticks are crossed. flipTick cannot revert for a tick that was initialized, since only aligned ticks can be initialized (src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:47-75). FullMath.mulDiv in Position.update cannot revert because the product of a 256 bit growth difference and a 128 bit liquidity divided by 2^128 fits in 256 bits. The casts of the principal amounts can revert for a very large position, and the owner then removes in parts. The sum of principal and fees can exceed int128, and the owner then collects fees with a zero delta first (src/PoolManager.sol:171). What remains is the known case of uncollected fees of 2^127 base units or more (F-005). I checked whether flash accounting gives a cheaper route to that bound: it does not. An account that is the only liquidity in range can donate to itself at no cost and wrap feeGrowthGlobal past 2^256, as the comment at Pool.sol:80-82 says, but positions out of range see no change in their fee growth inside, and after later tick crossings they are owed only real swap fees (six self donations of 2^127 - 1 units in the transcription, then swaps through both victim ranges). When a victim is in range, its share of a donation is real value the donor has to pay. Evidence: src/libraries/Pool.sol:159-238
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Hook deltas on liquidity changes: can afterAddLiquidity or afterRemoveLiquidity move more than the caller's own delta, which hook runs for a zero delta, and what a hook that calls modifyLiquidity itself can skip. Result: The caller delta after the hook is the pool delta minus the hook delta, and the hook is credited the hook delta, so the two always add up to principal plus fees (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:219-244, src/PoolManager.sol:171-183). The hook delta is read only when the matching return-delta bit is set, and then the return data must be exactly 64 bytes (Hooks.sol:159-168). A zero delta runs the remove hooks (Hooks.sol:201-205, 220-244). When the hook itself is the caller, the hook calls are skipped and no delta is taken (Hooks.sol:171-175, 217). A pool without a hook has none of these paths. The hazard for pools whose liquidity providers chose a hook is already recorded as F-004. One comment differs from the code: src/interfaces/IHooks.sol:50 and 81 say the delta passed to the after hooks includes the hook delta, while the code passes principal plus fees before the hook delta is known. This changes no balance. Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:195-245
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. donate from entry to the last delta: who is debited, who can receive, rounding, the tick and price mismatch at a boundary, and whether a donation can be redirected away from positions that were in range. Result: The donor is debited the two amounts, each cast to int128, and fee growth rises by amount times 2^128 divided by the liquidity in range, rounded down (src/libraries/Pool.sol:466-480, src/PoolManager.sol:256-276). A donation reverts when no liquidity is in range. The rounding remainder is below one base unit per donation and stays in the PoolManager. In the transcription each in range position was owed at most its exact share and the shares never added up to more than the donation, across all donations in 6,000 sequences. Positions out of range were unchanged. The two concrete values of test/PoolManager.t.sol:841-864 (34028236692093846346337 and 68056473384187692692674 for 100 and 200 units on 1e18 liquidity) come out of the source formula. Two things can redirect a donation, and both are stated in src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:150-155: liquidity added just before the donation takes a share, and after a zeroForOne swap that ends exactly on a tick, slot0.tick is one below the tick of the price, so the donation goes to the range below. Both cost the donor's intended recipients future income and take nothing that a position already holds. Evidence: src/libraries/Pool.sol:466-480
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Do the liquidity related tests in the repository hold against the source text: test/libraries/TickBitmap.t.sol, LiquidityMath.t.sol, Position.t.sol, SafeCast.t.sol, the modifyLiquidity fuzz in test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:43-84, the salt tests and the two fixed cases of test/ModifyLiquidity.t.sol, and the liquidity and donate cases of test/PoolManager.t.sol. Result: All hold. The 18 fixed vectors of TickBitmap.t.sol for nextInitializedTickWithinOneWord, the flip sequences, and the fuzz properties for compress, flipTick alignment, the search on the fixture bitmap and the search on an empty bitmap passed on the transcription (20,000 random inputs each). LiquidityMath: the three revert cases, addDelta(2^127, -2^127) = 0 and the int128 minimum fuzz passed. Position: the position hash and the revert conditions of the update fuzz passed. SafeCast: the conditions in the source are the ones the tests state. Pool.t.sol: the order of expected reverts (ticks misordered, lower bound, upper bound, underflow for a negative delta, empty position for zero, cap on the lower tick, misaligned lower, misaligned upper, int128 overflow of an amount) is the order in which the source reaches them. ModifyLiquidity.t.sol: the salt and router separation tests follow from the position hash, and the two fixed cases (spacing 32767 and spacing 1) are within one pip of the closed form, with differences of one base unit from rounding up. PoolManager.t.sol: ManagerLocked comes before PoolNotInitialized, and the donate reverts and values match. The JavaScript reference of the ffi fuzz test was not run. Evidence: test/libraries/TickBitmap.t.sol:130-320
- Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Zora, Worldchain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Monad, MegaETH, Arc, HyperEVM, cycle 2. Does the liquidity path give the same amounts on each network's EVM. Sent read-only eth_call probes to the PositionManager listed in networks.json: a multicall that initializes a new native pool and mints a position above the price, and a second set that mints and burns the same position in one call. Each probe was sent once with exactly the value the source formulas require and once with one wei less. Result: All 20 networks agree with the source formulas to the wei. Mint probes (9 per network): the highest tick filled to the cap for spacings 1, 60 and 200 (519766372, 1878783905959 and 20966766746469 wei, and TickLiquidityOverflow for one unit above the cap), a range next to a mid price, a range from tick -887190 to 887270 whose amount is 9185290247808691312573729382907766498, a range next to the lowest tick, spacing 32767, the largest liquidity whose amount stays below 2^127 (amount 170141183460469231731687013724867035278 accepted) and the next step above it (SafeCastOverflow). Mint and burn probes (6 per network): the caller owes exactly one wei, which is the gap between rounding up on add and rounding down on remove, and the call fails with zero value. These probes exercise TickMath, the 512 bit multiply and divide, signed tick arithmetic, the bitmap, the position hash, tick clearing, transient deltas and native settlement. Two side observations. The Soneium PositionManager holds 176652317140 wei that any caller's payment can draw on, so on Soneium the probe values were reduced by that balance, and the one wei less variant could not be tested for the spacing 1 mint and for the six mint and burn probes. On BNB Smart Chain the token id has to be read at a pinned block because new positions are minted every block. The probes ran against public RPC nodes at the latest block on 2026-11-22 and say nothing about validator builds. Donations and fee collection were not probed on chain because no deployed periphery contract exposes donate. Evidence: rpc endpoints listed in research/network-risk/state/networks.json
- Tempo, cycle 2. Same question for Tempo, where the node answers any call that carries value with 'value transfer not allowed' and eth_getBalance returns the constant 4242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242 for the PositionManager. Result: Partly covered. The value probes cannot run on Tempo. I used a probe that needs no payment: a position on ticks -887271 to -887270 of a new pool at the lowest price, with liquidity equal to a multiple of the product of the two sqrt prices, so that the amount on add and on remove is exact and the caller owes nothing. Mint and burn in one call succeeded on Tempo and on Ethereum for multiples 1 and 7, failed on both for liquidity one unit higher or lower (one base unit owed), and reverted on both with SafeCastOverflow for multiple 1000003, whose amount is above 2^127. An add that is paid in a TIP-20 currency was not probed. A pool with currency address(0) can be initialized on Tempo but can never receive a payment, so it holds nothing. Evidence: https://rpc.mainnet.tempo.xyz
- Zora, Base, cycle 2. Lead L-133, second half: is there a hook that must add liquidity on a tick an attacker can fill cheaply. Read the Zora coin hook, which adds liquidity inside afterSwap. Result: Not affected at realistic prices. CoinRewardsV4.mintLpReward runs inside afterSwap without a try block and adds a position one spacing wide that starts two spacings away from the current tick (CoinRewardsV4.sol lines 134-204, ZoraV4CoinHook.sol line 415 on the main branch). A full tick there would make every swap in the pool revert. The fill cost near the current tick is the cap times about 0.01 divided by the sqrt price in currency0, or times the sqrt price in currency1. With the cap of 3.8e34 for spacing 200 this is above the whole supply of a coin with 1e27 base units unless the price ratio in base units is beyond about 1e11, which only the far ends of the tick range reach. I read the repository source and did not check that the deployed hooks run this code. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ourzora/zora-protocol/main/packages/coins/src/libs/CoinRewardsV4.sol

## Reading of the source (flow-swap)

- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Line by line trace of a swap in a pool without a hook, from PoolManager.swap to the last delta written, for exact input and exact output in both directions. Result: swap rejects a zero amount and an uninitialized pool before anything else (src/PoolManager.sol:193-196). With hooks equal to address(0) beforeSwap returns the caller's amount unchanged and afterSwap returns a zero hook delta, because no permission bit is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:252-255, 298, 306). Pool.swap treats a negative amount as exact input and a positive amount as exact output at every place that branches on it (src/libraries/Pool.sol:313, 371, 453; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:61). For exact input the remaining amount rises toward zero by amountIn plus fee and the calculated amount grows by amountOut. For exact output the remaining amount falls by amountOut and the calculated amount falls by amountIn plus fee (Pool.sol:371-382). The final delta puts the specified amount in currency1 exactly when zeroForOne differs from exact input (Pool.sol:453-461), so the caller is debited the input currency and credited the output currency in all four cases. Both casts to int128 revert on overflow (Pool.sol:455, 459; src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43). The protocol fee is booked to the input currency (PoolManager.sol:216, 238). _accountPoolBalanceDelta writes amount0 to currency0 and amount1 to currency1 for msg.sender (PoolManager.sol:226, 381-384). I found no step where a sign, an operand order or a cast gives the caller more than the pool math computed. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:187-253, 368-384; src/libraries/Pool.sol:279-463; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:51-107
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. beforeSwap: the returned delta, the check that the swap type does not change, and the fee override word, including a hook that returns dirty upper bits. Result: The hook result must be exactly 96 bytes and start with the beforeSwap selector, otherwise the call reverts (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154, 259). The specified delta is read only when the address carries BEFORE_SWAP_RETURNS_DELTA_FLAG (Hooks.sol:266-270). It is added to the caller's amount with checked arithmetic, and the call reverts when an exact input amount becomes positive or an exact output amount becomes negative (Hooks.sol:273-278). An amount of exactly zero is allowed and makes Pool.swap return a zero delta without touching state (src/libraries/Pool.sol:320). The fee word is read only for a dynamic fee pool (Hooks.sol:263). parseFee assigns a full 32 byte word to a uint24 in assembly (src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:16-21). The value is then used only through isOverride, which ANDs with 0x400000, and removeOverrideFlag, which ANDs with 0xBFFFFF, followed by a comparison with 1,000,000 (src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78, Pool.sol:303-305). Both masks are 24 bit constants, so upper bits supplied by the hook cannot reach the fee, whatever the compiler does with the assignment. Without the override bit the stored fee is used. A hook can set the fee of its own dynamic fee pool to any value from 0 to 100 percent, which is the recorded hook trust finding F-004 and does not reach pools without that hook. Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:248-282; src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:9-28; src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78; src/libraries/Pool.sol:300-320
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. afterSwap and the two _accountDelta calls: does the caller delta plus the hook delta always equal the pool delta, and can a cast or a packing step lose a value. Result: afterSwap takes the specified and unspecified parts of the beforeSwap return, adds the afterSwap return to the unspecified part with a checked int128 cast and a checked addition (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:295-303), places the two parts in currency order with the same rule that Pool.swap uses (Hooks.sol:307-309 against src/libraries/Pool.sol:453), and subtracts the hook delta from the swap delta (Hooks.sol:312). The subtraction works on sign extended halves and reverts when a half leaves the int128 range (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:34-46). PoolManager.swap then credits the hook delta to the hook address and the remainder to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:221-226). The pool was run with the adjusted amount, so the two accounts together receive exactly the pool delta and each must reach zero before unlock returns (PoolManager.sol:112). I transcribed these lines and ran 20,000 random combinations of direction, amount and hook delta. Caller plus hook equalled the pool delta in every accepted case, and the accepted and rejected cases matched the conditions written in test/CustomAccounting.t.sol:195-209. Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:284-315; src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:14-71; src/types/BeforeSwapDelta.sol:9-37; src/PoolManager.sol:220-227, 368-384
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Fee split between protocol and liquidity providers in each step, and the unchecked subtraction of the protocol share. Result: The swap fee is the LP fee when the protocol fee is zero and protocolFee + lpFee - floor(protocolFee * lpFee / 1e6) otherwise (src/libraries/Pool.sol:307, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:38-46). It equals the protocol fee only when the LP fee is zero, because the protocol fee field is 12 bits wide and capped at 1,000. In that case the whole step fee goes to the protocol. Otherwise the protocol receives floor((amountIn + feeAmount) * protocolFee / 1e6) and the rest goes to fee growth (Pool.sol:391-405). In 300,000 random step shapes over the whole price range, with liquidity from 0 to 2^127 and amounts up to 2^255, the protocol share never exceeded the step fee, so the unchecked subtraction at Pool.sol:395 did not wrap. The transcribed swap reproduced the protocol fee totals that test/PoolManager.t.sol:779-818 and test/DynamicFees.t.sol:286-318 expect in 12,000 random cases, including the rounding up when the LP fee is zero. Rounding favours liquidity providers over the protocol and never the swapper. Evidence: src/libraries/Pool.sol:283-308, 384-407; src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:17-46; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-105
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Rounding of every amount in a swap step, asking who gains if a result is off by one unit. Result: Exact input: the amount after fee is rounded down, the input needed to reach the target is rounded up, the fee on a full step is rounded up, the fee on a partial step is the whole remainder, and the output is rounded down (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:64-86). Exact output: the output to the target is rounded down, the input and the fee are rounded up (SwapMath.sol:88-104). The next price is rounded up when currency0 comes in and down when currency1 comes in, which moves the price less than the exact result for an input and more for an output (src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:31-120, 146-148, 175-177). Every rounding step is against the swapper. The transcription returned the values asserted in test/libraries/SwapMath.t.sol:69-180 for seven fixed vectors and the Swap event values asserted in test/DynamicFees.t.sol:156-279, test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol:94, test/PoolManager.t.sol:501-503 and 608. Evidence: src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:51-107; src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:31-289; src/libraries/FullMath.sol:14-116; src/libraries/UnsafeMath.sol:12-28
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Tick crossing, the sign of liquidityNet, the tick stored after a step, and the price limit bounds. Result: The loop asks the bitmap for the next tick at or below the current tick when zeroForOne and above it otherwise (src/libraries/Pool.sol:347-348, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:94-119), clamps the result to MIN_TICK and MAX_TICK (Pool.sol:351-356) and uses the nearer of that tick's price and the limit as the target (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:25-36). A crossing happens only when the step ends exactly on the price of an initialized tick. It flips both fee growth outside values with the updated growth of the input currency and applies liquidityNet with its sign reversed for zeroForOne (Pool.sol:413-428, 602-612). After a zeroForOne step that ends on a tick the stored tick is one below it (Pool.sol:431). I traced the following oneForZero swap, a liquidity add on each side of that tick and a donate from that state. Each of them treats the pool as sitting just below the tick, which agrees with the liquidity value the swap left. A zeroForOne limit must be above MIN_SQRT_PRICE and a oneForZero limit below MAX_SQRT_PRICE (Pool.sol:322-338), so a swap cannot cross MIN_TICK downward or reach the price of MAX_TICK. Addition of liquidityNet reverts above 2^128 - 1 (src/libraries/LiquidityMath.sol:10-19) and the per tick cap keeps the sum over all ticks below that bound (Pool.sol:165-173, 565-582). The transcription returned the next tick and the initialized flag asserted in 19 fixed cases of test/libraries/TickBitmap.t.sol:130-293 and met its two fuzz properties in 40,000 random cases. Evidence: src/libraries/Pool.sol:322-359, 409-449, 596-612; src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:16-121; src/libraries/TickMath.sol:57-237
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Extremes of tick, price, liquidity, amount and fee, tested as solvency of one pool: can any sequence make a pool pay out more of a currency than it took in. This matters for every pool, because the PoolManager keeps no reserve per pool and a pool that overpays would draw on the balances of the others. Result: I wrote a third transcription of FullMath, UnsafeMath, BitMath, TickMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, LiquidityMath, TickBitmap, the position update and Pool.initialize, modifyLiquidity, swap and donate from the source text, with 256 bit wrapping where the source is unchecked or assembly. I checked it against the fixed values in the repository tests named in the other items. I then ran 8,000 random sequences of 5 to 40 operations: tick spacings 1, 10, 60, 200, 32767 and random, starting prices over the whole range including MIN_TICK and the ticks next to MAX_TICK, static fees from 0 to 100 percent, a per swap fee override in 40 percent of the swaps, protocol fees from 0 to 1,000 in both directions, liquidity up to 2^126, exact input and exact output amounts up to 2^255 with both the extreme and nearby price limits, and donations up to 2^126. After every operation, and after all positions were removed, the net amount the pool had received in each currency was at least the protocol fee accrued, in all 8,000 runs. 17 runs ended with a position that could not be removed. In each of them the fees paid into the pool in one currency exceeded 2^127 base units, which is the recorded finding F-005 and cannot happen for a token whose supply is below 2^127. Evidence: src/libraries/Pool.sol:94-612; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:20-107; src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:31-289; src/libraries/TickMath.sol:57-237; src/libraries/Position.sol:76-102
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Zero liquidity in range: a swap step with liquidity 0 moves the price for free. Can that give the swapper tokens or damage positions. Result: With liquidity 0 the input to the target, the output and the fee are all 0, the step reaches its target and no fee growth is added (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:66-74, 84-90; src/libraries/Pool.sol:401). In the transcription a swap of 1e18 exact input through an empty range returned the delta (0, 0) and only moved the price and tick. Positions are not affected, because a later add or removal computes its amounts from the price and tick of that moment with the usual rounding (Pool.sol:206-237) and the solvency runs above include such moves. The free move matters for contracts that read a pool price as an oracle and for the gas cost recorded in the finding of this unit. It does not move funds in core. Evidence: src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-105; src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Swap hook calls to an address that is a precompile, a system contract or an account without code: can the PoolManager be made to accept such a call during a swap. Result: callHook reverts unless the call succeeds and the return data is at least 32 bytes that start with the selector that was sent (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). An address without code returns nothing and fails this test. beforeSwap also needs exactly 96 bytes (Hooks.sol:259) and afterSwap with the return delta flag exactly 64 bytes (Hooks.sol:166). A contract that returns its input unchanged passes the selector test but returns the whole call data, which is longer than 96 bytes for beforeSwap and longer than 64 bytes for afterSwap, so it cannot act as a swap hook that returns deltas. It can only pass as an afterSwap hook without the return delta flag, where the return value is ignored (Hooks.sol:163). A failed hook call reverts the whole swap, so a side effect in the callee does not survive. Such a pool is one that somebody chose to create with that address as hook, and pools without a hook never make these calls. Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-168, 248-315
- Celo, Polygon, Arc, cycle 2. A native asset that also answers as an ERC-20 at some address: can sync, settle and take, in any order, credit one payment twice or credit more than was paid. Exhaustive search over a model of src/PoolManager.sol:279-297 and 349-364. Result: I modelled the PoolManager balance, the synced currency, the synced reserves, the two deltas and the attacker's wallet, with operations sync(0), sync(face), settle with value, settle without value, take in each currency, a transfer through the face and a native transfer that reaches the PoolManager without a call. I searched every sequence of up to 6 operations with amounts 1, 2 and 3. When the face reports the native balance one to one, no sequence left the attacker better off. The guard at PoolManager.sol:356 blocks the only order that would count a value twice. When the face reports floor(native / S) for S above 1, the best sequence gained S - 1 base units per round of sync and settle, and it needs native value to arrive without a call while the face is synced. On Arc the USDC contract at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 returns decimals 6 and its balanceOf for the PoolManager equalled floor(eth_getBalance / 1e12) at blocks 0x1f14a00, 0x1f14a63 and 0x1f14a79, with remainders of 930109466545, 178438878313 and 971982015932 base units. S is therefore 1e12 there and one round can gain less than 0.000001 USDC. I did not test whether native USDC can reach the PoolManager without a call on Arc, and I did not query the one to one property on Celo and Polygon again. For those two I rely on the earlier findings F-023 and F-008. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, 349-364; https://rpc.mainnet.arc.io eth_call decimals() and balanceOf(PoolManager) on 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 and eth_getBalance at blocks 0x1f14a00, 0x1f14a63, 0x1f14a79

## Reading of the source (invariants-bits)

- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Slot0 packing: field offsets, mask widths, sign handling of the tick and the effect of dirty upper bits passed to a setter. Result: The four fields sit at bit offsets 0, 160, 184 and 208 with widths 160, 24, 24 and 24, so they end at bit 232 and do not overlap (src/types/Slot0.sol:33-38). MASK_160_BITS is written with 42 hex digits, two of them leading zeros, and equals 2^160 - 1. Every setter ANDs the new value with its mask before the shift and clears only its own field in the packed word (Slot0.sol:66-93). The tick getter sign extends from 24 bits (Slot0.sol:47-51). I transcribed the eight functions into Python and ran 200,000 random cases in which each setter received a full 256 bit value. Every getter returned the input truncated to the field width, the top 24 bits of the word stayed unchanged, and the order of the setters did not change the result. No caller-supplied value can spill into a neighbouring field. The repository test test/types/Slot0.t.sol:8-35 states the same round trip and the source text satisfies it. Evidence: src/types/Slot0.sol:33-93; test/types/Slot0.t.sol:8-35
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. BalanceDelta and BeforeSwapDelta packing and unpacking, and the arithmetic on packed deltas. Result: toBalanceDelta shifts amount0 left by 128 bits and masks amount1 to 128 bits, so sign extension bits of a negative amount1 cannot reach amount0 (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:14-18). amount0 is read with sar 128 and amount1 with signextend 15 (BalanceDelta.sol:61-71). add and sub split both operands, add or subtract the halves as 256 bit numbers and pass each half through SafeCast.toInt128, which reverts when the result leaves the int128 range (BalanceDelta.sol:20-46, src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43). A carry from the low half therefore cannot enter the high half. BeforeSwapDelta uses the same layout with the specified amount in the high half (src/types/BeforeSwapDelta.sol:9-37). A Python transcription returned the inputs for 200,000 random int128 pairs and for the extreme pairs. The hook delta that reaches these functions is a full word chosen by the hook, and both halves are valid int128 values by construction, so no bit pattern is out of range. Evidence: src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:14-71; src/types/BeforeSwapDelta.sol:9-37; src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Fee fields: LP fee bounds and flag bits, the two 12 bit protocol fee halves, the combined swap fee and the unchecked subtraction of the protocol share. Result: MAX_LP_FEE is 1,000,000, which is below 2^20, so a valid fee never touches bit 22 (override flag 0x400000) or bit 23 (dynamic flag 0x800000) (src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:15-25). A pool is dynamic only when the fee field equals 0x800000 exactly (LPFeeLibrary.sol:30-32). isValidProtocolFee masks the low and the high 12 bits and compares them with 1001 and 1001 << 12 (src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32). I checked the function against the plain rule for one seventh of all 2^24 inputs. calculateSwapFee masks both inputs and returns p + l - floor(p * l / 1e6) (ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:38-46). For every p from 0 to 1000 and a grid of l up to 1,000,000 the result stayed at or below 1,000,000 and was at least p and at least l, and it equalled p only when l was 0. The step fee is at least amountIn * swapFee / (1e6 - swapFee) rounded up, or the whole remainder on a partial step (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:72-82, 104), so the protocol share floor((amountIn + feeAmount) * p / 1e6) cannot exceed it and the unchecked subtraction at src/libraries/Pool.sol:391-396 cannot wrap. The Slot0 setter masks the protocol fee to 24 bits before storing it (src/types/Slot0.sol:78-86). Evidence: src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:15-78; src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8-46; src/libraries/Pool.sol:286-316, 385-397; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-105
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Hook return data: which bits of the returned words the PoolManager uses, and whether dirty bits in a hook answer can change a value outside that hook's own pool. Result: parseSelector, parseFee and parseReturnDelta each load one full word at offsets 0x20, 0x60 and 0x40 of the returned bytes (src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:9-28). The selector is compared as bytes4, so only the first four bytes of the first word count (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152). The fee word is used only for a dynamic fee pool and only through an AND with 0x400000, an AND with 0xBFFFFF and a comparison with 1,000,000 (Hooks.sol:263, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78, src/libraries/Pool.sol:303-305), so bits above bit 23 are dropped whatever the compiler does with the assembly assignment, and a returned dynamic flag makes the fee fail validation. The delta word is split into two int128 halves and applied with checked arithmetic (Hooks.sol:266-279, 295-313). The hook is credited exactly what the caller is debited (src/PoolManager.sol:181-183, 224-226). Every value a hook can influence stays inside the pool that names that hook. The length rules are at least 32 bytes for every hook, exactly 64 bytes when a delta is parsed and exactly 96 bytes for beforeSwap (Hooks.sol:152, 166, 259). Evidence: src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:9-28; src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-168, 248-315; src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Hook flag bits and the validity rule: do the 14 flags overlap, does operator precedence give the intended test, and which special addresses pass the rule. Result: The 14 flags are the single bits 13 down to 0 and ALL_HOOK_MASK is 2^14 - 1 (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:27-47). In Solidity the bitwise AND binds tighter than the comparison, so hasPermission tests (address & flag) != 0 and the last line of isValidHookAddress tests (address & mask) > 0 (Hooks.sol:126, 337-339). I enumerated all 16,384 low bit patterns. With a static fee exactly 5,183 are accepted, which is 3^4 * 2^6 - 1: each of the four return delta bits needs its action bit, and the all zero pattern is refused. The zero address is accepted only with a static fee, and an address without flags only with the dynamic fee value (Hooks.sol:124-126). The fixed cases in test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol:940-990 agree, including the refusal of an address whose only set bit is bit 14. Low addresses that pass include 0x10, 0x64, 0x100 and 0x101. A precompile or a codeless account at such an address cannot answer with 32 bytes that start with the hook selector, so the hooked action of that pool reverts (Hooks.sol:152-154). That is the recorded hook trust finding F-004 and needs victims to choose a pool with that hook address. The identity precompile at 0x04 echoes its input and would pass the selector test, and its address carries bit 2 without bit 6, which the rule refuses (Hooks.sol:112). Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:27-47, 109-127, 152-154, 337-339; test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol:940-990
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Tick bitmap word and bit positions, the compress function, and the unchecked int24 products in the search for the next initialized tick. Result: position returns the signed tick shifted right by 8 as the word index and the low 8 bits as the bit index (src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:35-41). flipTick rejects a tick that is not a multiple of the spacing, divides, and builds the mapping slot from the 256 bit sign extended word index and the mapping slot, which is the encoding Solidity uses for an int16 index (TickBitmap.sol:47-75). For 200,000 random ticks and spacings the assembly compress equalled floor division, and the word index stayed inside int16 (-3466 to 3465 at spacing 1). The lte mask keeps bitPos + 1 low bits and the other mask clears the bits below bitPos (TickBitmap.sol:97, 110). The literal 1 in 1 << bitPos is evaluated as uint256. The largest magnitude the unchecked products can reach is 256 * 32767 = 8,388,352 for word index -1 at the maximum spacing, which is inside int24 (limit 8,388,608), and the swap loop then clamps the result to MIN_TICK and MAX_TICK (src/libraries/Pool.sol:351-356). MAX_TICK_SPACING is int16 max and initialize enforces the range 1 to 32767 (src/libraries/TickMath.sol:26-28, src/PoolManager.sol:119-120). Evidence: src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:16-121; src/libraries/Pool.sol:351-356; src/PoolManager.sol:119-120
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Tick info packing, LiquidityMath.addDelta and the liquidity cap per tick: can a width error let one account overflow gross, net or in range liquidity. Result: updateTick stores liquidityGross masked to 128 bits in the low half and liquidityNet shifted into the high half, which matches the declaration order of TickInfo (src/libraries/Pool.sol:68-77, 544-557). liquidityNet is computed with checked int128 arithmetic before the store (Pool.sol:543). addDelta masks x to 128 bits, sign extends y from 128 bits and reverts when any bit above bit 127 is set in the sum, which covers both overflow and underflow (src/libraries/LiquidityMath.sol:10-19). A transcription agreed with exact integer arithmetic on 200,000 random cases with dirty upper bits in x. tickSpacingToMaxLiquidityPerTick reproduces the four values in test/Tick.t.sol:115-141. For every spacing from 1 to 32767 the cap times the number of usable ticks is below 2^128 and the cap is below 2^127, so the sum of all tick liquidity fits uint128 and liquidityNet fits int128. Evidence: src/libraries/Pool.sol:68-77, 520-582; src/libraries/LiquidityMath.sol:10-19; test/Tick.t.sol:115-141
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. ERC-6909 id to currency conversion in mint and burn, and whether an id with high bits set can reach a balance or allowance of another id. Result: mint and burn truncate the id to 160 bits with fromId and use the truncated currency for the delta and toId of it for the claim balance, so an id with high bits set acts on the canonical id (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336, src/types/Currency.sol:110-118). The allowance and operator check in _burnFrom uses the same canonical id and the caller as spender (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22). transfer, transferFrom and approve use the raw 256 bit id (src/ERC6909.sol:25-56). A balance at an id with high bits can never be minted, so those ids always hold zero and every transfer of them reverts in the checked subtraction. mint casts the amount with toInt128 before the negation, so the unchecked block at PoolManager.sol:323-328 cannot wrap (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). The interface id 0x0f632fb3 equals the XOR of the seven ERC-6909 selectors. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:322-336; src/types/Currency.sol:110-118; src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22; src/ERC6909.sol:25-90
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Transient slot constants, the hash used for delta slots and the nonzero delta counter. Result: With a keccak implementation written for this unit and checked against the known digest of the empty string, keccak256 of ReservesOf, Currency, NonzeroDeltaCount and Unlocked minus one equal the four constants (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:11-13, src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:9-10, src/libraries/Lock.sol:8). A delta slot is keccak256 of the 64 bytes (target, currency), both masked to 160 bits, in the same order in getDelta and applyDelta (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41). A delta slot equal to a fixed slot would need a preimage of a hash minus one. sync stores the currency masked to 160 bits together with the reserves, and resetCurrency clears only the currency (CurrencyReserves.sol:21-32). applyDelta adds with checked int256 arithmetic. _accountDelta returns early for a zero delta, decrements the counter only when a slot returns to zero and increments only when it leaves zero, so the wrapping subtraction in decrement is never reached at zero (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:28-34). Evidence: src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:11-32; src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41; src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:9-34; src/libraries/Lock.sol:8-27; src/PoolManager.sol:368-378
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Position hash and pool id: byte layout of the assembly, dirty bits in the owner, and whether two different inputs can share a slot. Result: calculatePositionKey writes salt at offset 0x26, tickUpper at 0x06, tickLower at 0x03 and owner at 0 of free memory and hashes 58 bytes from offset 0x0c (src/libraries/Position.sol:54-66). I simulated the four overlapping writes on dirty memory for 2,000 random inputs with garbage above bit 160 of the owner. The result always equalled keccak256 of owner (20 bytes), tickLower (3), tickUpper (3) and salt (32), so the fields do not overlap and bits above the address fall outside the hashed range. The three words are zeroed afterwards. The owner is always msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161). The pool id is keccak256 of the five words of the PoolKey in memory (src/types/PoolId.sol:11-15). The struct reaches memory through the ABI decoder of the external functions, which rejects dirty address, uint24 and int24 words, so one logical pool has one id. Evidence: src/libraries/Position.sol:48-67; src/types/PoolId.sol:11-15; src/PoolManager.sol:117, 145, 161, 187, 256
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Assembly memory use and cleanup: the ERC-20 transfer block, the hook call, the wrapped revert, the scratch space users and the storage readers. Result: The ERC-20 transfer writes 68 bytes at the free memory pointer without moving it, evaluates the call before the return data test, accepts empty return data or at least 32 bytes whose first word is 1, and zeroes the three words it used (src/types/Currency.sol:55-80). The output area is scratch word 0, and with empty return data the test does not read it. callHook allocates 32 bytes plus the return size rounded up to 32 after the call, which I checked for sizes 0 to 399, and copies the full return data (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:140-149). bubbleUpAndRevertWith lays out selector, address, selector word, the two offsets 0x80 and 0xa0 plus the padded size, the reason and a 4 byte context, and then reverts, so its use of memory past the pointer has no later reader (src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119). The delta slot hash and flipTick use only bytes 0 to 63 (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:11-15, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:67-70). The revert helpers that take one argument write bytes 0 to 0x23, which is still scratch space (CustomRevert.sol:14-46). ## Reading of the source (invariants-settlement)

- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Which invariants of flash accounting and custody does the code enforce, and where. This is the list that the other items of this unit try to break. Result: I1, lock. Every function that writes a delta carries onlyWhenUnlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:96-99 and the modifiers at 147, 189, 258, 291, 300, 305, 310, 322, 332). The flag is set only at line 107, cleared only at line 113, and unlock reverts when it is already set (105). I2, closure. unlock returns only when NonzeroDeltaCount is zero (112). _accountDelta raises the counter when a slot leaves zero and lowers it when a slot returns to zero (368-378), so the counter equals the number of nonzero (account, currency) slots. I3, credits. A positive delta comes from four places only: settle, which adds msg.value when no ERC-20 is synced or the checked rise of balanceOf since sync (349-364); burn, which lowers an ERC-6909 balance by the same amount (332-336, src/ERC6909.sol:85-89); a pool action whose amounts Pool computes (159-183, 206-226, 268-270); and a hook delta that is subtracted from the caller in the same step (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:230, 242, 312). I4, debits. take and mint debit the nominal amount before any external call (294, 326). clear can only bring a positive delta to zero (310-319). I5, custody. The PoolManager sends assets only through Currency.transfer in take (295) and in collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56), each after an equal bookkeeping decrease (294 and ProtocolFees.sol:55). I6, one payment bracket. There is one synced currency slot. sync overwrites it (286) or resets it for the native asset (283), an ERC-20 settle resets it (361), and settle rejects msg.value while it is set (356). I7, claims. ERC-6909 balances change only in transfer, transferFrom, _mint and _burn with checked arithmetic (src/ERC6909.sol:25-48, 79-89). From I1 to I7 it follows that for every currency id the PoolManager balance stays at or above pool reserves plus claims plus accrued protocol fees, as long as four properties of the chain and the token hold: T1, balanceOf(PoolManager) of a currency changes only by transfers to or from the PoolManager and by the transferred amount; T2, no second currency id draws on the same balance in another unit; T3, msg.value arrives in full; T4, transient storage is one store per transaction that follows call and revert semantics. The code checks none of T1 to T4. Exhaustive search for a sequence of unlock, sync, settle, settleFor, take, clear, mint, burn, ERC-6909 transfer and direct payment by one account that leaves the account richer or the PoolManager short, in seven currency settings. Result: I wrote a state model of the settlement layer from the source lines and explored every reachable state, with claims per id capped at 2 and each delta capped at plus or minus 4, amounts 0, 1 and 2, and the whole sequence treated as one transaction so that a sync survives between unlocks. The search asserts in every state that the counter equals the number of nonzero delta slots and never goes below zero. Settings and results: native plus ERC-20, 35,859 states, no gain; native plus an ERC-20 face that mirrors the native balance one to one and can transfer (CELO token shape), with native sends that reach the PoolManager without a call, 31,628 states, no gain; the same face without a working transfer (Polygon 0x1010 and LegacyERC20ETH shape), 9,709 states, no gain; a face that reports floor(native / 3) and moves 3 base units per unit, without forced native sends, 48,488 states, no gain; a wrapper that credits the sender of native value (WETH9 shape), 214,118 states, no gain; a deposit ledger that credits the sender and has no transfer (EntryPoint shape), 10,872 states, no gain. In none of these did the PoolManager end below its obligations. The one setting with a gain is the scaled face together with forced native sends, which is recorded in the Arc item below. - all 21 networks, cycle 2. Re-entry into someone else's unlock: a recipient of a native payout, a token with callbacks or a hook gets control while a victim is between its pool action, sync, payment and settle. Can it take the victim's payment, make the victim pay twice, or leave the victim without what it paid for. Result: The victim script is unlock, an action that leaves it owing 1 unit and holding a claim, sync of the currency, payment, settle, return. The attacker may run up to two operations of its own in each of the six gaps, which is more than any real callback allows. Five settings were searched to the end: ERC-20 payment (2,235,193 states, 157 completed runs), native payment (1,211,637 and 130), payment through a one to one native face (1,696,802 and 48), native payment on a chain that has such a face (943,455 and 50), payment through a scaled face (3,811,569 and 393). In every completed run the attacker's wallet did not grow, the victim paid exactly its amount and kept its claim. Runs in which the attacker booked the victim's payment with settleFor, re-synced, or reset the sync with sync(address(0)) all end with a nonzero slot and revert at src/PoolManager.sol:112. A callee can therefore make the surrounding unlock revert, which it could also do by reverting itself, and cannot change who is credited in a transaction that succeeds. - all 21 networks, cycle 2. A stale sync: sync needs no lock, and its two slots are the only settlement state that can outlive an unlock. What can a party gain from a sync left behind inside one transaction, and what would follow if a network failed to wipe transient storage between transactions. Result: unlock ends with the flag false and the counter zero or it reverts (src/PoolManager.sol:105-113), so after any successful call the lock flag and all deltas are zero and only the synced currency and reserves can remain (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-32). The model treats a whole sequence as one transaction and found no gain from a sync that survives between unlocks. The effects that remain are these. A later settle with msg.value reverts with NonzeroNativeValue until someone calls sync again (src/PoolManager.sol:356). collectProtocolFees for that ERC-20 reverts (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52). The next settle without a new sync credits the caller with every rise of that balance since the stale sync, which inside one transaction can only be the caller's own payment or an inflow it triggered. If a network kept transient storage across transactions, the same reading gives two consequences and no more: native payers who do not call sync first would revert until the slot is reset, and a party could leave a sync in one transaction and book unsolicited inflows, such as a positive rebase, in a later one. Deposits of other users are not exposed, because every ERC-20 settle resets the slot and every payer that follows the interface comment calls sync first (src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:165-171). A leak of the lock flag or of a delta across transactions would be a different and total failure, and the code gives no path to it under call and revert semantics. Protocol fee collection at a moment chosen by an outsider, on networks where the controller is an adapter with a public collect function: before a sync, between sync and settle, inside an unlock, and on networks where the native asset has an ERC-20 face. Result: I added a third party fee withdrawal of one unit, allowed at any point except for the ERC-20 that is currently synced, to the model and searched the native plus ERC-20 setting (75,072 states), the one to one face setting (67,659) and the scaled face setting (100,064). No sequence gave the attacker a gain or left the PoolManager below its remaining obligations. The reading agrees: collectProtocolFees lowers protocolFeesAccrued with a checked subtraction before it transfers (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56), writes no delta and no transient slot, and reverts for the synced ERC-20 in both lock states (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52), so it can neither raise a settle credit nor pay out more than was accrued. _isUnlocked is declared and never called (src/ProtocolFees.sol:60, src/PoolManager.sol:392-394). That can only happen inside the transaction of the party that holds the bracket. - Arc, cycle 2. Arc: USDC is the native asset with 18 decimals and also answers at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 with 6 decimals. The face rounds down, so a settle bracket on the face can credit one face unit for less than 10^12 base units. How much can an ordinary account take that way. Result: In the model, a face that reports floor(native / S) gives a gain only when native value can reach the PoolManager without a call while the face is synced. Each round is sync(face), a forced send of the missing base units, settle, and a native take that restores the remainder, and it turns a native debt of 1 base unit into a credit of 1 face unit, a gain of at most S - 1 base units. With S = 3 the search found a sequence of 7 rounds inside one unlock that took all 13 base units of the toy PoolManager, so the mechanism is real and repeatable. Without forced sends the gain is zero, because settle rejects msg.value while the face is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356), the PoolManager has no receive or fallback function, and the face moves whole units only. On Arc S is 10^12 base units, which is 0.000001 USDC. At block 32,594,756 the PoolManager held 2,444,955,282,313,718,484,324,471 base units and the face reported 2,444,955,282,313, which is the floor of that figure divided by 10^12. The base fee was 20 gwei in each of 21 consecutive blocks ending at 32,597,012 and eth_gasPrice returned 25 gwei. A call that carries value costs at least 9,000 gas, which is 1.8 * 10^14 base units at 20 gwei, about 180 times the largest possible gain of one round, before the cost of sync, settle, take and the forced send. An account that pays the base fee loses money on every round. I did not test whether a forced send by SELFDESTRUCT is accepted on Arc; the stablecoin unit reports that it is. This agrees with the earlier clearance by that unit and adds the per round bound and the fee figures. Width and sign at the settlement entry points: amounts of 2^127 or more, accumulation of many deltas in one slot, an id with high bits in mint and burn, and the three unchecked blocks in PoolManager.sol. Result: take, mint, burn, clear and settle convert the amount with SafeCast.toInt128, which reverts for 2^127 or more (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59; src/PoolManager.sol:294, 313, 326, 334, 364). The unchecked blocks at lines 292, 316 and 323 cover only the negation of a value that is at most 2^127 - 1 and calls to functions whose own arithmetic stays checked, since a called function does not inherit the block. A delta slot holds an int256 and is updated with a checked addition (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:37), and each update is below 2^127 in size, so a slot cannot wrap. mint and burn truncate the id to 160 bits and use the truncated value for both the delta and the claim (src/PoolManager.sol:324-327, 333-335; src/types/Currency.sol:110-118). clear compares the int128 amount with the int256 slot, so it succeeds only for an exact positive match or for zero against zero (310-319), which is what test/PoolManager.clear.t.sol expects in its seven cases. - Arc, cycle 2. Arc: the CallFrom precompile at 0x1800000000000000000000000000000000000003 starts a call on behalf of Memo and Multicall3From. Does that inner call run with transient storage of its own, which would separate PoolManager deltas from payouts inside one unlock, and can a contract in the middle of a transaction use it to act as another account at the PoolManager. Result: No to both, in the main branch of the client. The precompile builds an ordinary CALL input with the chosen sender as caller and zero value (call_from.rs, decode_child_call). ArcEvm::init_subcall rejects static context and value, rejects a substituted sender that is neither the calling helper nor the transaction signer, and then pushes the child through the same frame stack and the same journal as every other call, with a journal checkpoint taken from that journal (evm.rs, init_subcall and complete_subcall). A child frame on the same journal sees and writes the same transient storage as its parent, so the lock flag, the deltas and the counter of the PoolManager stay one consistent store (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:12-34). Memo passes msg.sender as the sender (Memo.sol, memo), which closes the part the stablecoin unit left unread. A contract that is not the signer therefore cannot reach the PoolManager as someone else, and the ERC-6909 functions that trust msg.sender (src/ERC6909.sol:25-64) keep their meaning. I read the main branch and did not confirm which release mainnet runs, and I did not read revm itself for where transient storage lives; the stablecoin unit did. Tempo: from hardfork T5 three precompiles on the Implicit Approval List (FeeManager, StablecoinDEX, TIP20ChannelReserve) may move TIP-20 tokens out of any account without an allowance through system_transfer_from. Can an ordinary account make one of them pull tokens out of the PoolManager, which would lower a balance without a take. Result: No path found in the client source at commit 697ea97. system_transfer_from is not part of the token ABI and accepts only a listed precompile as caller (tip20/mod.rs:939-980). Every call site passes the direct caller of the precompile as the account to pull from: the DEX in transfer_from and decrement_balance_or_transfer_from, which its dispatcher feeds with msg_sender for place, placeFlip, withdraw, cancel and both swaps (stablecoin_dex/mod.rs:299-352, stablecoin_dex/dispatch.rs:17-66); the fee AMM in two places with msg_sender (tip_fee_manager/amm.rs:239 and 360); the channel reserve in two places with msg_sender (tip20_channel_reserve/mod.rs:215 and 380). Custody rule I5 of this unit therefore holds on Tempo apart from issuer roles, which are recorded elsewhere. - all 21 networks, cycle 8. Invariants of flash accounting and custody as this checkout writes them, restated for the opcode focus of this cycle: which instructions each settlement statement depends on, and whether any edge of those instructions can change a credit, a debit, the counter or the lock. Result: The invariants are the seven of cycle 2 (lock, closure, credits, debits, custody, one payment bracket, claims) and the four chain properties T1 to T4, and I found nothing in the current text that changes them. I read src/PoolManager.sol:96-114 and 279-384, src/libraries/Lock.sol:8-27, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:9-34, CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41, CurrencyReserves.sol:11-38, src/types/Currency.sol:40-118, src/ERC6909.sol:25-89, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22, src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59 and src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-70. The settlement path uses few instructions. The delta slot is KECCAK256 of two masked 32 byte words at memory 0 (CurrencyDelta.sol:12-14). The four fixed slots are literals. TLOAD and TSTORE hold the flag, the counter, the deltas and the bracket. The counter moves by ADD and SUB of 1 (NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:21, 31). The delta update is a checked int256 addition (CurrencyDelta.sol:37), so the compiler adds signed comparisons. The credit is a checked subtraction of two balances (PoolManager.sol:360). Every amount passes the cast at SafeCast.sol:56-59, which is a GT style comparison against 2^127. The counter cannot pass below zero: _accountDelta returns on a zero delta (PoolManager.sol:369), it decrements only when next is zero, which means previous was -delta and nonzero, and it increments only when previous is zero (373-377). Every input delta is below 2^127 in size, so the int256 sum at CurrencyDelta.sol:37 would need more than 2^128 calls to overflow. clear compares an int128 with the int256 slot value and can only bring a positive slot to zero (PoolManager.sol:310-319). mint and burn use the masked id currency.toId() for the claim and the truncated currency for the delta, so both sides name the same currency (PoolManager.sol:322-336, Currency.sol:110-118). None of these depends on SAR, SIGNEXTEND, SDIV, SMOD, MULMOD or BYTE. KECCAK256 over 64 bytes, TLOAD, TSTORE, ADD, SUB, AND and the comparisons are in the 185,529 vector battery that OPCODES.md reports clean on all 21 networks. The rollback behaviour of TSTORE inside the PoolManager's own frames is not covered by that battery and is tested in the next item. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:349-378
- all 21 networks, cycle 8. T4 on the deployed PoolManager of each network: after an unlock that fails inside a caller's frame (callback REVERT, callback out of gas, callback INVALID, callback that returns with an open delta), are the lock flag, the nonzero delta counter, the caller's delta slot, the synced currency slot and the caller's ERC-6909 balance back to zero, so that the caller cannot go on to call take, mint or burn without the closure check. Also: does a nested unlock revert, does settle with value revert while an ERC-20 is synced, and does take outside unlock revert. Result: Yes on all 21 networks. A driver placed by code override at an address with no code calls the deployed PoolManager seven times with eth_call; nothing is deployed or sent. In each callback the driver first calls mint(driver, 1, 1), which opens a delta of -1 for currency id 1 and writes a claim. Read from inside the callback before the revert, the lock flag was 1, the counter 1 and the delta slot -1 on every network, so the writes happened. After each failed unlock the driver read all five values through exttload and balanceOf and got zero on every network, for REVERT, for out of gas at 300,000 gas, for INVALID and for a callback that returned with the delta open, which unlock rejected with CurrencyNotSettled (0x5212cba1, src/PoolManager.sol:112). A callback that minted and burned the same amount returned success and left all five values zero. A nested unlock from inside the callback reverted with AlreadyUnlocked (0x5090d6c6, src/PoolManager.sol:105). After sync(0x04) inside the callback the synced currency slot held 0x04, and settle with 1 wei reverted with NonzeroNativeValue (0xb0ec849e, src/PoolManager.sol:356). take(address(0), driver, 0) after all of this reverted with ManagerLocked (0x54e3ca0d, src/PoolManager.sol:96-99). This confirms that inner writes are undone when the outer frame fails and that the lock cannot be left open by a caught failure, on the code path that eth_call uses on each endpoint. - all 21 networks, cycle 8. T3 on the deployed PoolManager of each network: does msg.value sent with settle arrive in the PoolManager's balance by the same amount inside the same frame, and does a native take of the same amount restore the balance, so that the credit at src/PoolManager.sol:354 matches a real payment. Result: Yes on all 21 networks. Inside the callback the driver read BALANCE(PoolManager), called settle with 5 base units, read it again, took 5 base units back with take(address(0), driver, 5), read it a third time and reverted. The second reading was the first plus 5 and the third equal to the first on every network, from 0 on Tempo (the driver's balance came from the state override) to about 3.18 * 10^24 on Polygon. The counter was 1 after settle and 0 after take. The PoolManager therefore sees the value as payment in the same unit as SELFBALANCE and BALANCE report it, and the native payout at src/types/Currency.sol:48 moves the stated amount. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/008/core-code-invariants-settlement.work/t4/rollback_all.json, field native and mode 6 of each network
- Monad, cycle 8. Monad compiles frequently used contracts to x86 code, and eth_call runs the interpreter, so the probe above did not run the compiled path. Do compiled TSTORE and TLOAD keep the same rollback as the interpreter. Result: Yes, by reading the client source on the main branch. The x86 emitter compiles TLOAD and TSTORE to calls of the runtime functions runtime::tload and runtime::tstore (emitter.hpp lines 492-501, dispatched from x86.cpp lines 250-254). The interpreter calls the same runtime::tstore (instruction_table.hpp lines 1357-1375). runtime::tstore exits with an error under a static call and otherwise calls host set_transient_storage, and tload calls get_transient_storage (storage.hpp lines 38-62). The host writes into the current account state of the versioned State object (state.cpp lines 326-329 and 409-413), which is the version stack that the cycle 3 reading found to be popped on a failed frame. Compiled and interpreted code therefore share one transient store and one rollback, and the probe result holds for both. The remaining gap is that I did not confirm that main equals the mainnet release v0.16.5; web3_clientVersion on rpc.monad.xyz returned Monad/unknown. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/emitter.hpp; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86.cpp; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/interpreter/instruction_table.hpp; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/runtime/storage.hpp; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/execution/ethereum/state3/state.cpp
- Polygon, cycle 8. Bor puts two shared caches in front of the interpreter: a cache of KECCAK256 results for 64 byte inputs and a jump destination analysis cache shared by the BlockSTM V2 workers and the prefetcher. Every delta slot (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:12-14), every ERC-6909 balance and allowance slot and every mapping slot of the pools is a 64 byte KECCAK256 input. Can either cache return a wrong slot or a wrong jump answer for the PoolManager. Result: No, as read at tags v2.11.0, v2.11.1 and develop. opKeccak256 uses the cache only when the input is exactly 64 bytes, keys it by the whole 64 bytes copied into an array, and stores a common.Hash value, which Go copies, so the shared hasher buffer cannot alias a stored entry (instructions.go lines 259-290 at v2.11.1, evm.go line 179 for the type of hasherBuf). The cache is a sync.Map with a size cap, and a speculative execution that is later discarded can only leave entries that are true hashes, because the value is a pure function of the key (keccak_cache.go, bounded_cache.go). The jump destination cache is keyed by the code hash as in go-ethereum and stores the bitmap computed from that code (contract.go lines 82-112). A collision in either cache needs a KECCAK256 collision. I could not confirm which bor release the endpoint runs; polygon.drpc.org answers web3_clientVersion with Geth/v10.0.0/drpc. The 64 byte cache is present at all three revisions read. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/instructions.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/keccak_cache.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/bounded_cache.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/contract.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/evm.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.0/core/vm/instructions.go
- all 21 networks, cycle 8. Re-entry through the four places where the PoolManager hands control to outside code while settlement state is open: the unlock callback, hooks, the ERC-20 transfer and balanceOf of a currency, and the recipient of a native take. Does any of them run before the PoolManager has written the debit or after it has read a value it then trusts. Result: No ordering gap in the current text. take writes the debit before the transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295). mint writes the debit before the claim (326-327) and burn writes the credit before the burn, and the burn reverts the whole call when the balance or allowance is short (334-335, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22, src/ERC6909.sol:85-89). _settle reads the synced currency, rejects value for an ERC-20, reads the balance, resets the slot and then credits, and the only outside call in it is the balanceOf staticcall, which cannot write state (349-364, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). sync makes the same staticcall and then writes both slots (279-288). Hooks run inside the pool functions and their deltas are booked after the hook returns (178-183, 221-226, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-160). A re-entering party shares the lock but not the caller's delta slots, which are keyed by msg.sender (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16), and unlock returns only when every slot of every party is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:112). The cycle 2 victim and two account searches cover the sequences; this item confirms that the text they model has not changed in the lines they cite. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:291-336

The proxy forwards take, settle, mint, burn and clear by delegatecall and expects them to run, so the double is consistent with production functions that accept delegatecall. I checked whether the missing modifier matters for funds. A delegatecall runs PoolManager code against the storage, transient storage and balance of the calling contract. The lock flag, the deltas, the claims and every transfer then belong to that contract. Nothing held by the PoolManager can be reached this way. The same holds for an account that points an EIP-7702 delegation at the PoolManager, because the delegated code runs in the context of that account. EIP-7702 says that CALL loads the code at the delegated address and executes it in the context of the authority, and EIP-7 says that the call created by DELEGATECALL has the same sender and value as the original call. I fetched both texts in this session. I did not test how the client of each network implements DELEGATECALL and delegation, so for the 20 networks other than Ethereum this rests on the two specifications. ProtocolFeesImplementation mirrors ProtocolFees without change and adds a lock toggle that nothing reads. - all 21 networks, cycle 3. The test double src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol puts noDelegateCall on unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint and burn, and the production PoolManager does not. Is that a gap in the source. Result: No. The proxy exists to delegatecall into the real manager, and test/NoDelegateCall.t.sol:63-82 expects DelegateCallNotAllowed only from modifyLiquidity, swap and donate, which carry the modifier at PoolManager.sol:148, 190 and 259, as does initialize at line 117. No test expects the modifier on the other functions. A delegatecall into take, settle, mint, burn, clear or unlock runs the manager's code on the storage, transient storage and balance of the calling contract, so it can move only what that contract holds and cannot reach a pool. The proxy also differs from the manager in the position of the Initialize event (ProxyPoolManager.sol:90-94 against PoolManager.sol:136-141), so it is not kept as an exact mirror. ## Reading of the source (theme-callvalue-without-debit)

- all 21 networks, cycle 3. On-chain differential for value semantics. A probe contract placed by state override made a CALL with 5 wei, a CALLCODE with 3 wei and a DELEGATECALL to a second probe that returns CALLVALUE, SELFBALANCE and BALANCE(CALLER). Runs: funded sender with value 7, funded sender with value 0, and an unfunded probe. Result: All 21 endpoints returned the Ethereum result. The CALL moved exactly 5 wei from caller to callee and the callee read CALLVALUE 5. The CALLCODE frame read CALLVALUE 3 with the caller's balance unchanged. The DELEGATECALL frame read the parent's CALLVALUE with no balance change. From an account with balance 0 the CALL and the CALLCODE with value failed. On Tempo the run with transaction value was rejected with 'value transfer not allowed' and the run with an overridden balance behaved as on Ethereum. CALLCODE and DELEGATECALL frames show value without a debit on every client by design. They run in the caller's own storage, so they cannot set msg.value inside the PoolManager, which makes no DELEGATECALL or CALLCODE (src/types/Currency.sol:48 and 73 and src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134 are its only raw calls). A value CALL from an account lowers that account's balance by the value on every endpoint, which answers the second half of lead L-203 for ordinary recipients. Evidence: eth_call with state overrides on the 21 RPC endpoints of state/networks.json, block latest, 2026-11-22
- all 21 networks, cycle 3. Whether the PoolManager can be made to call itself with value, which would give a frame with CALLVALUE and no net debit on any client, and whether the deployed contracts accept plain value. Result: No. The only value-bearing call in src is the native payout call(gas(), to, amount, 0, 0, 0, 0) with empty calldata (src/types/Currency.sol:48). Token transfers and hook calls pass value 0 (src/types/Currency.sol:73, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134) and the unlock callback is a plain high-level call (src/PoolManager.sol:110). The contract has no receive or fallback function, so empty calldata reverts and a take of native currency to the PoolManager's own address fails. On all 21 endpoints a call with value 1 and empty calldata to the PoolManager reverted with empty data, both from a funded account and with the PoolManager as sender, and settle() and settleFor(address) with value reverted with ManagerLocked (0x54e3ca0d). Evidence: src/types/Currency.sol:44-52, src/PoolManager.sol:104-114 and 300-307; eth_call on the 21 RPC endpoints, 2026-11-22
- all 21 networks, cycle 3. SELFDESTRUCT to a third party, to self and to the PoolManager: does any client credit the beneficiary without emptying the source, and does a forced credit give anyone a native delta. Result: On all 21 endpoints a probe with 9 wei that self-destructs to a third address ended with balance 0 and the target with 9, and the same toward the PoolManager raised the PoolManager balance by exactly 9 with no code run. A forced credit is credited to nobody because native credit is msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354) and sync(address(0)) stores no balance (src/PoolManager.sol:281-283). Self-destruct to self kept the 9 wei on 19 endpoints, reverted on Arc (the client rejects source equal to target) and left 0 on Monad. I did not establish whether the Monad result is a burn rule or an effect of the state override. The PoolManager bytecode has no SELFDESTRUCT, so neither case reaches it. Evidence: eth_call with state overrides on the 21 RPC endpoints, 2026-11-22; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/circlefin/arc-node/main/crates/evm/src/opcode.rs lines 64 to 143
- Ethereum, cycle 3. Ethereum: system caller rule in go-ethereum and whether anything a public account sends runs with caller 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe. Result: go-ethereum master skips the balance check and the transfer for that caller. Its only uses as caller are the EIP-4788, EIP-2935 and request queue calls, each with value zero and a fixed target. revm, which the queried endpoint runs (reth v2.11.0), moves value for every caller: the frame calls transfer_loaded, which fails with OutOfFunds when the balance is short, and its system call builder sets no value. The address holds 42 wei on mainnet and a funded probe call from it moved value normally on this endpoint. - Optimism, Base, Unichain, Zora, Worldchain, Ink, Soneium, cycle 3. OP Stack chains with ETH gas: can a deposit transaction with a mint field, or any predeploy, give a frame value that its sender did not pay. Result: No. op-revm adds the mint to the sender's balance, subtracts gas spending and leaves the value to the frame transfer, which fails when the balance is short. The branch that lifts the balance to the transaction value runs only when the balance check is disabled in configuration, which the code marks as not consensus critical and used in testing. The Base handler at v1.5.6 and the op-revm commit that World Chain pins have the same text. op-geth adds the mint and then checks CanTransfer for the value. The mint equals the ETH locked on Ethereum: depositTransaction with 0.001 ETH succeeded in eth_call on the OP Mainnet and Base portals. A deposit sender equal to the system address would need an Ethereum contract at 0xeeeeffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffeeed or a signature for the system address. ETHLiquidity, SuperchainETHBridge, NativeAssetLiquidity and LiquidityController hold 0 native balance on all seven chains, so no predeploy can release native value. All seven endpoints rejected an unfunded call with value from the system address with OutOfFunds.
