- X Layer, cycle 4. Securitize wrappers on X Layer (v4CRCL, v4MSTR, v4COIN, v4HOOD, v4VOLOROST2) and the multiplier tokens BMNRx and ANTx: does a payout from the PoolManager count against a limit of the wrapper or of the Securitize token behind it. Result: No limit found. The wrappers expose allow list, hook list and wrapper list functions and no limit or rate function. A payout from the PoolManager to an address that the wrapper permits burns the wrapper token and moves the Securitize token from the wrapper to the recipient. In the traced payout of half the v4MSTR balance to 0x10b5b66491d8f91310a85b49cf7a15ef6bbc936a the wrapper wrote its total supply and the PoolManager balance, the Securitize token wrote four balance words, and the compliance contract 0x2fc11ad109c41ab1d347d45d32a31eb3d09e66f6 was called and wrote nothing. A payout of the full balance also updates the wallet list of the Securitize token. Transfers to addresses outside the allow list revert with TRANSFER_FAILED, so an account without Securitize onboarding cannot do the round trip at all. BMNRx and ANTx had a clean round trip diff. Evidence: rpc eth_getLogs on https://rpc.xlayer.tech blocks 76,638,564 and 76,638,591; debug_traceCall (prestateTracer and callTracer) on https://xlayer.drpc.org; selector lookup at https://api.openchain.xyz/signature-database/v1/lookup
- Ink, Base, Worldchain, Soneium, Celo, HyperEVM, Tempo, cycle 4. Tokens that refuse a transfer of the full PoolManager balance: is the refusal a quota that other users share. Result: No, apart from ViciCoin on Polygon. ChimeraToken404 tokens on Ink (WIRED, BLOOP, CHIMERIA, GM+) revert with SYNC_LIMIT when one transfer changes the NFT count of a party that has not opted out by more than 64 units. The PoolManager is opted out at initialisation and cannot change that, so the rule binds the recipient of one transfer and a smaller take or an opted out recipient passes. BSTONK and VCAT on Base revert with MaxWalletExceeded for the recipient. In the BSTONK source the PoolManager is exempt at construction and a launcher role can remove the exemption, which is an issuer power. I did not read the VCAT source. BEAN on Base fails only when the test recipient has contract code, and fee on transfer tokens fail on the return leg of my probe because the recipient received less than it tries to send back. The remaining refusals are issuer or author states: IDRX, WRC, CAKE and DogeX on World Chain are paused or locked, Mikami on World Chain answers Sender is frozen for the PoolManager, whose balance is 15,912e18 base units, MOCHI refuses the recipient, RSNC on Soneium is non transferable, rii on Celo has transfers locked, nine HyperEVM tokens revert with InvalidTransfer for every amount, and THBT on Base refuses the test recipient with AccountInvalid. Evidence: https://explorer.inkonchain.com/api/v2/smart-contracts/0xE2F8d7bE0f19a6F00Bf4dd8adA9422Ef617d8806 (ChimeraToken404 _sync and MAX_SYNC); https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/8453/0x0f61edbfe6cd86024c0f210c0695b08df55fdfc9?fields=sources,proxyResolution,compilation (AdvancedLaunchToken); rpc eth_call from the PoolManager address on the endpoints of chain ids 57073, 8453, 480, 1868, 42220, 999 and 4217, 2026-11-23; https://api.openchain.xyz/signature-database/v1/lookup
- Tempo, cycle 4. Tempo storage credits (TIP-1060): the PoolManager has one credit balance at 0x1060000000000000000000000000000000000000 that every user of the PoolManager shares. Can an ordinary account use it up, and what does the next user lose. Result: Gas only. Clearing a PoolManager slot mints one credit for the PoolManager account, and the clearing refund of EIP-3529 is zero on Tempo. Creating a PoolManager slot costs 245,000 gas more unless a credit is available, in which case the sender of that transaction gets the amount back at the end of the transaction. balanceOf(PoolManager) at the precompile returned 13 at block 50,377,344. Any account can spend these credits by creating slots it pays 5,000 gas for, such as ERC-6909 balances of one base unit under fresh ids (src/PoolManager.sol:322-328). A liquidity provider who clears slots when leaving gets no refund, and the next creator of a slot gets the benefit or pays the full price. No call fails and no balance moves. The same counter exists per token: a transfer to a new holder used one credit of stcUSD (2 to 1) in my trace and a round trip restored it. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tempoxyz/tempo/main/tips/tip-1060.md; https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/releases/tag/v1.10.1 (TIP-1060 listed in the T7 upgrade); rpc eth_call balanceOf and eth_getStorageAt on 0x1060000000000000000000000000000000000000 and debug_traceCall on https://rpc.mainnet.tempo.xyz at block 50,377,344, client tempo/v1.19.0-697ea97
- Tempo, MegaETH, Monad, cycle 4. Network rules that could throttle the PoolManager address after another account used it: TIP-403 policies on Tempo, resource limits on MegaETH, the reserve balance on Monad. Result: None of them keeps state per called contract. A TIP-403 policy is a white list, a black list or a compound of three such lists, and isAuthorized is a view that reads set membership. It holds no amount, count or time, and only the policy admin changes it. MegaETH enforces compute gas, data size, KV update and state growth limits per transaction and per block and has no limit per account. The block limit on state growth is covered by F-042. The Monad reserve balance applies to externally owned accounts that pay gas, as an earlier cycle confirmed in the client source. Evidence: https://tempo.com/developers/docs/protocol/tip403/spec; https://docs.megaeth.com/spec/megaevm/resource-limits; https://docs.monad.xyz/developer-essentials/reserve-balance
- all 21 networks, cycle 4. Rate limited bridged tokens: do xERC20 limits, OFT rate limits, CCTP limits or Superchain token bridge limits sit on the plain transfer path that take uses. Result: No case found. In every bridged token I traced, a transfer between two holders changed two balance slots only. That includes USDT0 on Ink, Unichain, X Layer, MegaETH, HyperEVM and Tempo, USDC and bridged USDC.e and WBTC on the trace networks where the PoolManager holds them, and the Paxos tokens. AGL is an OFT whose limit of 1.8e19 AGL per send sits in the send path, and its transfer path was read in source. Bridge limits are read in mint, burn and send functions, which the PoolManager never calls (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75 calls transfer only). On the five networks without a trace endpoint this rests on the 25 round test. Evidence: debug_traceCall results of this unit on the sixteen trace endpoints; https://celo.blockscout.com/api/v2/smart-contracts/0x0000000000109de411eabc9f04906d79f06fda0e (AGL sharedDecimals and OFT send path)

## Reading of the source (theme-assigned-balance)

- Optimism, Base, Unichain, Zora, Worldchain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Avalanche, Monad, MegaETH, Tempo, Arc, HyperEVM, cycle 5. Lead L-319 on the eighteen networks other than Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and Polygon: is there a pooled token where an ordinary account can assign units to the PoolManager that balanceOf counts and transfer cannot move. Method: code of every currency with a balance was grouped by selector set (own code plus implementation behind the usual proxy slots), every function with a name that suggests locking, vesting, staking, granting, minting, distributing, claiming, burning or transferring was called by an ordinary account that had just received a third of the PoolManager balance, with the PoolManager as address argument, and a stub at the PoolManager address then tried to send out the full balance and the balance minus the amount. Result: No token on these networks ended a trial with a higher reported balance and a refused full transfer. Coverage: Optimism 1594 tokens, 403 families, 7242 trials; Base 9108 tokens, 594 families, 10487 trials; Unichain 4562 tokens, 247 families, 2830 trials; Zora 41 tokens, 18 families, 302 trials; Worldchain 851 tokens, 271 families, 3600 trials; Ink 3438 tokens, 184 families, 2794 trials; Soneium 70 tokens, 53 families, 806 trials; Celo 92 tokens, 43 families, 700 trials; X Layer 96 tokens, 27 families, 512 trials; Arbitrum One 5502 tokens, 1188 families, 20591 trials; Robinhood Chain 738773 tokens, 7616 families, 80866 trials; Elysium 129491 tokens, 577 families, 6606 trials; Avalanche 1841 tokens, 521 families, 9100 trials; Monad 8375 tokens, 405 families, 6452 trials; MegaETH 67 tokens, 32 families, 559 trials; Tempo 73 tokens, 19 families, 237 trials; Arc 261204 tokens, 1143 families, 11682 trials; HyperEVM 262 tokens, 68 families, 934 trials. On Robinhood Chain the 294,326 distinct code hashes were covered through one token per hash shared by more than three tokens (2,156 hashes, 440,634 tokens) and three sampled tokens per code size for the rest (5,551 sizes), so a rare one off contract there can have been missed. Tokens that run as precompiles (TIP-20 on Tempo, B20 on Base) have no selectors in code and were covered only by the full balance transfer test and by the earlier source readings. Limits everywhere: names come from a public signature database that knew 85,092 of 137,912 selectors, arguments follow fixed patterns, and a lock that only takes effect later or needs a second token as deposit is not seen. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-assigned-balance.work/raw/summary.json:1
- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Does the PoolManager already hold units that it cannot send. Full balance transfer test: a measuring stub at the PoolManager address (state override, eth_call) sent the whole balance of every currency to an address without code and read both balances after. Result: Refused per network: Ethereum 1119 of 60024, Optimism 110 of 1594, Base 27 of 9108, Unichain 37 of 4562, Zora 0 of 41, Worldchain 43 of 851, Ink 39 of 3438, Soneium 1 of 70, Celo 3 of 92, X Layer 5 of 96, Arbitrum One 178 of 5502, Robinhood Chain 2439 of 738773, Elysium 14 of 129491, Polygon 104 of 6776, BNB Smart Chain 21 of 3369, Avalanche 20 of 1841, Monad 62 of 8375, MegaETH 0 of 67, Tempo 1 of 73, Arc 115 of 261204, HyperEVM 9 of 262. For the seventeen generator tokens and the two QANX contracts the frozen and locked readings for the PoolManager are zero. The refusals with a price above 1,000 USD are whole balance states set by an issuer or author (block, pause, recipient rule), and the five largest are in the issuer finding of this unit. Others seen: VIBESTR on Ethereum, which rejects nonzero transfers outside its own trading flow, G$ on Celo, BSTONK, BEAN and THBT on Base, PGOLD on Arbitrum One with the message blacklist, PNIC on Avalanche, uPEG on Ethereum where a large transfer runs out of gas and one unit passes, and the Polygon system token at 0x1010. I classed only the refusals above 1,000 USD. On Robinhood Chain the 2,439 refusals spread over 972 distinct code hashes. In a sample of 60 of them repeated one by one, 26 accepted the transfer on the second attempt, 17 refused the full balance and accepted one base unit with a custom error, which fits a limit on the amount per transfer or per recipient and would also fit a locked part, 14 refused every amount and 3 ran out of gas or gave another result. I did not class them further. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-assigned-balance.work/xfer_sweep.py:1
- Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Zora, Worldchain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer, Arbitrum One, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Monad, MegaETH, Tempo, HyperEVM, cycle 5. Part two: can any transfer start a rise of the reported balance, as an automatic rebase or a reflection does. - Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Arbitrum One, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Monad, cycle 5. Part three: public triggers of a rebase on pooled tokens beyond the named ones. For 114 tokens with rebasing indicators on eleven networks (rebase, gonsForBalance, stakingContract with index, monetaryPolicy, rebaseOptIn, rewardMultiplier) the related contracts were read from public getters, and every function with at most two simple arguments on them was called by an ordinary account while the PoolManager balance was measured. Result: The staking rebase is open to any caller on sVALUES 0x8d8b9044662644e2502e4a6747846f6b0fdaf0bd on Polygon (1,133.70 pooled), on sOHM 0x04906695d6d12cf5459975d7c3c03356e4ccd460 (249.39 pooled), the older sOHM 0x04f2694c8fcee23e8fd0dfea1d4f5bb8c352111f (12.37) and sVEC 0x66d5c66e7c83e0682d947176534242c9f19b3365 (135.07) on Ethereum, and on sT 0x14194a883fc79af1180a9294dff9e6e8d8933330 on Arbitrum One (dust). The fourth word of epoch() is zero for all five, so the next rebase distributes nothing and nothing can be booked today. They join the class of the Polygon finding if distribution resumes. Of the named tokens, sKLIMA would rise by 851,020 base units and sNVB by 54,992,087 base units at the time of the test, and sLGNS, sATH and sSAC were not due. On the vaults of OUSD, OETH, their Base counterpart and Sperax USDs no call changed the PoolManager balance, which fits contracts being outside the rebase unless they opt in. Two Ethereum tokens named Ti have an owner contract with a public poke() that raised the calling account's balance and left the PoolManager balance unchanged. A trigger that needs more than two arguments or a contract two steps away from the token is not covered. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-assigned-balance.work/hop.py:1
- Ethereum, Optimism, Unichain, Worldchain, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Polygon, Monad, Arc, HyperEVM, cycle 5. Tokens where a call by an ordinary account raised the PoolManager balance at no cost to the caller (class free raise in the trial sweep). Result: Apart from TITHE these are tokens with a mint function open to any caller, mostly test tokens: 27 on Ethereum, 20 on Polygon, 19 on Robinhood Chain, 16 on Arbitrum One, 12 on Unichain, 5 each on Monad and Arc, 2 each on Optimism, World Chain and Elysium, 1 on HyperEVM. - Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum One, Monad, Soneium, cycle 5. Tokens with a pooled value above 10,000 USD whose function list contains lock, freeze, vest, cooldown or escrow words: FOLD, WLFI, sUSDe, sENA, apyUSD, aptUSD, syrupUSDC, syrupUSDT, yUSD, ondo, skl, DPR, AST, RNDR and TITANX on Ethereum, SPA on Arbitrum One, and the launch pad tokens with lockPool and vesting data on Base (blueagent, Surplus and about forty others). - Base, Tempo, Arc, cycle 5. Network native token standards: do B20 tokens on Base, TIP-20 tokens on Tempo or the USDC token of Arc count amounts in balanceOf that the holder cannot transfer, and can a third party assign such amounts. Result: No evidence of it. The B20 introduction describes an ERC-20 superset with roles, per feature pause, policies, mint, burn and seize, and names no held, locked or vesting balance. The full balance transfer from the PoolManager address succeeded for the B20 token OUSD on Base (5.33 million pooled), for 72 of 73 Tempo currencies (the exception is the token frozen by its issuer, already recorded) and for USDC on Arc. Earlier cycles listed every balance write of the TIP-20 precompile and found none that a third party can direct at the PoolManager. I did not read B20 or Arc node source for this question in this cycle. Evidence: https://docs.base.org/specifications/b20/introduction

## Reading of the source (theme-claim-operators)

- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Reading of the claim transfer and burn checks in this repository: src/ERC6909.sol:35-48 (transferFrom), src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22 (_burnFrom), src/PoolManager.sol:322-336 (mint and burn), src/types/Currency.sol:110-118 (toId and fromId), src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59. Result: transferFrom skips the allowance step only when msg.sender is the sender or isOperator[sender][msg.sender] is true. Otherwise it reads allowance[sender][msg.sender][id] and writes allowed - amount with checked arithmetic unless the allowance is the maximum uint256, so a spender without enough allowance reverts. The balance of the sender is reduced with checked arithmetic. _burnFrom applies the same test with from in place of sender and then calls _burn. PoolManager.burn credits the delta of msg.sender and burns from the named account, so an operator or spender receives the value of what it burns. That is the intended meaning of an approval. mint and burn truncate the id to 160 bits before use and transfer, transferFrom and approve use the full 256 bit id, so an id with high bits set can be held and approved and can never be burned. That strands only the holder's own claim. An operator right covers every id and both transferFrom and burn and has no expiry. I found no way in this code for an account without an approval to move another account's claims on any network. Evidence: src/ERC6909.sol:36
- Zora, Soneium, MegaETH, Tempo, cycle 5. OperatorSet (topic 0xceb576d9) and Approval (topic 0xb3fd5071) logs of the PoolManager over its whole history on Zora (blocks 25,434,534 to 54,369,267), Soneium (2,473,300 to 31,148,811), MegaETH (7,009,653 to 32,635,361) and Tempo (6,455,926 to 50,420,652), read twice on 23 November 2026 with no failed window. Result: Answer no on all four. The PoolManager has emitted no OperatorSet and no Approval log, so no address holds a right over another account's claims. - all 21 networks, cycle 5. Do the shared contracts that run command lists or batches for any caller hold an approval? I matched every operator and spender address of all 21 networks against Multicall3, Multicall2, Permit2, the Across MulticallHandler, the 1inch v6 router, the 0x exchange proxy and AllowanceHolder, the CoW settlement contract, the three ERC-4337 EntryPoint versions, the Safe MultiSend contracts, the LiFi diamond, the Kyber meta router, CreateX and every Uniswap contract listed in networks.json. Result: Six kinds of match, all without effect today. (1) The Universal Router is operator of owner 0xd7c7200e8d781013e16db8418ded4767a5beb598 on Robinhood Chain (0x8876789976decbfcbbbe364623c63652db8c0904) and holds allowances from three owners on Base (0x6ff5693b99212da76ad316178a184ab56d299b43, ids USDC, 0x2105 and 0). Its verified source rejects every v4 action other than swaps, SETTLE_ALL, TAKE_ALL, SETTLE, TAKE and TAKE_PORTION with UnsupportedAction (V4Router.sol:34-82 on Robinhood Chain, line 78 on Base) and its Dispatcher makes low level calls only to Permit2, the v3 position manager, the v4 PositionManager, itself and poolManager.initialize. Its token payments use the ERC-20 selectors, which the PoolManager does not have. Its bytecode has no constant for burn (0xf5298aca) or the ERC-6909 transferFrom (0xfe99049a), also in the shifted form the optimizer writes. (2) The PositionManager is operator of one owner on Base and spender for one id on BNB Smart Chain and on Robinhood Chain. It refuses actions 0x17 and 0x18 and has neither constant. (3) Permit2 is spender for one owner on Base and one on BNB Smart Chain. It calls transferFrom(address,address,uint256) with selector 0x23b872dd, which the PoolManager does not have. (4) The PoolManager itself is spender or operator for seven owners on Ethereum, Base, Unichain, Robinhood Chain, Monad and Elysium. It never calls itself. (5) The zero address is operator of one account on BNB Smart Chain and spender on Robinhood Chain, and the native token contract 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 is operator of one account on Polygon. None of these owners holds a claim, and the token contract makes only value transfers. (6) No Multicall, EntryPoint, bridge handler, aggregator or settlement contract of the list appears on any network. These approvals stay safe only while the approved code has no path to burn or transferFrom. The Actions library already reserves BURN_6909, so a later router that handles it with a payer chosen by the caller would make the existing approvals usable by anyone. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/4663/0x8876789976decbfcbbbe364623c63652db8c0904?fields=sources,compilation and https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/8453/0x6ff5693b99212da76ad316178a184ab56d299b43?fields=sources,compilation; research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/raw/triage_8453.json, triage_4663.json, triage_56.json
- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Call shape probe with a positive control. From an unrelated account, each approved contract whose owners hold claims was sent 25 shapes that wrap PoolManager.transferFrom(owner, receiver, id, amount): the four Multicall3 functions, execute, executeBatch, call, forward, exec, multicall, functionCall, invoke, the ERC-7821 and ERC-7579 execute modes, Safe multiSend and the inner calldata sent raw. Each shape ran with amount 1 and with amount balance plus 1, and a shape counts when the first succeeds and the second does not. Result: 489 contracts on 16 networks, no positive. Control on Ethereum: with a state override that makes Multicall3 an operator of a claim holder the probe reports aggregate, aggregate3, tryAggregate and aggregate3Value as positive, and without the override it reports none. Evidence: https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com eth_call with stateDiff override; research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/probe.py and raw/probe_<chainId>.json
- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Caller test of unlockCallback. For each of 714 approved contracts the same calldata was sent once with from set to the PoolManager and once from an unrelated account, with five payloads. A contract whose callback has no caller check can be driven by any account that has unlocked the PoolManager itself. Result: 309 contracts have an unlockCallback. 292 answer the two callers differently. 17 answer alike and were looked at one by one: 12 revert with the same custom error for both callers before any call to the PoolManager and their owners hold no claims or the trace reached nothing, 2 are the tx.origin bound contracts described for Ethereum and Arc, 2 are test contracts on Robinhood Chain whose callback returns without a caller check, which have no burn or transferFrom constant and whose owners hold no claims, and 1 on BNB Smart Chain has no burn or transferFrom constant. Limit: the test looks for the callback selector in the code at the approved address or at its EIP-7702 delegate. The 264 clone proxies (Bunni tokens and Panoptic collateral trackers) were therefore covered through their verified implementations, which check the caller at BunniToken.sol:255-258, CollateralTracker.sol:352-353 and SemiFungiblePositionManager.sol:520-521. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/guard.py and raw/guard_<chainId>.json
- Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Ink, Celo, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Monad, HyperEVM, cycle 5. Reach test with debug_traceCall. For 201 code groups of approved contracts (one representative per implementation, chosen by exposure) every dispatcher selector was called from an unrelated account with six argument fillings that place an approving owner, a claim id of that owner, the caller and small numbers in the argument words: 5,388 selectors and about 32,000 traces. The call tree was searched for calls to the PoolManager and the first argument of each burn and transferFrom was compared with the caller, the contract and the approving owner. Result: 50 contracts have a selector that reaches the PoolManager from an unrelated account. In every burn or transferFrom seen, the debited account is the caller or the contract itself, with one exception that pays the debited owner (redeemFees on Robinhood Chain, see that entry). 33 traces failed at the endpoint. Five approved addresses are 677 byte proxies with a private implementation slot (Ethereum, OP Mainnet, Unichain, Base, Robinhood Chain, one owner each, 4 to 84 USD of claims). The main run saw only their two proxy functions, so I traced the selectors of the implementation through the proxy on Ethereum, OP Mainnet and Unichain (5,350 and 8,926 bytes, with owner and authorized lists) and nothing reached the PoolManager. The Base and Robinhood Chain copies were not finished. This test shows what happened for the fillings I used. A function that needs a well formed struct or a signature before it reaches unlock shows up as not reaching, so the test supports the answer no and does not prove it for unverified code. Evidence: https://eth.drpc.org, https://base.api.pocket.network, https://unichain.drpc.org, https://arbitrum.drpc.org, https://robinhood.drpc.org, https://polygon.drpc.org, https://avalanche.drpc.org, https://hyperliquid.drpc.org, https://rpc.monad.xyz, https://bsc.api.pocket.network, https://rpc-qnd.inkonchain.com, https://op.api.pocket.network, https://celo.api.pocket.network debug_traceCall; research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/reach.py, raw/reach_<chainId>.json and raw/reach_proxy677.txt
- Ethereum, Base, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Monad, Robinhood Chain, cycle 5. EIP-7702 delegated accounts among the approved addresses. Code 0xef0100 followed by a delegate address was found at 56 approved addresses: 47 on Ethereum (all delegate to 0xb0c75276657e80ff04c98a3809dfc39a409a8736 and all are operators of the one account 0x82ccba35ad0c7a62230ef8ff337ac67f4cce0ea5, itself a delegated account with claims of about 740 USD), 3 on Robinhood Chain, 2 on Polygon, 2 on Base, 1 on BNB Smart Chain and 1 on Monad. The delegates are 0x63c0c19a282a1b52b07dd5a65b58948a07dae32b, 0x612373d7003d694220f7800eeaf8e3924c0951d3, 0x7702cb554e6bfb442cb743a7df23154544a7176c, 0x69007702764179f14f51cdce752f4f775d74e139 and 0x1c08930b2d330447e6c05b5be8c4caf172b4a174. Result: No public batch function was found. The 47 accounts on Ethereum were part of the call shape probe. For the nine delegated accounts on the other five networks I sent the 25 execute and batch shapes from an unrelated account with one inner call that must succeed and one that must fail: eight accounts revert on every shape and the ninth returns the same data for both, so none executes the inner call. The delegate 0xb0c75276 dispatches on msg.sender: the PoolManager, the account itself, or an address stored in transient slot 0 by the account's own flow. One handler (selector 0x10d1e85c) runs without that stored address and makes the account call PoolManager.take(currency, msg.sender, amount) with values from calldata for any caller. Inside another account's unlock this pays the caller and leaves the delegated account with a negative delta that only a payment through settleFor or the account's own actions can clear (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 305-307), so the caller gains nothing from this handler alone. I did not decompile the rest of the 24,384 byte delegate. The right of a delegated operator follows whatever code its signer delegates to next (assumption A7). Evidence: https://eth.drpc.org debug_traceCall of 0x04f9af14b8d9eccd220c91109a1f3b5e608f713e with selector 0x10d1e85c, https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com eth_getCode; research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/raw/triage_1.json, raw/reach_1.json, raw/probe_delegated.json

## Reading of the source (theme-shared-hooks)

- Ethereum, cycle 5. Hook census for Ethereum: count pools per hook from the Initialize logs of the PoolManager, then for the most used hooks test initialize from an ordinary account with seven PoolKey variants (two codeless currencies, native with a codeless currency, a real currency pair that the hook does not serve, each with a static and a dynamic fee, and the pair of an existing pool with another tick spacing), call each flagged callback from the PoolManager address with a PoolKey the hook did not create, and read what the hook holds. Result: 210501 pools in the Initialize logs read (blocks 21688329 to 26476694). 49114 name a hook and 11557 distinct hook addresses appear. Most used hooks. (1) 0x322dcec4958c14e021a9f1cd49df11b9457968cc LaunchHook (6691 pools, 10185 bytes; flags beforeInitialize, beforeAddLiquidity, beforeSwap, afterSwap, beforeSwapReturnDelta, afterSwapReturnDelta): initialize by an ordinary account reverts in all 7 PoolKey variants (NotSelf). Callbacks called from the PoolManager address with a PoolKey the hook did not create: beforeAddLiquidity reverts (LiquidityLocked); beforeSwap reverts (UnknownPool); afterSwap returns with zero delta. It holds ERC-6909 claims in 14 and token balances in 1 of the 14 pool currencies checked. (2) 0x0d62529346ac2c61f5c0582210d01214687bc0cc FeeHookV3 (5116 pools, 12266 bytes; flags beforeSwap, afterSwap, beforeSwapReturnDelta, afterSwapReturnDelta): initialize by an ordinary account succeeds in all 7 PoolKey variants. Callbacks called from the PoolManager address with a PoolKey the hook did not create: beforeSwap reverts (PoolMustHaveEthAsCurrency0); afterSwap returns with zero delta. It holds a native balance and nothing in the 14 pool currencies checked. (3) 0x96b893683afbfec071e90f78d00de4bb932fe0cc UniversalKlikHook (2240 pools, 7030 bytes; flags beforeInitialize, beforeSwap, afterSwap, beforeSwapReturnDelta, afterSwapReturnDelta): initialize by an ordinary account succeeds in all 7 PoolKey variants. Callbacks called from the PoolManager address with a PoolKey the hook did not create: beforeSwap returns with zero delta; afterSwap returns with zero delta. It holds no claims, token balances or native balance in the 14 pool currencies checked. (4) 0x6c24d0bcc264ef6a740754a11ca579b9d225e8cc ClankerHookStaticFeeV2 (1293 pools, 16405 bytes; flags beforeInitialize, beforeAddLiquidity, beforeSwap, afterSwap, beforeSwapReturnDelta, afterSwapReturnDelta): initialize by an ordinary account reverts in all 7 PoolKey variants (UnsupportedInitializePath). (1) 0x94f802a9efe4dd542fdbd77a25d9e69a6dc828cc, source not verified (4726 pools, 16405 bytes; flags beforeInitialize, beforeAddLiquidity, beforeSwap, afterSwap, beforeSwapReturnDelta, afterSwapReturnDelta): initialize by an ordinary account reverts in all 7 PoolKey variants (UnsupportedInitializePath). Callbacks called from the PoolManager address with a PoolKey the hook did not create: beforeAddLiquidity returns; beforeSwap reverts (UnauthorizedDynamicLPFeeUpdate); afterSwap returns with zero delta. It holds ERC-6909 claims in 2 of the 14 pool currencies checked. - Ethereum, cycle 5. FeeHookV3 at 0x0d62529346ac2c61f5c0582210d01214687bc0cc (5,116 pools, no initialize flag, both return delta flags, 5.31 ETH held): can a pool created by a stranger move the ETH that the hook owes to creators and partners?. Result: No. The hook has no initialize callback, so any PoolKey can be initialized. beforeSwap reverts unless currency0 is native (FeeHookV3.sol, PoolMustHaveEthAsCurrency0). Every fee credited in ethOwed is taken from the PoolManager in the same callback (poolManager.take of the same amount that is returned as the hook delta), and claim() pays only ethOwed[msg.sender]. Fee settings are stored per token, and only the address returned by token.factory() may register a creator, a recipient list, a partner or a custom fee for that token. A stranger's pool therefore adds real ETH that the stranger's swappers paid and cannot debit another token. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0x0d62529346ac2c61f5c0582210d01214687bc0cc
- Ethereum, cycle 5. UniversalKlikHook at 0x96b893683afbfec071e90f78d00de4bb932fe0cc (2,240 pools) and 0x07f17023db9cec3f8c6bb53c6940e29dffb0a0cc (1,290 pools): beforeInitialize accepts every caller. Does the hook keep state or funds that a foreign pool can reach?. Result: No. beforeInitialize only stores block.number under the pool id, and a second initialize of the same id reverts in the PoolManager, which undoes the write. The swap callbacks take the fee in ETH from the PoolManager and forward it in the same call to the platform treasury and to the token address. The hook keeps no ledger and both addresses hold no ETH, tokens or claims. This is an older Klik hook (VERSION 2) without the pending fee ledger of the finding. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0x96b893683afbfec071e90f78d00de4bb932fe0cc
- Unichain, cycle 5. UniMemeHook 0xb4960cd4f9147f9e37a7aa9005df7156f61e4444 (777 pools) and UniderpHook 0xcc2efb167503f2d7df0eae906600066aec9e8444 (114 pools), no initialize flag, afterSwap return delta: the referral ledger is per account, with no pool id. Can a stranger's pool or a stranger's hookData set the referrer of a token creator and collect or block that token's fees?. Result: No. The verified UniMemeReferral source writes referrerOf[creator] from hookData, where creator comes from a call to the pool currency. The deployed referral proxy 0x3622415b9fcb69b4395d1ad152ea002309c34fed behaves differently: in an eth_simulateV1 run of afterAddLiquidity from the PoolManager address with a referrer in hookData, the RefferalInfo event names the simulated sender (the PoolManager address, which was both the transaction origin and the caller of the hook) as invitee, and referrerOf(creator) stays zero. A swapper therefore cannot write the referrer of a token creator through hookData. In afterSwap the sum of the take calls equals the returned delta in each of the four possible referral tree shapes, and referrerOf[address(0)] cannot be written, so the mismatch case in distributeReferralFee cannot be reached. Both hooks hold no claims or balances. A token contract that reverts on receiving native currency in creator() position blocks exact input sells of its own pool only, which is a pool creator matter. Evidence: https://unichain.blockscout.com/api/v2/smart-contracts/0xb4960cd4f9147f9e37a7aa9005df7156f61e4444 and https://mainnet.unichain.org (eth_simulateV1 at block 64,676,429)
- Ethereum, Base, Unichain, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, BNB Smart Chain, Monad, cycle 5. Clanker hooks (ClankerHookStaticFeeV2, ClankerHookStaticFee, ClankerHookDynamicFee; 0x6c24d0bc... on Ethereum, 0xb429d62f... on Base, 0xbc6e5abd... on Unichain, 0xf7ac6695... and 0xfd213be7... on Arbitrum One, 0x48b8f6ad... on Robinhood Chain, 0xc5d30902... on BNB Smart Chain, 0x94f802a9... on Monad): they hold ERC-6909 claims and offer initializePoolOpen to every caller. Can a pool opened by a stranger take those claims?. Result: No. A direct PoolManager.initialize always reverts with UnsupportedInitializePath (ClankerHookV2.sol line 581). The hook creates pools itself through initializePool (factory only) and initializePoolOpen (any caller, any two tokens), and the PoolManager skips the callback when the hook is the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175). All per pool state (locker, mevModule, poolExtension, clankerIsToken0, poolCreationTimestamp) is stored under the pool id. The protocol fee is minted as claims in the paired currency, and _hookFeeClaim burns the whole claim balance of that currency and sends it to the immutable factory (lines 413 to 432). A stranger's pool can only trigger that sweep to the factory earlier. Read in the Robinhood Chain source. The other addresses returned the same errors in the probe and were not read line by line. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/4663/0x48b8f6ad3a1b4aa477314c9a23035b8f84dde8cc
- Robinhood Chain, Base, Arc, BNB Smart Chain, Monad, cycle 5. Doppler initializer hooks (DopplerHookInitializer 0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544 with 244,744 pools on Robinhood Chain, 0xf0d631d54c7e1040ccfa1c2ed737973d6a652544 on Arc and BNB Smart Chain, 0xbdf938149ac6a781f94faa0ed45e6a0e984c6544 and DecayMulticurveInitializerHook 0xbb7784a4d481184283ed89619a3e3ed143e1adc0 on Base, 0x580ca49389d83b019d07e17e99454f2f218e2dc0 on Monad): the hook owns the positions of every pool and holds collected fees. Can a pool from a stranger reach them?. Result: No. _beforeInitialize requires sender == address(this) (DopplerHookInitializer.sol line 497), and the PoolManager does not call the hook when the hook itself initializes, so only the hook's own initialize function, which is limited to the Airlock, creates pools. afterSwap looks the pool id up in getAsset and does nothing for an unknown id. FeesManager stores cumulated fees, shares and the PoolKey per pool id and pays a beneficiary only from fees that _collectFees returned for that pool. Read in the Robinhood Chain source. The other four addresses reject an ordinary initializer with the same OnlyInitializer error. Pools that an ordinary account creates through the Airlock with a quote currency of its choice were not examined. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/4663/0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544
- Ink, cycle 5. AegisHook 0xe449e013004db4a5681e9622ca10c5ba0ea610cc (102 pools): afterInitialize accepts any caller when the fee is dynamic, and the hook mints ERC-6909 claims for its fee and burns them when it reinvests. Can a foreign pool spend claims that belong to another pool?. Result: Not through the hook. The fee share hookFeePpm is zero for a pool until the owner sets it, so a foreign pool charges no hook fee. Pending fees, the per swap fee cache, the runtime data and the reinvest cooldown are stored per pool id, and _tryReinvest burns at most the pending amount of the pool that is swapping. The engine, the oracle manager, the dynamic fee manager and the limit order manager that the hook calls with the foreign PoolKey were not read. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/57073/0xe449e013004db4a5681e9622ca10c5ba0ea610cc
- Zora, cycle 5. StrategyHookV2 hooks on Zora (0x1f141a2f..., 0x7ae8de96... and two unverified addresses with the same flags, one pool each): initialize succeeds for a second pool with the same currency pair. What can that pool do?. Result: Nothing after launch. beforeInitialize only checks that currency1 is the strategy token. beforeAddLiquidity allows one deposit per hook, tracked in a single flag, so a second pool cannot receive liquidity once the real pool has it, and a swap without liquidity moves nothing and produces no fee. Before the first deposit an account could use the one allowed deposit on its own pool and block the launch, which concerns the deployer only. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/7777777/0x1f141a2f4eb256c58a6e008885c6fdc966576844
- Optimism, Polygon, Celo, Arbitrum One, Avalanche, BNB Smart Chain, Monad, Soneium, Worldchain, MegaETH, Ethereum, cycle 5. Hooks with flags beforeSwap and beforeSwapReturnDelta only (addresses ending in 8088, for example 0xf0e1b03731fa1c94b30e90a9a61368e2f5968088 on Optimism, 0x1743c5352f4e11aadb8a6023a10499703b600088 on Polygon, 0x8ca169714fc17174e5c6ef29bf2833f9bdb1c088 on BNB Smart Chain) and the variant with afterInitialize (0x987105e9... on Optimism, 0xc9987661... on Polygon, 0x89fcd097... on Arbitrum One, 0x8d92ff0a... on Monad): initialize is open. Does a pool from a stranger get served?. Result: The first group answers beforeSwap with PoolNotRegistered, InvalidPoolKey or HookPaused for a pool it did not register. The Optimism hook reports version UniswapV2LPHook v1.1.1, stores a Uniswap V2 pair per pool id, and its registration, setPoolFee, setPaused and execute functions revert with OnlyOwner for an ordinary caller. Existing pools were registered by the owner 0x2a315c59a6a95aeeec085c73badac801c2f4209f in a call to the hook. The variant with afterInitialize pairs an ERC-4626 vault with its asset. Its afterInitialize registers any pool whose pair passes the vault check: in an eth_simulateV1 run on Polygon an ordinary account initialized a second pool for USDC and waUSDC, getPoolCount rose from 89 to 90 and pools(id) of the new pool equals that of the existing one. A stranger can therefore register a pool for a vault contract it wrote. None of these hooks holds claims, tokens or native currency between transactions, except 0x60451c7c... on Polygon and 0x92385e5b... on MegaETH, which hold token balances and reject a foreign PoolKey with InvalidPoolKey. No path to funds of other pools was found. The owner's execute function can make the hook call any address, which is an owner power. Evidence: https://mainnet.optimism.io and https://polygon.drpc.org (eth_call and eth_simulateV1, 23 November 2026)
- Arc, cycle 5. Arc hook 0x4ab0bf61327761fffc5910052d9e0b9a94f960cc (1,260 pools, unverified, holds 35.4 units of native claims, selectors owed(address,address), claim(address), poolConfig(bytes32)): initialize succeeds for a second pool of a factory token with another tick spacing. Can that pool reach the claims?. Result: No path found. beforeInitialize rejects tokens that the token factory did not create (NotFactoryToken). In an eth_simulateV1 run the second pool was initialized, poolConfig(new id) still reverted with PoolNotConfigured, poolConfig of the real pool was unchanged, and beforeSwap for the new pool reverted with PoolNotConfigured, so the pool cannot be swapped. The hook has no liquidity callbacks. The configuration function 0x7e19851a rejects an ordinary caller and the token factory with OnlyStrategy(address). Who the strategy is was not established. Evidence: https://arc.drpc.org (eth_simulateV1) and https://rpc.mainnet.arc.io (eth_call), 23 November 2026
- MegaETH, cycle 5. HOMIEHook 0xeecbbd7ceb246684b8f621dc9dddca8f72b200c4 on MegaETH (3 pools, no initialize flag, afterSwap return delta). Result: The fee logic runs only for pool ids that the owner registered with registerPool, which requires the HOMIE token as one currency. afterSwap returns zero for any other pool. The hook holds nothing. Evidence: https://megaeth.blockscout.com/api/v2/smart-contracts/0xeecbbd7ceb246684b8f621dc9dddca8f72b200c4
- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Across the 111 hooks probed on the 21 networks: is there a hook with a return delta flag that accepts initialize from an ordinary account for arbitrary currencies and then returns a non zero delta, or calls take, mint, burn or settle, for that pool?. Result: Three groups do. FeeHookV3 and UniversalKlikHook on Ethereum and UniMemeHook, UniderpHook and hook 0x782d2a5624cfac246fd8f001ccd4d7582a0b8444 on Unichain charge their fee on any pool and pay it out or credit it in the same callback from the amount they take, which is covered above (0x782d2a56... is unverified and was judged from its probe result only). OmniHook 0x03f4051e621ee3f3652adef2c453458a777e40cc on World Chain (14 pools) does the same: it takes its fee to itself and credits five fixed recipients in owed[currency][recipient], so the ledger is per currency and each entry is backed by tokens taken in that currency. The Klik fee hooks are the third group and are the finding. Every other probed hook with a return delta flag either rejects the stranger's initialize or reverts or returns zero for a pool it does not know. A callback that reverted with ManagerLocked in the direct call shows that the hook tried a PoolManager call that needs an unlocked manager, which is how fee taking hooks were recognised. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-shared-hooks.work/raw/probe: one JSON file per chain and hook with the eth_call results

## Reading of the source (loose-guards)

- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Lead L-313, first item: collectProtocolFees never reads the lock and skips the synced check for address(0) (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52 against src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40). Result: Answered in cycle 1 and not repeated: the cleared items for chain ids 1, 137, 56 and 5042 walked a native collection while a native face is synced and found that it lowers the settler own credit, and the critic of cycle 5 confirmed on Ethereum, Polygon and Arc that the deployed contracts collect inside an unlock. This unit added one read. The fee controllers of the eight networks that have one (chain ids 1, 10, 8453, 42161, 4663, 137, 56 and 5042) all expose the same sixteen selectors, among them 0xe0511234 for collect((address,uint256)[]) and 0x06ab95ba for triggerFeeUpdate with a PoolKey argument, and each answers POOL_MANAGER() with the PoolManager of its network and TOKEN_JAR() with one fixed address. Seven of them are 4,544 bytes long and the one on Arc is 3,480 bytes. I did not read the adapter code on the seven networks other than Ethereum, so that the recipient is fixed there rests on the getter and on the shared selector set. Evidence: eth_getCode and eth_call on the rpc URLs of chain ids 1, 10, 8453, 42161, 4663, 137, 56 and 5042 on 2026-11-23, script controllers.py, results in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-loose-guards.work/raw/controllers.json; src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57; research/network-risk/state/ledger.json criticNotes of cycle 5
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. sync has no lock check (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288), while src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 names initialize and updateDynamicLPFee as the only functions that run without an unlock. What can an ordinary account do with that, and which network feature turns it into a gain or a freeze for others. Result: An ordinary account can set the synced currency and the reserves value while the manager is locked, and nothing else. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers a sync(T) from a plain contract outside any unlock succeeded for a stub T that answers balanceOf with 32 bytes. exttload then returned T in the currency slot and the answer in the reserves slot, the lock flag read 0, and sync(address(0)) cleared the currency slot. The tests of the repository expect this (test/Sync.t.sol:36-41, test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1008) and the test double declares sync without a modifier (src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:139-148), so only the interface comment disagrees. A lock check would not narrow what an account can reach. Any contract can call unlock, call sync inside its callback and return with every delta at zero (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). On all 21 networks such an unlock closed and the synced currency stayed in place afterwards, with the lock flag and the delta counter back at 0. A later settle with value in the same call then reverted with NonzeroNativeValue, and it passed once the payer called sync(address(0)) first. That effect is finding F-071 and stays as recorded there. The other network features of the task were walked against the two slots. Code that runs between another payer transfer and its settle: the PoolManager makes no call between those two steps, so such code can come only from the token or from the payer own router. It would not need sync or the missing lock check, because settle and settleFor are open to every caller while the manager is unlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:300-307). A credit captured that way leaves the payer delta open, and the payer unlock reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:112 unless the payer code ignores the amount that settle returns. This is the same on Ethereum. A failed frame: on all 21 networks an unlock whose callback reverted left no lock flag and no delta behind, since the next unlock in the same call opened and closed normally. Transient storage across transactions and inside protocol level batches (assumption A1) was read from client sources by the units of cycle 3 and was not repeated here. Evidence: eth_call with state overrides on the 21 rpc URLs of research/network-risk/state/networks.json on 2026-11-23 at the latest block of each endpoint (near Ethereum block 26,477,978, Celo 83,537,894, Polygon 97,822,132, Arc 32,737,892 and Tempo 50,432,381, the others as listed in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-loose-guards.work/raw/tests_<chainId>.json), scripts tests.py and stale.py, results raw/tests_<chainId>.json and raw/stale.json in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-loose-guards.work; src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 279-288, 300-307, 349-365; test/Sync.t.sol:36-41; src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:139-148
- Celo, Arc, Polygon, cycle 6. A sync of a native face made before an unlock on Celo, Arc and Polygon, where an ERC-20 address measures the native balance: can one payment be credited under address(0) and under the face, and what does a native payout do while the face is synced. Result: No double credit on any of the three. One eth_call per network ran the walk on the deployed PoolManager at blocks 83,538,264 (Celo), 32,738,581 (Arc) and 97,822,371 (Polygon), with a funded stub as the ordinary account. With the face synced before the unlock, settle with 1000 wei reverted with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:356). After a zero value settle cleared the slot, settle with 1000 wei credited 1000 under address(0). A new sync of the face stored the higher balance and the next settle paid 0, so the face delta stayed 0 and the native delta 1000. On Celo a transfer of 1000 through the CELO token 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438 was credited as 1000 under the face id, and take under that id paid 1000 wei of CELO to the recipient. On Arc one unit sent through 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 was credited as 1 under the face id, and take under that id paid 10^12 wei. On Polygon the transfer through 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 failed and take under that id reverted, so that id can be neither paid in nor paid out. On all three the native balance of the PoolManager ended at its starting value and every delta read 0. A native take while the face is synced made the next settle revert with a Panic on the checked subtraction (src/PoolManager.sol:360), which costs the settler and nobody else. An account whose EIP-7702 designator names 0x1010 on Polygon also reports the native balance of the PoolManager, as does any contract that returns the balance of its argument (src/test/NativeERC20.sol:46-48 models one). Such a face gives a credit only for value that arrives while it is synced, and its transfer function cannot move native funds of the PoolManager. Evidence: eth_call with state overrides on https://forno.celo.org, https://rpc.mainnet.arc.io and https://polygon.drpc.org on 2026-11-23, script faces.py, results raw/faces_42220.json, raw/faces_5042.json, raw/faces_137.json and raw/deleg_token.json in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-loose-guards.work; src/PoolManager.sol:349-365
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. A take of a currency address without code succeeds because the transfer accepts empty return data (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), while src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:174 says take reverts if the amount is not available. What can an ordinary account do with that, and can a pool, a claim or a debt exist under such an address. Result: The account can make take report success without any transfer, at its own cost. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers, inside one unlock: take of 5 units of a codeless address returned success, the caller delta slot read minus 5 and the delta counter 1. sync of that address reverted with empty data, because balanceOf is a high level call whose empty answer cannot be decoded (src/types/Currency.sol:94). settle with nothing synced paid 0. mint of 7 units added a debt of 7 and a claim of 7. clear reverted with MustClearExactPositiveDelta. A separate unlock that only took 5 units reverted with CurrencyNotSettled, and one that took amount 0 closed, on all 21 networks. The ecrecover address 0x01 gave the same answers as the codeless address. For the identity precompile 0x04 take reverted and sync stored a constant, so the next settle paid 0. Under a codeless id a positive delta could come only from settle, from burn, from a pool or from a hook delta. settle is closed because sync reverts. burn needs a claim, and a claim needs a positive delta to pay for the mint. Pool amounts are rounded against the caller (an add owes the amount rounded up and a removal returns it rounded down, src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:261-288 and src/libraries/Pool.sol:206-237) and a hook delta is subtracted from the caller delta (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:230, 242 and 312), so the deltas of all accounts in that currency sum to zero or less. No claim and no debt therefore exists under a codeless id. A pool that names it can be initialized (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142) and can hold only positions that need the other currency alone. The only party that loses from the silent take is the caller that asked for it. A holder of a real credit could lose it this way only if the code of a token disappeared after deposits, which needs a token built for that, for example an account whose owner clears its EIP-7702 delegation. That is the pool creator class of F-013. Evidence: eth_call with state overrides on the 21 rpc URLs of research/network-risk/state/networks.json on 2026-11-23 at the latest block of each endpoint (near Ethereum block 26,477,978, Celo 83,537,894, Polygon 97,822,132, Arc 32,737,892 and Tempo 50,432,381, the others as listed in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-loose-guards.work/raw/tests_<chainId>.json), scripts tests.py (real_script) and codeless_close.py, results raw/tests_<chainId>.json, raw/compare.json and raw/codeless_close.json in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-loose-guards.work; src/types/Currency.sol:55-96; src/PoolManager.sol:279-336
- BNB Smart Chain, Base, Tempo, cycle 6. Lead L-423, second item: which addresses change from no code to code at a scheduled fork or on demand, what do they answer to the call shapes of take and sync before and after, and can a pool, a claim or a debt exist under them before. Enshrined token ranges on BNB Smart Chain (Jenner), Base (B20) and Tempo (TIP-20). Result: BNB Smart Chain: the client sets JennerTime for mainnet to 1796697000, which is 2026-12-08 02:30 UTC, and from that time resolves every address of the CAS20 family from its prefix (params/config.go line 256, core/vm/evm.go lines 46 to 58). At block 135,275,526 the addresses 0xca52000000000000000001217954ab5467577565, 0xca5200000000000000000069e5bbadfec8b9075a and 0xca52000000000000000000000000000000abcdef held no code and answered balanceOf, transfer of 0, transfer of 1 and empty calldata from the PoolManager with success and no data. Until the fork a take that names such an address succeeds and moves nothing and sync reverts, as for any codeless address. On the Chapel testnet, where the fork has been active since 2026-10-29, the first two addresses hold the one byte code 0xef and answer balanceOf with 32 bytes, and the third, which was never created, reverted on all four shapes at block 144,409,446. Base and Tempo show the same state after activation today. Created B20 and TIP-20 tokens hold the code 0xef. The B20 range addresses 0xb200000000000000000000000000000000abcdef and 0xb2000000000000000000000000000000deadbeef, which hold no token, reverted on all four shapes at block 61,242,809, and the TIP-20 range addresses 0x20c00000000000000000000000000000deadbeef and 0x20c0000000000000000000000000000000abcdef reverted with Uninitialized at block 50,432,878. The address 0x20c0ffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff lies outside the token id range and answers as a codeless account. By the item above no claim, debt or funded position can exist under an address while it is codeless, so nothing is carried over an activation. A pool can be initialized on a future token address at a price of the creator choice, which is the same on Ethereum for any address that can be predicted. Not confirmed: that BNB Smart Chain mainnet will treat never created CAS20 addresses as Chapel does, because the fork is not active there yet. - all 21 networks, cycle 6. unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint, burn, clear and sync carry no noDelegateCall, while the test double puts the modifier on six of them (src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:58, 151-183). Lead L-423, third item: call them through DELEGATECALL from a stub and say what an account that points its EIP-7702 delegation at the PoolManager exposes. Result: A delegatecall runs these functions against the storage, the transient storage and the balance of the calling account, and nothing the PoolManager holds is reached. Test on all 21 deployed PoolManagers, one eth_call each with state overrides: a stub P that forwards every call to the PoolManager by DELEGATECALL, and a funded stub E as the ordinary account. Outside an unlock P.sync succeeded, P.settle reverted with ManagerLocked, P.initialize reverted with DelegateCallNotAllowed, and P.owner and P.protocolFeeController returned zero. E then called P.unlock. Inside the callback P.take of 1000 wei of native currency paid the recipient out of the balance of P. The delta of minus 1000 and the unlocked flag sat in the transient storage of P, while the flag and the delta of the PoolManager read 0. P.mint and P.burn moved a claim in the storage of P, while balanceOf at the PoolManager for the same account read 0. P.settle with 1000 wei returned 1000, P.swap reverted with DelegateCallNotAllowed, and P.sync and P.clear ran. The unlock closed, the native balance of the PoolManager was the same before and after, and a second unlock that only took reverted with CurrencyNotSettled. An account D that carries the designator 0xef0100 followed by the PoolManager address gave the same 29 answers on 20 networks. The Avalanche endpoint (avalanchego 1.15.3) executed the designator as code and failed with invalid opcode 0xef, so a delegated account could not be tested there. What such an account exposes: any caller can borrow its whole native and token balance for the length of one unlock and must return it, a caller can book as its own payment any balance rise it can trigger at the account between sync and settle, and anyone can write claim and operator entries into the storage of the account. owner and protocolFeeController read zero there, initialize, swap, modifyLiquidity and donate revert, and no protocol fee can accrue, so collectProtocolFees has nothing to pay. The exposure is limited to the account that made the delegation. The tests of the repository need the production functions without the modifier, because the double forwards take, settle, mint, burn and clear by delegatecall and expects DelegateCallNotAllowed only from modifyLiquidity, swap and donate (src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:151-183, test/NoDelegateCall.t.sol:63-82). - all 21 networks, cycle 6. fromId drops the upper 96 bits of a claim id (src/types/Currency.sol:114-118) and mint and burn accept any uint256 id (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). Can an id with high bits reach another balance, allowance or currency. Result: No. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers a mint with the id (0xabc << 160) | X raised the claim balance at the plain id X by the amount and left the balance at the raw id at 0. A burn with other high bits lowered the balance at X, and the delta moved under currency X both times. The source uses the truncated currency for the delta and toId of it for the claim and for the allowance check (src/PoolManager.sol:324-327 and 333-335, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22), and the interface states the truncation (src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:200-201 and 208-209). transfer, transferFrom and approve use the raw id, so a balance at an id with high bits can never be minted and every transfer of it fails on the checked subtraction (src/ERC6909.sol:26 and 41). The id never reaches a call: mint and burn make no external call, and the currency that sync, take and initialize receive is an address type. - all 21 networks, cycle 6. Caller identities that a network creates, against the functions that trust msg.sender without a lock or a role: unlock, sync, the ERC-6909 functions, and the controller check, which the zero address passes on 13 networks. Result: unlock from an address without code reverted with empty data on all 21 networks, because the answer of the callback cannot be decoded (src/PoolManager.sol:110). The zero address holds no code on any of the 21 networks, so no contract code and no delegation can act from it. Its nonce is nonzero on nine OP Stack networks (10 on OP Mainnet, Zora and World Chain, 8 on Base, 7 on Unichain, Ink and Soneium, 5 on Celo, 2 on X Layer) and zero on the other twelve. On seven of the nine (Unichain, Zora, World Chain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer) protocolFeeController is the zero address. This unit did not trace which transactions raised the nonce. The open leads L-100 and L-129 ask that for upgrade deposits, and the nonce values belong with them. Arc: the CallFrom precompile lets two helper contracts name the sender of a child call. Both helpers pass their own msg.sender (Memo.sol line 43, Multicall3From.sol lines 43, 58, 81 and 161), and the client rejects a named sender that is neither the calling helper nor the transaction signer (crates/evm/src/evm.rs lines 946 to 955) and rejects every scheme other than CALL (lines 895 to 903). A contract that runs in the middle of another account transaction therefore cannot reach unlock or the ERC-6909 functions as that account. Called by an outside sender it forwards the calldata to the PoolManager; called by the PoolManager it runs the inner calls passed in the unlock data and returns their success flags and first return words. The claim id was the address 0xb01b749eb983d41e87c2dc1f975774bc526b52e3, which has no code on any of the 21 networks. Result: All 21 endpoints returned the same words, the 24,050 byte Unichain predeploy included. Outside an unlock, settleFor, clear, settle, take, mint and burn revert with 0x54e3ca0d (ManagerLocked) and sync(address(0)) succeeds. mint to the stub followed by burn from the stub: unlock succeeds. mint only: unlock reverts with 0x5212cba1 (CurrencyNotSettled). mint to a third address followed by burn from that address by the unapproved stub: unlock reverts with CurrencyNotSettled, so the burn gave no credit. Two mints of 5 and 3 followed by one burn of 8: unlock succeeds, so a delta that moves between two nonzero values is counted once. Inside one unlock: settleFor without payment succeeds, clear of 1 with a zero delta reverts with 0xbda73abf, mint, take and burn of 2^127 revert with 0x93dafdf1 (SafeCastOverflow), a take of amount 0 in the codeless currency succeeds, sync of the codeless currency reverts without data, and a nested unlock reverts with 0x5090d6c6. These results describe the deployed contracts, which are other bytecode than a build of this checkout. Evidence: rpc: eth_call with a state override on the 21 endpoints of research/network-risk/state/networks.json on 2026-11-23, scripts and raw answers in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-test-pins.work/probe.py and raw/probe_results.json (blocks: Ethereum 26478014, Unichain 64690717, Celo 83538337, Arc 32738822, Tempo 50433255, HyperEVM 52035167)
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Deployed PoolManagers, read-only: is the lock closed when unlock returns, and does settle reset the synced currency (the two statements that the tests pin only without --isolate). Result: Same words on all 21 endpoints. Inside the callback exttload of the lock slot returns 1. After sync of the stub, which answers balanceOf with a fixed word, exttload of the currency slot returns the stub address; after settle, which returns 0, the slot returns 0, and a second settle returns 0. With a second stub that makes two more calls after unlock has returned, in the same eth_call: exttload of the lock slot returns 0 and take reverts with 0x54e3ca0d (ManagerLocked). Evidence: rpc: eth_call with a state override on the 21 endpoints of research/network-risk/state/networks.json on 2026-11-23, scripts and raw answers in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-test-pins.work/probe2.py and raw/probe2_results.json (blocks: Ethereum 26478031, Unichain 64690913)
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Lead L-217 for Unichain and the same walk on the other 20 networks, read-only with a stub that can attach value to inner calls (state override of code and balance). Result: Same words on all 21 endpoints. After sync of a token stand-in, settle with value 1 reverts with 0xb0ec849e (NonzeroNativeValue). After sync(address(0)), settle with value 1 returns 1 and the delta slot of the stub for address(0) reads 1. clear of 2 reverts with MustClearExactPositiveDelta. take of 1 native unit to the stub succeeds and the delta reads 0. mint of 5 raises balanceOf(stub, id) to 5, the delta reads -5 and the nonzero count reads 1; burn of 5 returns all three to 0. The synced currency guard of collectProtocolFees was tested on the eight networks that have a fee controller; Unichain has none, so that item of the lead cannot be tested there. On Tempo the value steps ran because the state override gave the stub a native balance. Whether an account can hold a native balance there was a question of earlier cycles, and this probe does not answer it. The Avalanche endpoint answered with a rate limit page once and gave the same words on the rerun. Evidence: rpc: eth_call with a state override on the 21 endpoints of research/network-risk/state/networks.json on 2026-11-23, scripts and raw answers in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-test-pins.work/probe3.py and raw/probe3_results.json (blocks: Unichain 64691062, Ethereum 26478042, Avalanche 101167638)
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Unpinned statements that stand against assumption A1 (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 113, 305, 310): can an ordinary account use them on any of the 21 networks. Result: No path in the text. Line 112 reads the transient counter that every _accountDelta call maintains (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378) and line 113 writes the lock slot; both hold for a caller as long as transient storage lives for exactly the transaction and rolls back with a reverted frame. settleFor and clear carry the same modifier as take and settle, so a locked manager rejects them. The feature that would break these lines is a transaction boundary inside or across user calls (protocol batches, system calls, nested runs with an empty transient map), which is the per network question of assumption A1 that earlier cycles answered from client source and simulation. The reading adds nothing that depends on a network. The cycle 3 critic probe showed on all 21 RPC nodes that these slots are scoped by address and that a second transaction reads zero where simulation is offered. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:96-99, 104-114, 305, 310; research/network-risk/state/ledger.json criticNotes cycle 3
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Unpinned statements that stand against assumption A2 (src/PoolManager.sol:360, 361, 364): a balance that falls between sync and settle, a balance rise credited twice, and a balance reading of 2^127 or more. Result: As written, a fall makes the checked subtraction revert, the reset after settle means a rise is credited once, and a rise of 2^127 or more reverts in toInt128. An ordinary account can still book a rise that a third party or the token itself causes between its own sync and settle, which is the class of F-041 and its variants and needs no unpinned line. I found no way to use these three statements beyond that class. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:349-365
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Unpinned statements that stand against assumptions A4 and A7 (src/types/Currency.sol:48, 64-74, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152, 166): a currency or hook address without code or at a precompile, and the gas forwarded to a native recipient. Result: A take of a currency whose address returns success and no data debits the caller and moves nothing, so the caller loses and no one else does; a credit in such an id needs sync, which reverts when balanceOf returns no data (confirmed on all 21 deployed contracts in the probe above for an address without code). A hook answer shorter than 32 bytes is rejected. A native payout forwards all gas to the recipient, which is lever P1 of ASSUMPTIONS.md and was swept per network in earlier cycles (F-021, F-047, F-048, F-049). These lines give an ordinary account no way to take or lock funds of others in the text as written. Evidence: src/types/Currency.sol:44-87, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-168
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Unpinned statement that stands against assumption A8 (src/PoolManager.sol:335): burn takes claims from a named account and credits msg.sender. Result: burn calls _burnFrom, which requires msg.sender to be the holder, an operator of the holder, or to have an allowance of at least the amount for that id (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22). The credit goes to msg.sender, so the only question a network can change is who msg.sender is. A caller identity that the chain forges (aliased cross domain senders, system callers) would still need the holder's approval for that identity. On all 21 deployed contracts a burn of another address's claims by an unapproved caller gave no credit. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:332-336, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22

Result: All 13 are dividend trackers of pooled tokens (names such as ETHBack_Dividend_Tracker and DIVIDEND_TRACKER). A tracker repeats the balance that each holder has in the main token and logs a Transfer when it changes, so its figure for the PoolManager falls when a pool pays the main token out. None is a currency of a pool. A transfer of one unit from the PoolManager reverts on each of them, for 11 with the text No transfers allowed, so a pool created with a tracker as currency could be credited through sync and settle and never paid out, as with the mirror tokens of F-008 and F-050. The PoolManager is not excluded from dividends on the trackers that answer excludedFromDividends. The reward tokens are USDT, BUSD, DOGE, ASTER, BNCB and DogeZilla. withdrawableDividendOf(PoolManager) is zero on 10 trackers and dust on the others today. Rewards that a tracker pays to the PoolManager are not recorded by any pool. A lead asks how much has been paid and whether a public claim lets a caller book it. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/006/theme-currency-lists.work/raw/bnb_trackers.json
