Monad v0.16.5 inline CALLER, CALLVALUE and RETURNDATASIZE, which decide who is credited (src/PoolManager.sol:301, 306, 369), how much native currency a settle credits (src/PoolManager.sol:354) and whether a token transfer counts as successful (src/types/Currency.sol:68). Result: No mismatch. CALLER: 50,000 addresses including all limb edges give the 160 bit value, with the top limb zero and the 32 bit movbe clearing the upper half of its register. CALLVALUE: 100,000 values through both the general register and the AVX destination. RETURNDATASIZE: every size from 0 to 4,096 and 5,000 random sizes below 2^24. RETURNDATASIZE reads the low 32 bits of a 64 bit field (static_assert at emitter.cpp 3072-3074); this is exact for return data below 2^32 bytes, which a transaction cannot produce under Monad's memory limit. When a comparison is held in the CPU flags, the three readers write zero with mov instead of xor, so the flags that Currency.transfer's gt(returndatasize(), 31) and eq(mload(0), 1) feed into are kept. - Monad, cycle 11. How compiled CALL and STATICCALL return into the caller on Monad v0.16.5: the return data buffer, the caller's memory and the transient storage journal when the callee reverts, and whether a revert inside compiled code undoes TSTORE through the same journal as the interpreter. Result: Both paths run runtime::call_impl. It clears the return data before the call, stores the callee's output as the new return data after host->call, copies min(retSize, output size) into the caller's memory whatever the status, and pushes 1 only for EVMC_SUCCESS (call.cpp 58-196). The journal sits outside the VM: execute_call_message runs pre_call, which pushes a State version, then VM::execute on either path, then post_call, which accepts the version on success and rejects it otherwise (execute_message.cpp 110-174, 305-350). Transient storage lives in the versioned account state (state.cpp 126-180, 318-330, 406-410), so a revert in compiled code is undone exactly as in the interpreter. VM::execute_raw picks interpreted or native code inside that bracket (vm.cpp 142-190), and both end in rt_ctx.copy_to_evmc_result (vm.cpp 232-256). This repeats the cycle 4 and cycle 8 readings, which were taken from the main branch, on the v0.16.5 tag. The scripts make 26,221 PoolManager calls. Inside the settlement functions (Currency.transfer, balanceOfSelf, CurrencyDelta, CurrencyReserves, unlock, CustomRevert) the transcribed RETURNDATASIZE ran 2,818 times and CALLER 584 times. Across all contracts of the scripts, CALLDATALOAD with a non-literal offset took the register, AVX and stack paths 84,578 times. - Monad, cycle 11. Lead L-623, first half: does debug_traceTransaction with callTracer on Monad execute the transaction again, or return the frames that block execution recorded?. Result: It returns recorded frames. In monad-rpc, debug_traceTransaction replays only for prestateTracer (requires_replay matches Tracer::PreStateTracer only); for callTracer it calls monad_debug_traceTransaction, which reads the RLP call frames stored for the transaction (get_transaction_call_frame) and decodes them. Block execution writes those frames to the database through CommitBuilder::add_call_frames. The executor behind eth_call and debug_traceCall builds its VM as InterpreterOnly. So a recorded trace shows what the block, with the PoolManager compiled once hot, computed, and debug_traceCall shows what the interpreter computes. The monad-rpc reading is from the master branch of monad-bft; which commit rpc.monad.xyz runs was not confirmed (web3_clientVersion returns Monad/unknown). Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad-bft/master/monad-rpc/src/handlers/mod.rs lines 381-398; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad-bft/master/monad-rpc/src/handlers/debug.rs lines 557-591, 639-720; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad-bft/master/monad-rpc/src/handlers/debug_replay.rs lines 51-54; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.5/category/execution/ethereum/db/commit_builder.cpp lines 234-260; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.5/category/rpc/monad_executor.cpp lines 1297-1300

Recorded block execution against interpreter replay for the first user transaction of a block (index 1; index 0 of every Monad block is the staking system call to 0x...1000) in 2,400 mined PoolManager transactions of blocks 124,987,459 to 125,011,397. Each was replayed with debug_traceCall at the parent block with its sender, target, input, value, gas and access list. Result: No difference that the PoolManager produced. The 2,400 trees hold 287,515 frames and 28,811 PoolManager frames: 5,369 unlock, 5,690 swap, 4,778 sync, 5,468 settle, 5,926 take, 1 mint. 1,078 transactions replay with an identical event sequence (every call, input, value, output, error and log in execution order), covering 6,017 PoolManager frames. In the other 1,322 the first differing event never belongs to the PoolManager. It is the staking precompile's answer (846), a bot contract that logs the block number (286), or a contract whose behaviour depends on the block (190). Pairing PoolManager frames by position and input gives 22,930 pairs, and 22,893 have identical outputs, errors, logs and outgoing calls. The other 37 come after an earlier divergence elsewhere in the same transaction: a token's balanceOf returned another balance, so settle returned another amount. 285 transactions hold a reverted frame that had entered unlock, followed by an unlock that completed. In 282 of them every PoolManager pair is identical. The first comparison without access lists gave false differences: the replay ran out of gas where the block had warm slots. Passing the access list removed every PoolManager-owned divergence. Evidence: rpc https://rpc.monad.xyz eth_getLogs, eth_getTransactionByBlockNumberAndIndex, eth_getTransactionByHash, eth_getTransactionReceipt, debug_traceTransaction (callTracer, withLog) and debug_traceCall (callTracer, withLog) on 2026-11-24; research/network-risk/cycles/011/theme-monad-settlement-path.work/scan.py, scan.json, frames_monad.py, frames.json, pmframes.py, pmframes.json
- Monad, cycle 11. The settlement calls as block execution ran them in 12,000 mined PoolManager transactions (blocks 124,991,690 to 125,011,402), checked from the recorded frames alone against src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, 300-308, 349-364 and src/types/Currency.sol:40-96, with the synced currency and reserves rolled back over reverted frames as transient storage is. Result: No mismatch. 17,640 token syncs each made one balanceOf(PoolManager) staticcall to the named currency, and 1,331 native syncs made none. 17,640 token settle and settleFor calls each made one balanceOf staticcall to the synced currency, sent no value and returned exactly the balance minus the synced reserves. 2,846 native settle and settleFor calls returned exactly msg.value and made no call. Of 18,208 token takes and 3,558 native takes, all 21,765 that succeeded made one call: transfer(to, amount) to the token with no value, or a call to the recipient with value amount and empty input. Each token transfer returned nothing or a 32 byte 1. This exercises the compiled TLOAD and TSTORE of CurrencyReserves (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:15-37), CALLVALUE at src/PoolManager.sol:354, RETURNDATASIZE in balanceOfSelf and transfer, and STATICCALL and CALL, as far as block execution ran the PoolManager compiled (see the last lead). Evidence: rpc https://rpc.monad.xyz debug_traceTransaction (callTracer) on 2026-11-24; research/network-risk/cycles/011/theme-monad-settlement-path.work/settlecheck.py, settlecheck.json
- Monad, cycle 11. Do the credits and debits that block execution recorded inside each completed unlock net to zero per account and currency, as unlock requires (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 368-379)? Summed over swap, modifyLiquidity, donate, settle, settleFor, take, mint, burn and clear frames, outside reverted frames, in 12,000 mined transactions. Result: Yes for all 13,635 completed unlocks checked, which hold 48,268 accounted operations. 11 unlocks on pools with a hook were left out, because a hook can move deltas to its own account. A planted error of one unit in each settle credit made 191 of 192 unlocks fail the check, so the check sees an over-credit. - Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Zora, Worldchain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Tempo, Arc, cycle 11. Across the other networks: does block execution run the settlement opcodes on a code path that a simulated call does not reach?. Result: No for these 18. Their blocks and their eth_call run the same interpreter: go-ethereum and its forks (BNB Smart Chain, Polygon, Avalanche, the three Nitro chains), revm on the OP Stack and Arc, and evm2 on Ethereum's reth nodes and Tempo, whose published binaries have no compiler. The opcode battery, the call semantics tests and the script sets therefore test the block path there. ## Reading of the source (theme-bytecode-coverage)

- all 21 networks, cycle 12. Part one of L-655: every unexecuted range and every one-sided or never-taken JUMPI of the 24,009 byte build, mapped to its source construct through the solc 0.8.26 source map of a rebuild with the settings of compile.js (runtime byte-identical to build/PoolManager.json). Result: Before set 6: 9,959 of 10,418 instructions, 255 JUMPI both ways, 129 one way, 3 never. Of the 132, 51 were ABI decoder or callvalue guards (jump to revert(0,0) at pc 816), 9 lock checks (ManagerLocked), 7 Panic 0x41, 3 Panic 0x11, 2 Panic 0x12, 7 SafeCast reverts, and the rest hook paths, ERC-6909 allowance paths, clear, settle with value, delegatecall guard, bounds checks and large-number branches of SqrtPriceMath and FullMath. The map with source file, line and instruction context for each is jumpmap-before.json. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/012/theme-bytecode-coverage.work/jumpmap-before.json
- all 21 networks, cycle 12. Part two of L-655: pmdiff6.py, 706 scripts and 25,681 calls in the reference interpreter (pyevm.py) on the build, with a driver that can send value, delegatecall, staticcall, run outside unlock and return malformed callback data, hook doubles for every permission bit and return-delta combination, hook self-calls, a token whose balanceOf reverts or returns short data, failing native payouts with revert data of 0 to 1000 bytes, bounds of initialize, modifyLiquidity and swap, the overflow fallback of getNextSqrtPriceFromAmount0RoundingUp, the 512 bit branch of mulDiv by 2^128 in Position.update, protocol fee collection while synced, and truncated calldata for every function. Result: Coverage of the six sets together: 10,288 of 10,418 instructions (98.75 percent, up from 95.6), 338 JUMPI both ways, 46 one way, 3 never. 83 of the 132 jumps now go both ways. jumpmap-after.json gives each remaining one with what it decides and why its other side is unreachable: 39 decide a revert, 9 a payout or price and 1 a credit, and none of the 49 can be reached by an ordinary caller in a transaction that pays out. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/012/theme-bytecode-coverage.work/jumpmap-after.json
- all 21 networks, cycle 12. pmdiff6 on all 21 endpoints by eth_call with state override, each record compared with the reference interpreter (705 scripts; one is too long for the reference). Result: Per network, scripts equal to the reference: 1 703/705; 10 705/705; 8453 705/705; 130 703/705; 7777777 703/705; 480 705/705; 57073 703/705; 1868 703/705; 42220 703/705; 196 703/705; 42161 703/705; 4663 703/705; 99901 703/705; 137 700/705; 56 704/705; 43114 703/705; 143 703/705; 4326 703/705; 4217 703/705; 5042 701/705; 999 701/705. Every difference falls into one of three groups. (a) Four scripts in which a swap at tick spacing 1 walks the whole price range (8.1 to 14.9 million reference instructions): the first differing call is that swap failing with empty return data on the endpoint with less gas, and on 279 the whole record is empty (all networks except OP Mainnet, Base and World Chain for 277 and 279; Polygon, Arc and HyperEVM also for 275 and 276). (b) Script 682: take(currency 0x1000) succeeds in the reference because 0x1000 has no code there, and reverts with WrappedError(ERC20TransferFailed) on Polygon and BNB Smart Chain, where 0x1000 holds a system contract (eth_getCode returned 14,347 and 29,871 bytes), and on Monad. (c) Scripts 681 and 682 on Monad return nothing: 0x1000 is the staking precompile there, which reverts with 'method not supported' and consumes all gas given to it, so after about three such calls the script runs out of gas. Every other record, including all hook, ERC-6909, clear, settle, fallback and fee-growth paths, is byte-identical on all 21 networks. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/012/theme-bytecode-coverage.work/pmdiff6.json
- Monad, cycle 12. Monad staking precompile at 0x1000 consumes all gas on a failing call, met through sync(0x1000) and take(0x1000) in pmdiff6. Result: An eth_call of three sync(0x1000) calls returns nothing while one or two return the full record, and eth_estimateGas of one call is 22,596,024. Monad documents that calls with invalid arguments consume all gas and that STATICCALL reverts (https://docs.monad.xyz/reference/staking/api, https://docs.monad.xyz/reference/staking/overview). The PoolManager reaches 0x1000 only as a currency or recipient the caller names, so the gas loss falls on the caller of its own pool. Earlier cycles already cleared 0x1000 as a currency and hook on Monad. Evidence: https://docs.monad.xyz/reference/staking/api
- Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, cycle 12. System contracts at 0x1000 on Polygon and BNB Smart Chain revert transfer(address,uint256) called by the PoolManager. Result: take of that currency reverts with ERC20TransferFailed (pmdiff6 script 682). This only makes a caller-chosen currency unusable; no pool of real tokens uses it. Polygon's native face at 0x1010 is F-008 and F-077. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/012/theme-bytecode-coverage.work/pmdiff6.json
- all 21 networks, cycle 12. Credit-deciding jumps that went one way in the first five sets: clear of an exact positive delta (PoolManager.sol:314-318), the infinite and finite allowance paths of transferFrom and burn (ERC6909.sol:155-158, ERC6909Claims.sol:224-229), afterSwap, afterAddLiquidity and afterRemoveLiquidity without the return-delta flag (Hooks.sol:163, 220-243, 298-302), the hook-as-caller returns (Hooks.sol:172, 217, 253, 293), native settle and settleFor with value (PoolManager.sol:349-365), and the 512 bit branch of mulDiv by 2^128 in Position.update (Position.sol:263-268). Result: All now go both ways in the reference and the results match the source: clear of the exact delta zeroes it and unlock completes, a finite allowance drops by the amount moved and an infinite one does not, a hook without the return-delta flag gets a zero delta, a hook calling the PoolManager itself skips its own callbacks and deltas, and the 512 bit fee branch always ends in SafeCastOverflow at Pool.sol:192 because the fee is then at least 2^128. The answers are byte-identical on all 21 networks. Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:159-168
- all 21 networks, cycle 12. The overflow fallback of getNextSqrtPriceFromAmount0RoundingUp (SqrtPriceMath.sol:42-52), taken by no earlier script. Result: A swap step stops short of its target only while the input left is below what the target needs, and each position's deposit is capped below 2^127 by toInt128 (Pool.sol:212-235). For amount times price to pass 2^256, the step must start below price 2^96 and run toward the bottom of the range, which needs an input above 2^160. pmdiff6 reaches the fallback that way, including the window where numerator1 plus the product wraps, and the swap then always reverts with SafeCastOverflow at Pool.sol:455-459. So the fallback never sets a price that is paid out. The same bound makes the amount > 2^160 branch of getNextSqrtPriceFromAmount1RoundingDown (SqrtPriceMath.sol:102-106, pc 20776 and the never-reached 20942, 20963, 20971) need about 2^33 deposits. Evidence: src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:42-52
- all 21 networks, cycle 12. Dead or redundant branches left one-sided: SELFBALANCE in Currency.balanceOfSelf (pc 15021), second success tests after the unlockCallback CALL and the balanceOf STATICCALL (pc 9048, 15094), and bytes4(data) of a hook call shorter than 4 bytes (pc 16370). Result: balanceOfSelf is only called for a nonzero currency (PoolManager.sol:281-285 and 353-359), so its native branch cannot run. The two success tests repeat a test that already left on failure (pc 9042, 15088), and hook calldata always comes from abi.encodeCall. None of them can be steered by a network that executes the earlier test correctly, and that earlier test is covered both ways on all 21 networks. Evidence: src/types/Currency.sol:90-96
- all 21 networks, cycle 12. A full read of src/ for this cycle's question (PoolManager, ERC6909, ProtocolFees, Extsload, Exttload, NoDelegateCall, and the libraries TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, UnsafeMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap, Position, LiquidityMath, Pool, SafeCast, Hooks, CustomRevert, CurrencyDelta, CurrencyReserves, NonzeroDeltaCount, Lock, Slot0, BalanceDelta, LPFeeLibrary, ProtocolFeeLibrary). Result: No line computes a credit, payout or fee that disagrees with what its comment and the tests intend. The transient slot constants equal keccak256 of their names minus 1 (recomputed). Every one-sided jump left in the build maps to a guard that the bounds above make unreachable, so no credit decision in the bytecode stays untested on the 21 networks. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:349-378

## Reading of the source (theme-code-cache-consistency)

- Polygon, cycle 12. bor v2.11.1 BlockSTM V2: can one Call build a Contract whose CodeHash and Code come from two state versions, so that the bitmap of one bytecode is stored under the PoolManager's code hash in the per-block JUMPDEST cache that V2 workers and the prefetcher share (lead L-645). Result: No. The production parallel path is V2 (core/blockchain.go line 975 builds NewV2StateProcessor), and its workers read code through ParallelStateDB, not through the MVHashMap path of core/state/statedb.go. ParallelStateDB.GetCode and GetCodeHash both go through readCodeKey (core/state/parallel_statedb.go lines 359-381), which caches the first CodePath read of each address for the whole incarnation in codeReadCache, with a comment that names exactly this hazard: the two GetCode(addr) reads of resolveCode and resolveCodeHash (core/vm/evm.go lines 363-370, 721-748) must follow one delegation target. The destruction index is cached the same way (priorDestructedAt, lines 597-620). Both caches are cleared per incarnation in Reset (lines 302-304). For code written by an earlier transaction of the block, GetCodeHash returns cachedCodeHash(addr, val), which is keccak256 of the very bytes GetCode returned (lines 875-888, 897-905). For code from the parent state, both come from SafeBase, a pool of copies of one parent StateDB that is never written (core/state/safe_base.go lines 52-63, 181-209), and a StateDB loads code by its hash. Code set inside the transaction comes from localCode, and every change of localCode clears codeHashCache (SetCode line 949, revertCode and revertCreate in core/state/parallel_statedb_journal.go lines 93-124). So the cache key is always the hash of the bytes analysed, or the trie hash of those same bytes. A bitmap stored by an incarnation that later fails validation is left in syncMapJumpDests (core/vm/jumpdests.go lines 57-78 has no delete), but it is the correct bitmap for the bytes whose hash keys it, so leaving it is harmless. The prefetcher runs each transaction on its own Copy of the parent state (core/state_prefetcher.go lines 240-249), a single-threaded StateDB in which the two reads see the same account. The serial processor (bc.cfg.VmConfig, core/blockchain.go line 1487), the stateless witness path (ExecuteStateless with bc.cfg.VmConfig, line 6477) and the block producer (miner/worker.go lines 3588-3597, which copies the chain VmConfig without the shared cache) each use a per-EVM map, not the shared cache. The same codeReadCache code is in every release since BlockSTM V2 arrived: v2.10.1, v2.10.2, v2.10.3, v2.11.0, v2.11.1 and v2.11.2 all contain it, and core/state/parallel_statedb.go is byte-identical in v2.11.1 and v2.11.2. An ordinary account sending type 4 transactions in any order therefore cannot pair one bitmap with another code hash, and no block producer role changes that. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/state/parallel_statedb.go lines 170-181, 302-304, 359-381, 597-620, 843-949; also https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/state/parallel_statedb_journal.go lines 93-124, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/evm.go lines 363-370 and 721-748, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/contract.go lines 65-113, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/blockchain.go lines 975, 1268-1349, 1487, 6477, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/state_prefetcher.go lines 213-257, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/state/safe_base.go lines 52-209, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/miner/worker.go lines 3588-3597
- Polygon, cycle 12. What a wrong JUMPDEST bitmap could do to this PoolManager if one were ever paired with its code hash: list the 0x5b bytes inside push data of the 24,009 byte runtime and whether any jump could reach them. Result: validJumpdest first requires the byte at the destination to be 0x5b in the real code (bor core/vm/contract.go lines 65-78). The runtime has 610 valid JUMPDESTs and 29 bytes of value 0x5b inside push data, at offsets 50, 261, 470, 885, 1877, 6220, 9058, 9969, 9973, 10775, 11255, 12643, 12678, 12724, 12759, 16550, 17125, 17743, 18038, 19380, 20374, 21025, 23215, 23246, 23300, 23397, 23428, 23486 and 23512. No PUSH constant anywhere in the runtime equals any of these offsets, and the compiler's jump targets are pushed constants (internal returns jump to pushed return addresses), so no jump of the PoolManager can name one of those bytes. A wrong bitmap could only turn valid destinations invalid, which reverts the call on the node that holds it. It could not redirect control. Since the pairing cannot happen (previous item), neither outcome is reachable. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/012/theme-code-cache-consistency.work/pushdata_jumpdest.json (scripts/pushdata_jumpdest.py over research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json)
- Polygon, cycle 12. bor v2.12.0-beta (pre-release, not on mainnet) adds a one-entry memo of the reciprocal of a full-width MULMOD modulus (#2310). FullMath.mulDiv uses mulmod with modulus 2^256-1, which takes this path. Result: core/vm/mulmod_memo.go lines 55-66 compares the whole 256-bit modulus before reusing the reciprocal, recomputes uint256.Reciprocal on a miss, and is per-EVM state with no sharing. holiman/uint256 v1.3.2 MulMod (uint256.go lines 720-730) computes mu = Reciprocal(m) and calls reduce4(p, m, mu), and MulModWithReciprocal (lines 688-697) runs the same umul and reduce4 with the supplied mu, so the result equals stock MulMod for every input. Moduli with a zero top limb, which includes the 2^96 and 2^128 constants of the bytecode, bypass the memo. Nothing to fix; read it again if the final v2.12.0 differs. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.12.0-beta/core/vm/mulmod_memo.go lines 55-66; https://proxy.golang.org/github.com/holiman/uint256/@v/v1.3.2.zip uint256.go lines 688-730
- BNB Smart Chain, cycle 12. BNB Smart Chain v1.8.2: JUMPDEST caches shared across transactions or workers, and the pooled Contract objects (lead L-646). Result: BSC keeps the per-EVM map of upstream and adds a process-wide LRU of 2,048 bitmaps keyed by code hash (core/vm/contract.go lines 27-34 and 101-113), shared by block import, the prefetcher, the miner and every RPC call on the node. The LRU is mutex-protected (common/lru/lru.go lines 25-60). The key is the CodeHash set next to the code in Call, CallCode, DelegateCall and StaticCall (core/vm/evm.go lines 353-363, 420-423, 464-467, 517-520), and both come from one single-threaded StateDB; the prefetcher gives each transaction or worker its own statedb.Copy() (core/state_prefetcher.go lines 72 and 154). Every write of code computes the hash from the bytes: StateDB.SetCode (core/state/statedb.go lines 509-514), the journal revert (core/state/journal.go line 408), and the RPC state override, which calls SetCode (internal/ethapi/override/override.go line 108). SetStorage (statedb.go lines 545-548) copies the old object's hash with its lazily loaded code field, and stateObject.Code() loads the bytes by that hash when the field is empty (state_object.go lines 568-587). So a cached bitmap is always the analysis of the bytes whose keccak is its key, and even a poisoned RPC call cannot put a wrong bitmap into the process-wide cache. The Contract pool (core/vm/contract_pool.go lines 17-38) resets Code, CodeHash and analysis on every GetContract. v1.8.2 has no parallel block executor; block processing is serial. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bnb-chain/bsc/v1.8.2/core/vm/contract.go lines 27-34, 101-113; also https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bnb-chain/bsc/v1.8.2/core/vm/contract_pool.go lines 17-46, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bnb-chain/bsc/v1.8.2/core/vm/evm.go lines 353-363, 700-725, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bnb-chain/bsc/v1.8.2/core/state/statedb.go lines 509-548, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bnb-chain/bsc/v1.8.2/core/state/journal.go line 408, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bnb-chain/bsc/v1.8.2/internal/ethapi/override/override.go line 108
- BNB Smart Chain, cycle 12. reth-bsc v0.1.4 (bsc-rpc.publicnode.com answers reth-bsc/v0.1.4-hotfix-23b510f): where its JUMPDEST analysis lives. Result: reth-bsc v0.1.4 builds on the bnb-chain/reth fork tag v0.1.3 with revm 38.0.0 and revm-bytecode 10.0.0 (Cargo.toml lines 19-86). In revm-bytecode the jump table is a field of the Bytecode value itself, computed from the bytes by analyze_legacy in new_legacy (src/bytecode/mod.rs lines 43 and 128-139 in 10.0.0). The analysis travels with the bytes and is not looked up by a hash read separately. The hotfix suffix names a build whose source was not found, and the reth fork's own storage encoding of Bytecode was not read (the file path of crates/primitives-traits at that tag returned 404). Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bnb-chain/reth-bsc/v0.1.4/Cargo.toml lines 19-86; https://static.crates.io/crates/revm-bytecode/revm-bytecode-10.0.0.crate src/bytecode/mod.rs lines 43, 128-139
- Avalanche, cycle 12. avalanchego 1.15.3 with libevm d398bc4dbe41: sharing of JUMPDEST analysis, and EIP-7702 delegation. Result: libevm keeps the go-ethereum 1.13 design: each Contract inherits the jumpdests map of its parent frame and a new map is made for the outermost frame of each message (core/vm/contract.go lines 63-72, 99-125), so analysis is never shared across transactions or threads. Call reads code and code hash from one StateDB (core/vm/evm.go lines 243-251). The prefetcher runs each transaction on its own statedb.Copy() (core/state_prefetcher.go lines 64-100) and the processor is serial, so the code hash and the code of one Call come from one single-threaded StateDB (core/vm/evm.go lines 343-350 and 812-821), and the key is the hash of the bytes analysed. - Monad, cycle 12. Monad v0.16.5, and v0.16.7 which rpc.monad.xyz now reports: can the varcode cache (interpreter code and native code keyed by code hash) store or find analysis or machine code of one bytecode under the PoolManager's code hash, for a 7702-delegated account or for an account created and called in the same block under optimistic parallel execution (lead L-647). Result: No. Monad never pairs a code hash with code read separately. execute_call_message reads the hash with state.get_code_hash(msg.code_address) and then fetches the code by that hash, state.read_code(hash), and passes both to the VM (category/execution/ethereum/execute_message.cpp lines 326-330). For a delegated account the delegate address is read first (category/vm/evm/delegation.cpp lines 57-80) and the hash and code are then those of the delegate, the code again fetched by hash. read_code looks up the transaction's own code map, then BlockState, then the code trie, each keyed by hash (state3/state.cpp lines 523-532, state2/block_state.cpp lines 129-153). Every entry of those stores has a key computed from its bytes: State::set_code computes keccak256(code) (state3/state.cpp lines 576-587), BlockState::merge copies a transaction's code map entries under the same hashes (block_state.cpp lines 194-216), and the RPC state override goes through set_code (category/rpc/monad_executor.cpp line 171). VarcodeCache::try_set_raw returns an existing entry for a hash without comparing bytes (category/vm/varcode_cache.cpp lines 74-82), which is safe only because of that invariant, and the invariant holds on every insert path read. Under optimistic execution a transaction that read an account before an earlier transaction changed its code fails can_merge, which compares the recorded code_hash (state3/state.cpp lines 664-666), and runs again. Compiled code is keyed by the same hash and recompiled when the chain revision changes (category/vm/vm.cpp lines 142-160). state.cpp, varcode_cache.cpp, vm.cpp and delegation.cpp are byte-identical in v0.16.7, and the v0.16.7 changes to execute_message.cpp and block_state.cpp touch only the ripemd touch and include comments. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.5/category/execution/ethereum/execute_message.cpp lines 326-330; also https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.5/category/execution/ethereum/state3/state.cpp lines 523-587, 664-666, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.5/category/execution/ethereum/state2/block_state.cpp lines 129-216, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.5/category/vm/varcode_cache.cpp lines 41-82, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.5/category/vm/evm/delegation.cpp lines 57-80, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/ (same files)
- Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Zora, Worldchain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer, Tempo, Arc, MegaETH, HyperEVM, cycle 12. revm and evm2 based clients (reth v2.11.0 on Ethereum, op-reth on OP Mainnet, Unichain, Ink, Soneium, Base reth v2.5.2, conduit-op-reth on Zora, world-chain, Celo reth, X Layer reth, Tempo v1.19.0, Arc, mega-reth replicas on MegaETH, the HyperEVM public replay clients): does any cache pair a jump table with a code hash read separately from the code. Result: In revm-bytecode 10.0.0 and 11.0.1 (revm 38 and 40) the jump table is a field of the Arc-shared Bytecode, computed from the bytes by analyze_legacy (src/legacy/analysis.rs lines 10-62; src/bytecode/mod.rs lines 22-43 and 131-142 in 11.0.1). reth v2.11.0 (on evm2 via reth-core 275ce4cf) persists the jump table next to the bytes in one Compact record and rebuilds the Bytecode with new_analyzed from that record (crates/primitives-traits/src/account.rs lines 348-421 in reth-core), so the table belongs to the bytes it is stored with. A cache keyed by code hash in front of the database returns that record for that hash. Nothing in these designs reads a hash and code from two state versions. The code caches of the engine tree in each reth build were not read line by line, and the closed MegaETH sequencer and HyperEVM validator cannot be read (see leads). Evidence: https://static.crates.io/crates/revm-bytecode/revm-bytecode-11.0.1.crate src/legacy/analysis.rs lines 10-62; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paradigmxyz/reth-core/275ce4cf5befeb9f1e8acd935ff2882d2d25fc61/crates/primitives-traits/src/account.rs lines 348-421; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paradigmxyz/reth/v2.11.0/Cargo.toml lines 436-439, 682-684
- Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Zora, Worldchain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Monad, MegaETH, Tempo, Arc, HyperEVM, cycle 12. Read-only test of the delegated call path on every network: eth_call owner() and extsload(0) on an EOA whose code is overridden with 0xef0100 followed by the PoolManager address and whose slot 0 is overridden with a marker. Result: On 20 networks both calls return the marker word, so the node resolved the delegation, ran the PoolManager's 24,009 bytes under the delegate's code hash with every jump of the owner() and extsload paths accepted, and read the EOA's storage. Avalanche rejects the designator (EIP-7702 not active). The test cannot reach a cross-transaction race inside a block, which only block import can exercise; that question is settled by the source readings above. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/012/theme-code-cache-consistency.work/delegated_call.json (scripts/delegated_call.py, eth_call with state override on each RPC in state/networks.json, 2026-11-24)
- Monad, cycle 12. PoolManager bytecode under EIP-8024 style immediates: revm-bytecode 11.0.1 pads for DUPN, SWAPN and EXCHANGE (0xe6 to 0xe8) whose immediates the jump scan does not skip. Result: A linear disassembly of the runtime finds no 0xe6, 0xe7 or 0xe8 in opcode position, and the only 0xfe is the terminator before the CBOR metadata, so that rule cannot change any jump destination of this contract on a network that activates it. Evidence: https://static.crates.io/crates/revm-bytecode/revm-bytecode-11.0.1.crate src/legacy/analysis.rs lines 38-67; research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json

From them 1,354 transactions were traced: all 17 with an ERC-6909 Transfer to the zero address (burn), all 182 with an event on one of the 89 pools whose key names a hook (keys from 81 Initialize logs in the range and from the PositionManager), 400 of the 671 with a mint and 800 others at random. netcheck2.py keeps hooked pools and credits the hook's delta to the hook address as the source does (src/PoolManager.sol:178-183, 221-226): for swap the Swap event delta minus the caller delta the frame returned (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:285-315), for modifyLiquidity the BalanceDelta the after-liquidity hook frame returned when the hook address carries the return-delta flag (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:159-168, 215-244). settlecheck2.py is settlecheck.py on the same list. Result: All 1,905 completed unlocks that could be summed net to zero per account and currency, among them 244 operations on hooked pools, 205 of which moved a nonzero delta to the hook, 17 burns and 467 mints; one unlock with an unknown selector was skipped (raw/netcheck2.json). Dropping the hook deltas makes 74 of the 159 hooked unlocks fail, so the check sees them (raw/netcheck2-planted.json). settlecheck2.py finds no mismatch over 3,358 token settles, 328 native settles, 3,761 takes, 18 burns and 469 mints in blocks 124692446 to 124990852 (raw/settlecheck2.json). The traced set holds no settleFor and no clear. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/012/theme-mined-liquidity-2.work/netcheck2.py, research/network-risk/cycles/012/theme-mined-liquidity-2.work/settlecheck2.py, research/network-risk/cycles/012/theme-mined-liquidity-2.work/monad_scan.py
- all 21 networks, cycle 12. Whether hooks with return-delta permissions change what the PoolManager pays out in total, which decides whether such pools can be checked from events. src/PoolManager.sol:178-183 credits hookDelta to the hook and callerDelta minus hookDelta to the caller after modifyLiquidity (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:209-244), and src/PoolManager.sol:221-226 does the same after swap (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:285-315). unlock reverts unless every account's delta is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). Result: The two credits add up to the pool delta of the event, and both accounts must reach zero through take, settle, mint, burn or clear before unlock returns, so the PoolManager's net token flow in a completed unlock equals the sum of the pool deltas of the events, adjusted by ERC-6909 mints and burns and by clear. A hook cannot change that total; it can only move it between its own account and the caller's. analyze3.py therefore checks pools with return-delta hooks (243 transactions on Arc, 41 on Monad, 30 on Elysium, 25 on Robinhood Chain). Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:178-183
- all 21 networks, cycle 12. Whether clear leaves value that someone else can claim. clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-319) lowers the caller's own positive delta to zero only when the amount equals it exactly, and moves no token. The cleared tokens stay in the PoolManager's balance. Result: A later sync records the whole balance as reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288), so the cleared amount is never credited to a later settler, and no function pays it out. It is lost to the caller who chose to clear it and is taken from nobody else. The 9 Polygon transactions above cleared 797 to 9,999,999,974,048 units this way. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:310-319

Wasm.rules lines 102-138 lower a shift by a variable amount to Select(shift, 0, amount < 64) unless the prove pass shows the amount below 64, which is Go's own semantics; the uint256 shifts by 64 - shift (uint256.go:520-580, 1042-1149) are therefore 0 for shift 0 as on x86. ## Reading of the source (own-check)

- Monad, cycle 12. Monad v0.16.7 says reverted state depends on whether code ran compiled or interpreted. Can a reverted inner frame leave a CurrencyDelta credit or a synced currency behind (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:21-39, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32) while the payment is rolled back?. Result: Read at v0.16.5 and v0.16.7; the four journal files are byte-identical in the two releases. Every account's balance, nonce, storage, transient storage, touched flag, warm flag and warm slot set live in one AccountState object held in a VersionStack per address (state3/state.hpp line 62, account_state.hpp lines 49-70, account_substate.hpp lines 31-40). The first write in a frame copies the object under the frame's version (version_stack.hpp current(), state.cpp lines 73-86), and a failed frame pops that copy for every address the frame touched (state.cpp pop_reject lines 155-181, version_stack.hpp pop_reject). Logs use the same stack, and post_call asserts a zero refund for every failed frame (execute_message.cpp). So nothing a frame wrote survives its revert on either path: a CurrencyDelta or reserves word set by TSTORE inside a reverted frame is gone together with the token transfer. The developers' comment describes what happens inside a frame that is about to fail: compiled code checks gas once per basic block, so it stops before the block, while the interpreter stops part way through it. The partial work is discarded in both cases. v0.16.5 had one exception, a touch of the ripemd address kept after a revert; v0.16.7 removed it. That flag only decides whether an empty account at address 3 is deleted and no PoolManager path reads it. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.7/category/execution/ethereum/execute_message.cpp lines 143-162 ; state3/state.cpp lines 73-86 and 126-181 ; state3/version_stack.hpp ; state3/account_state.hpp ; state3/account_substate.hpp (same text at v0.16.5)
- Monad, cycle 14. On Monad every served receipt, log and trace comes from RPC nodes that interpret (F-130). Do those nodes check their execution against what the validators agreed on, so that mined results stand for validators that may run compiled code? (lead L-737). Result: Own reading of monad-bft at tag v0.16.7 (commit 670b8ce5). A proposal for block N carries delayed_execution_results, the full Ethereum header of block N-D (monad-consensus-types/src/block.rs line 92; EthHeader wraps the alloy Header, monad-eth-types, so it holds state root, receipts root, logs bloom and gas used). EthBlockPolicy::check_coherency reads the header the node's own execution wrote to its triedb (monad-eth-block-policy/src/lib.rs lines 1182-1196 and 1271-1290; monad-triedb-utils/src/lib.rs lines 124-154 and 314-342) and returns ExecutionResultMismatch when the two differ. The block tree then leaves the block incoherent and counts rx_bad_state_root (monad-blocktree/src/blocktree.rs lines 280-308). A block that is not coherent is never committed: get_high_committable_qc skips it (blocktree.rs line 369), try_commit returns early (monad-consensus-state/src/lib.rs lines 1459-1467) and prune asserts coherency (blocktree.rs lines 153 and 169). Only newly coherent blocks are handed to execution (lib.rs lines 1542-1558). A node that is not in the validator set runs the same consensus state; only its votes, timeouts and proposals are filtered out (monad-state/src/consensus.rs lines 591-637). So a full node, tracing or not, whose execution of block N-D gave a different state root, receipts root, logs bloom or gas used than the header the validator quorum certified stops committing at block N. rpc.monad.xyz follows the finalized tip, so its interpreter results equal the quorum's for every block it serves, receipts and logs included. If validators run compiled code, its state root, receipts root, logs bloom and gas used have therefore agreed with the interpreter on every mined block, including the 129,567 swaps through the 512 bit branch of FullMath.mulDiv found in cycle 14. What stays without evidence is input that no mined transaction has used. Evidence: https://github.com/category-labs/monad-bft/tree/v0.16.7
- Tempo, cycle 14. Does the Tempo v1.19.1 release binary contain the evm2 LLVM compiler, now that reth v2.11 ships it by default? (lead L-743). Result: Own reading at tempo/v1.19.1. Tempo depends on reth-evm-ethereum with default features, and at reth 167933d that crate's default is ["std"]; jit is a default feature of the reth binary crate only (bin/reth/Cargo.toml). Tempo's own hook-up of the compiler is behind its jit feature (crates/evm/src/lib.rs lines 19-20, 183-184, 239-265; crates/node/src/node.rs lines 72-79 and 590), which the release workflow and the Dockerfile do not pass (features asm-keccak, jemalloc, otlp). TempoEvmConfig builds evm2::Evm without configure_jit in such a build, so no JitBackend exists in the release binary. Evidence: https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/tree/tempo/v1.19.1
- Polygon, cycle 16. L-799: in bor v2.12.0-beta, can the widened keccak result cache return the hash of a different input (key aliasing EVM memory, a fingerprint key, or an entry from an aborted speculative execution), which would give a wrong storage slot for a pool id (160 bytes) or a position key (58 bytes)?. Result: Read on 2026-11-25 in 0xPolygon/bor at tag v2.12.0-beta (core/vm/instructions.go 258-330, interpreter.go 50-71, shared_cache.go, bounded_cache.go, keccak_cache.go). The widened cache keccakResultCache is a sync.Map from string(data) to common.Hash. Store copies the input (string(data)), so a stored key never points into EVM memory, and it takes the hash by value. Load builds a string view of memory without a copy, which sync.Map.Load compares and does not keep, and the calling goroutine owns that memory for the length of the call. The key is the full input, with no fingerprint, so inputs of different lengths or contents cannot share an entry. An entry written by a speculative execution that BlockSTM later discards is still keccak of its own key, since the hash is computed from the same bytes immediately before Store. On a miss the handler falls through to the ordinary path with the freshly computed hash. The cache exists only when a node sets the precompile cache flag (default false) and is dropped at the end of each block. The legacy path for 64 byte inputs, which v2.11.1 already has, copies the key into a [64]byte array. A standalone copy of the Load and Store logic (cycles/016/own-check.work/keccak_cache/main.go, sha256 standing in for keccak) was run with 16 goroutines on inputs of 58 and 160 bytes that differ in one byte, in buffers overwritten after every call: 12,800,000 lookups, 4,809,737 hits, 0 wrong, every stored key still maps to the hash of its own bytes, and a shorter run under the Go race detector reports no race. v2.12.0-beta is the only tag with this code; v2.12.0 does not exist yet and Polygon's endpoint reports v2.11.1. Whether Polygon's validators will set the flag is not known and does not matter for correctness as read. L-664 and L-668 keep the rerun of the opcode checks against a v2.12 node. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.12.0-beta/core/vm/shared_cache.go ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.12.0-beta/core/vm/instructions.go ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/instructions.go ; research/network-risk/cycles/016/own-check.work/keccak_cache/main.go
- HyperEVM, cycle 17. L-837: do the seven v3 style swaps of HyperEVM's closed validator that cycle 17 could not reproduce differ from the formulas of src/libraries/FullMath.sol and SqrtPriceMath.sol?. Result: No. The same 7,000 groups (filter m512?, seed 3, limit 20,000, first 7,000 of the sorted sample) were rerun with every mismatch saved. The counts equal the cycle 17 log: 7,282 swaps reproduced, 3,008 with a call on the 512 bit branch of mulDiv, 7 mismatches. Six are in pool 0x0d3e8f6949dcaca02cbd1aaf7ca840f4f36216b7 and one in 0x12e5f773134a6df0fcc74aedddcca0429a08eaa6. Each of the seven blocks holds a 0xd78218c0 Mint variant for the pool before the swap, which the collector does not read, and no other unread topic. With the variant applied, all seven reproduce price, tick, liquidity and both amounts to the unit. About 57,000 groups of the sample are still not run (L-826). Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/017/own-check.work/NOTES.md, v3check_own.py, v3recheck.py, results/mismatches.jsonl, results/recheck.json (https://rpc.purroofgroup.com, 2026-11-25)

- Arc, cycle 13. Arc arc-node v0.8.6, the complete set of instruction, gas and call hooks it adds to revm 38.0.0 (lead L-681). The endpoint answers web3_clientVersion with arc/v1, which names no release. Result: Instruction table: only SELFDESTRUCT is replaced (evm.rs lines 114-134, three variants by hardfork); the PoolManager bytecode has no SELFDESTRUCT. Frame hook: every CALL or CREATE with nonzero value passes check_blocklist_and_create_log (evm.rs lines 516-605), recorded as the finding of this unit; the PoolManager reaches it only at the native payout of src/types/Currency.sol:48, and the success flag differs from Ethereum only for a recipient that is address(0), blocklisted or destroyed earlier in the same transaction. A rejected frame returns all of its gas, so the PoolManager has more gas left than after a stock failure. Subcall registry: calls to 0x1800..03 are diverted to CallFrom with an allow list (evm.rs lines 669-711 and 1805-1820), and a caller outside the list gets a 100 gas revert (lines 137-151). Precompile set: the stock Osaka set plus four stateful precompiles at 0x1800..00 (NativeCoinAuthority), 0x1800..01 (NativeCoinControl), 0x1800..02 (SystemAccounting) and 0x1800..04 (PQ) (precompile_provider.rs lines 46-71, pq-precompile lib.rs line 26). Their state-changing selectors run check_staticcall first, which spends all gas (helpers.rs 540-555), but the only staticcall the PoolManager makes is balanceOf(address) at src/types/Currency.sol:94, which none of them implements, so it takes the 200 gas invalid-selector revert. Measured from the PoolManager address: 0x1800..00 to ..04 revert with 100 bytes for 323 to 2,829 gas on all five call shapes; 0x1800..05 to ..09 hold the one byte code 0xef and consume all forwarded gas, which is ordinary EVM semantics for an undefined opcode. KECCAK256, MCOPY, RETURNDATACOPY, TLOAD, TSTORE, SSTORE, LOG and the arithmetic are the stock revm handlers, as cycle 12 and the stablecoin-l1 unit of this cycle found for v0.8.0 to v0.8.6. - MegaETH, cycle 13. MegaETH mega-evm (main branch; state/cleared.json records Rex6 active on mainnet since 25 August 2026): the handlers it replaces and whether any changes a value, a success flag, return data or gas left for the PoolManager's operands. Result: From MINI_REX on, all 256 table entries are rebuilt (instructions.rs lines 859-916 and following). Arithmetic, comparison, shift, KECCAK256, CALLDATA*, RETURNDATA*, MCOPY, TLOAD and TSTORE are the revm handler inside compute_gas_ext, which only records compute gas. SSTORE and LOG gain storage gas and data-size limits (storage_gas_ext, additional_limit_ext). CALL, STATICCALL, DELEGATECALL and CALLCODE go through forward_gas_ext, which caps the gas given to the callee at 98/100 of what remains instead of 63/64 (lines 1064-1180), and from Rex4 through volatile_data_ext, which reverts a call to the block beneficiary only when the calling frame has disabled volatile access and caps later compute gas after an oracle or beneficiary access (lines 40-140, 405-445). SELFBALANCE gains the same beneficiary guard. Measured with a callee that returns GAS: a hook or token called from the PoolManager address gets 97.87 percent of the parent's gas on MegaETH against 98.31 percent on 19 other networks (raw/fwdgas.json). The PoolManager keeps more gas after each callee returns, so its own revert wrapping cannot run short; a callee gets about 0.44 percent less, which changes gas only. The PoolManager never touches the beneficiary and never disables volatile access, so the guard cannot fire on its own calls, and an attacker cannot set that flag in a victim's frame (F-018 records the hook author case). Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/evm/instructions.rs lines 40-140, 284-480, 859-916, 1064-1180, 1283-1340; research/network-risk/cycles/013/theme-callee-gas-and-overrides.work/raw/fwdgas.json (fwdgas.py)

Result: From the PoolManager address the precompiles 0x05 to 0x11 consume all forwarded gas for malformed input on Ethereum as well; that is how the EVM treats a failing precompile. A take to such an address, or a pool whose hook is such an address, therefore fails the same way on Ethereum, and the special addresses found on other networks add nothing an attacker could not already do on Ethereum in its own transaction. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/013/theme-callee-gas-and-overrides.work/raw/cg_<chainId>.json and research/network-risk/cycles/013/theme-callee-gas-and-overrides.work/raw/calleegas.json (calleegas.py, eth_call with a driver placed by state override at the PoolManager address, 1,000,000 gas forwarded)
- all 21 networks, cycle 13. Callee gas: can an ordinary account make a precompile, predeploy or system contract that burns forwarded gas the recipient of a take or native payout, the hook or a currency inside a transaction that a victim sends through a normal router on an honest pool (lead L-684). Result: No on all 21 networks, on the text of the code. The PoolManager makes outbound calls at four places only: the native payout and the token transfer of src/types/Currency.sol:48 and :73, whose target is the currency of the take and whose recipient is the `to` argument chosen by the caller of take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297); the balanceOf staticcall of sync at src/types/Currency.sol:94, whose currency the caller chooses (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288); the hook call of src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134, whose target is key.hooks, part of the PoolKey that the pool id hashes (src/PoolManager.sol:132, 151); and the unlock callback to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:110). In a victim's swap or removal on an honest pool, the currencies and the hook are fixed by the pool and the recipient and the callback target are fixed by the victim's router and calldata. No storage that a third party can write steers any of these targets. A gas-burning address can therefore appear only in a transaction the attacker builds, where it costs the attacker gas and reverts the attacker's own unlock. Where a hook address is a special address, the low 14 bits decide which callbacks run: HyperEVM 0x0800 to 0x0813 all set BEFORE_ADD_LIQUIDITY (Hooks.sol:32), so no deposit can enter such a pool; Monad 0x1000 sets AFTER_INITIALIZE (Hooks.sol:30), so the pool cannot be created; Arc 0x1800..00 has no flag bits and is never called. Gas forwarding is 63/64 everywhere except MegaETH (98/100), so after a callee burns its gas the PoolManager keeps at least 1/64 to revert. A victim's swap or removal therefore cannot be made to fail or to cost far more on any of the 21 networks through callee gas. Evidence: src/types/Currency.sol:48, src/types/Currency.sol:73, src/types/Currency.sol:94, src/PoolManager.sol:110, src/PoolManager.sol:132, src/PoolManager.sol:151, src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:30-47, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-124, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134; research/network-risk/cycles/013/theme-callee-gas-and-overrides.work/raw/cg_<chainId>.json and research/network-risk/cycles/013/theme-callee-gas-and-overrides.work/raw/calleegas.json (calleegas.py, eth_call with a driver placed by state override at the PoolManager address, 1,000,000 gas forwarded)
- all 21 networks, cycle 13. Whether any client override found in this unit changes what the PoolManager computes, as opposed to gas. Result: No. The handlers replaced on Arc (SELFDESTRUCT, value-call frame hook, CallFrom intercept), MegaETH (gas wrappers, 98/100 forwarding, volatile guards), Tempo (0x4f, SSTORE, 0xef) and Nitro (GASPRICE, BLOCKHASH, NUMBER, SELFDESTRUCT, filter touches) leave every arithmetic, hashing, memory, return data and transient storage result unchanged. The PoolManager's five GAS reads only feed call gas, so a different amount of gas left cannot steer its logic. The one value-visible change is Arc's success flag for value calls to three recipient classes, recorded as the finding. Evidence: research/network-risk/OPCODES.md lines 146, 118; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/circlefin/arc-node/v0.8.6/crates/evm/src/evm.rs; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/evm/instructions.rs; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/instructions.go

## Reading of the source (theme-proof-builds-2)

- Optimism, Unichain, Ink, cycle 13. Lead L-682: which routines ruint 1.20.0 uses on the kona mips64 target for 64 by 64 to 128 bit products and 128 by 64 divisions, and whether the opcode vectors pass through them. Result: ruint 1.20.0 divides with MG10 reciprocals (reciprocal_mg10 by table and 64 bit products, div_2x1_mg10, div_3x2_mg10, Knuth div_nxm), so no u128 division and no compiler-builtins call (__udivti3, __umodti3, __multi3) occurs: the linked object of the handlers references none, products are DMULTU and DMULT with MFHI and MFLO, and the only divisions are three DDIVU for one-limb operands. The big-endian path of pu128::get (lib.rs:107-118) joins limbs in the right order. Compiled with rustc 1.97.0 for kona's target spec and run in a Cannon-semantics emulator, all 85,544 targeted and 96,876 battery vectors and the pool math checks match; planted faults (MOVN on bit 0, 5 bit DSLLV mask, a DMULTU high word error) give 624, 895 and 1,797 mismatches on 4,278 sampled targeted vectors. - all 21 networks, cycle 13. For each of the 21 networks: could an opcode the PoolManager runs give another result in the build that settles state than on the node, and could an ordinary account use it. Result: No on all 21 as far as tested. Ethereum, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Monad, MegaETH, Tempo, Arc and HyperEVM settle on the client that produces blocks (no separate proof build; covered by OPCODES.md checks 1 to 4). OP Mainnet, Unichain, Ink: kona-client 1.9.0 on MIPS64, permissionless games, no divergence in the compiled handlers or the prestate scan (this unit). World Chain: op-program 1.9.0 on MIPS64, permissioned, no divergence (cycle 12). Zora and Soneium: no proof program, operator only (cycle 12). Base: SP1 range program on RV64IM, permissionless challenges, no divergence (this unit). - all 21 networks, cycle 13. Event semantics for pools with hooks that return deltas: the Swap event carries the pool delta of Pool.swap, computed from amountToSwap after the beforeSwap delta, before afterSwap adjusts the caller delta. Result: src/PoolManager.sol:202-250 emits delta.amount0(), delta.amount1() of pool.swap(params) with amountSpecified = amountToSwap, so a hook delta changes the specified amount the loop starts from and never the arithmetic the event reports. The replay therefore needs no special case for return-delta hooks: it derives the specified amount from the event, and all swaps on return-delta hook pools in the windows match. Hook and token behaviour was not swept (owner instruction). Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:230-250

The fault is caught only for even denominators. With an odd denominator, twos is 1 and add(div(sub(0, twos), twos), 1) is 0 (src/libraries/FullMath.sol:59-75), so prod1 drops out and the result is prod0 times the inverse modulo 2^256, which is exact whenever the quotient fits. oddden.py confirms this on 400,000 inputs: 0 wrong results for 200,129 odd denominators and 199,871 of 199,871 wrong for even ones. A fault in the high word for an odd denominator therefore cannot change a PoolManager amount unless it moves prod1 between zero and nonzero or across the require at src/libraries/FullMath.sol:30. - Monad, MegaETH, HyperEVM, cycle 14. The Q128 copy of mulDiv at pc 22358 (src/libraries/FullMath.sol:33 inside Position.update, src/libraries/Position.sol:93-96) and what its 512 bit branch can decide. Result: The constant denominator at pcs 22330-22377 is 2^128, so this copy computes feesOwed. prod1 is nonzero only when the fee growth delta times liquidity is at least 2^256, which makes feesOwed at least 2^128. Pool.modifyLiquidity casts feesOwed with toInt128 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:192), which reverts for any value of 2^127 or more (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-57). On a node that follows the specification, this branch therefore always ends in a revert and its quotient never reaches state. Reaching it needs at least 2^128 units of fees credited to one position, which only a token whose author mints that much can supply (pool-creator). No mined instance exists on the three networks, and none is expected. Evidence: src/libraries/Position.sol:93-96; src/libraries/Pool.sol:188-192; src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-57; research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json runtime pcs 22275-22382

Memory differs in that 0e44603 reuses pooled capacity; Free clears the used bytes first and growth past capacity zero-fills, so unused bytes are always zero in both.
